[p. 366]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah An-Nur

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The fornicating woman and the fornicating man, flog each one of them with a hundred lashes﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that every fornicating woman and every fornicating man must be flogged, each of them, with a hundred lashes. This is because the *alif* and *lam* in His statement ﴿the fornicating woman and the fornicating man﴾, if we say that they are a relative pronoun (*ism mawsul*) whose relative clause (*silah*) is the descriptive phrase, which is the active participle ﴿al-zaniyah wa al-zani﴾, then relative pronouns are among the forms of generality.

And if we say that they are for definition, by abstraction from the descriptive sense, and that the perpetrator of that immorality is called "the fornicator" just as names of genera are applied, then this gives comprehensiveness (*istighraq*). So the generality that includes every fornicating woman and every fornicating man is the apparent meaning of the verse, according to all possibilities.

The apparent meaning of this generality is that it includes the slave and the free, the female slave and the free woman, the virgin and the married (*muhsan*), among men and women.

Its apparent meaning also is that the fornicating woman and the fornicating man are not exiled for a year together with the flogging. But some Qur'anic verses indicate that the generality of "the fornicating woman" is specified in two ways.

The first: the specification of the ruling of her flogging with a hundred lashes by her being free. As for if she is a female slave, then she is flogged half of the hundred, which is fifty. This is in His statement, exalted is He, concerning the slave women: ﴿So if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment of free [married] women﴾ [An-Nisa: 25]. The meaning of "free [married] women" here is free women, and the punishment is flogging. Concerning the free fornicating woman it is a hundred lashes, and the female slave's punishment is half of it by the explicit text of this verse of *An-Nisa*, which is fifty. So the verse ﴿then for them is half the punishment of free [married] women﴾ specifies the generality of His statement ﴿the fornicating woman and the fornicating man﴾ with respect to the female fornicator.

As for the second specification of the generality of "the fornicating woman" in this verse of *An-Nur*, it is by a verse whose recitation has been abrogated (*mansukh al-tilawah*) while its ruling remains (*baqi al-hukm*), which requires that the generality of "the fornicating woman" here is specified by her being a virgin.

[p. 367]

As for if she is married (*muhsanah*), meaning that she had been married before the fornication and her husband had had intercourse with her in a valid marriage, then she is stoned.

The verse by which I specified it with this ruling that I mentioned, which is abrogated in recitation while its ruling remains, is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit fornication, then stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾.

This specification is only according to the view of those who say that the married fornicator is not combined with flogging and stoning, but is stoned only, without flogging.

As for the view of those who hold that the two are combined, then there is no specification, but rather the stoning verse adds to the flogging, so each of the two verses established a ruling that the other did not establish. This will be clarified, Allah willing, not long hence, along with the statements of the people of knowledge on it and the discussion of their evidences.

As for the male fornicator, the verse we mentioned has indicated, being abrogated in recitation while its ruling remains, that the generality of his ruling is specified: the one who is flogged one hundred is the virgin male fornicator, and as for the married one, he is stoned. This specification regarding the male is also only according to the view of those who do not hold the combination of flogging and stoning, as we clarified shortly with regard to the female.

As for the view of those who hold the combination of the two, there is no specification, but rather each of the two verses established a ruling that the other did not establish.

The generality of the male fornicator in this verse of *An-Nur* is also specified, according to the majority (*al-jumhur*), a second time: the flogging of one hundred is specific to the free male fornicator. As for the male fornicator who is a slave, he is flogged half of the hundred, which is fifty.

The basis of this specification: the attachment of the slave to the female slave in halving the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) for fornication because of slavery. The criterion of halving is undoubtedly slavery, because maleness and femaleness, with respect to the prescribed punishments, are incidental attributes (*wasfan tardiyyan*) upon which no ruling is based. So His statement, exalted is He, in the verse of *An-Nisa* concerning the slave women: ﴿then for them is half the punishment of free [married] women﴾ [An-Nisa: 25], indicates that slavery is the criterion for halving the punishment for fornication, since there is no difference between male and female in prescribed punishments. So what specifies the generality of "the male fornicator" in reality is what the verse ﴿then for them is half the punishment of free [married] women﴾ conveys. And although the jurists of legal theory (*al-usuliyyun*) call it specification by analogy (*qiyas*), in reality it is the specification of one verse by what is understood from another verse.

* *

[p. 368]

Issues related to this noble verse.

The first issue: know that the stoning of the two married fornicators is established by two verses from the Book of Allah. One of them has had its recitation abrogated while its ruling remains, and the second remains in both recitation and ruling. As for the one whose recitation was abrogated while its ruling remains, it is His statement: ﴿The elderly man and the elderly woman﴾ to its end, as will come. The fact that stoning is established by the Qur'an is established in the authentic (*sahih*) reports.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his *Sahih*, in the chapter on stoning a pregnant woman who committed fornication when she is married (*ahsanat*):

"Abd al-Aziz ibn Abd Allah narrated to us: Ibrahim ibn Sa'd related to me, from Salih, from Ibn Shihab, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah ibn Mas'ud, that Ibn Abbas said: I used to teach some men from the Emigrants (*muhajirin*), among them Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. While I was in his house at Mina, and he was with Umar ibn al-Khattab during the last pilgrimage he performed, he returned to Abd al-Rahman and said: If you had seen a man who came to the Commander of the Faithful today and said: O Commander of the Faithful, what do you think about so-and-so who says: 'If Umar dies, I will pledge allegiance to so-and-so. By Allah, the pledge to Abu Bakr was only a hasty matter that was completed.' Umar became angry and then said: Indeed, if Allah wills, I will stand this evening among the people and warn them against those who wish to seize their affairs from them. The hadith in full."

And in it: "Indeed Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) with the truth and revealed the Book to him. Among what Allah revealed was the verse of stoning. We recited it, understood it, and memorized it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned, and we stoned after him. I fear that if a long time passes over the people, someone will say: 'By Allah, we do not find the verse of stoning in the Book of Allah,' and they will go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah revealed. And stoning in the Book of Allah is a truth upon whoever commits fornication when he is married (*ahsana*), men and women, when evidence is established, or there is pregnancy, or confession." End of the point of relevance from the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari.

And in it: that stoning was revealed in the Qur'an in a verse from the Book of Allah, and its not being read in the written pages (*suhuf*) indicates the abrogation of its recitation while its ruling remains, as is established in the mentioned hadith.

In another narration in al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed I feared that a long time would pass over the people until someone says: 'We do not find stoning in the Book of Allah,' and they go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah revealed. Verily, stoning is a truth upon whoever commits fornication when he is married, when evidence is established, or there is pregnancy, or confession."

Sufyan said: "Thus I memorized it: Verily the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned, and we stoned after him."

[p. 369]

Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari*, in his commentary on this last narration: al-Isma'ili transmitted it from the narration of Ja'far al-Firyabi, from Ali ibn Abd Allah, the teacher of al-Bukhari in it, and he said after his statement "or confession": "And we recited it: ﴿The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit fornication, then stone them absolutely﴾, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned, and we stoned after him." So the part from his statement "And we recited it" to his statement "absolutely" fell out of al-Bukhari's narration. Perhaps al-Bukhari himself deliberately omitted it. For al-Nasa'i transmitted it from Muhammad ibn Mansur, from Sufyan, like the narration of Ja'far, then he said: "I do not know anyone who mentioned in this hadith: 'The elderly man and the elderly woman...' other than Sufyan, and it should be that he erred in that."

I say: The imams have transmitted this hadith from the narrations of Malik, Yunus, Ma'mar, Salih ibn Kaysan, Aqil, and others of the memorizers, from al-Zuhri.

This addition has also occurred in this hadith in the narration of the *Muwatta'*, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "When Umar returned from the pilgrimage and came to Medina, he addressed the people and said: O people, the sunnahs have been established for you, and the obligations have been prescribed for you, and you have been left upon the clear path. Then he said: Beware lest you perish through the verse of stoning, lest someone say: 'We do not find two prescribed punishments in the Book of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned, and we stoned. By Him in whose hand my soul is, were it not that people would say 'Umar added to the Book of Allah,' I would have written it with my own hand: ﴿The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit fornication, then stone them absolutely﴾." Malik said: "al-shaykh and al-shaykhah: the *thayyib* (previously married man) and the *thayyibah* (previously married woman)."

It occurred in *al-Hilyah*, in the biography of Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Umar: "I would have written it at the end of the Qur'an."

This addition also occurred in this hadith in the narration of Abu Ma'shar, which will be pointed out in the chapter that follows it. He said continuously after his statement: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned, and we stoned after him. And were it not that they would say: 'Umar wrote what is not in the Book of Allah,' I would have written it. We recited: ﴿The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit fornication, then stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾."

This sentence was also transmitted by al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim authenticated it, from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "Indeed it was in it, i.e., in Surat al-Ahzab, the verse of stoning: ﴿The elderly man﴾," and he mentioned the like of it.

[p. 370]

And from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The elderly man and the elderly woman'," the like of it, up to his statement "absolutely."

And from the narration of Usama ibn Sahl, that his maternal aunt informed him, she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indeed taught us the verse of stoning," and he mentioned it up to his statement "absolutely," and she added "for what the two of them enjoyed of pleasure."

Al-Nasa'i also transmitted that Marwan ibn al-Hakam said to Zayd: "Will you not write it in the codex (*mushaf*)?" He said: "No. Do you not see that the two married young men are stoned? And we have mentioned that." Umar said: "I will suffice you." He said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), write for me the verse of stoning." He said: "I cannot."

And we have related in *Fada'il al-Qur'an* by Ibn al-Durays, through the chain of Ya'la, who is Ibn Hakim, from Zayd ibn Aslam, that Umar addressed the people and said: "Do not doubt in stoning, for it is a truth. I had intended to write it in the codex, so I asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and he said: 'Did you not come to me while I was teaching it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and you pushed me in my chest and said: Teach him the verse of stoning, while they were copulating like donkeys?'" Its narrators are trustworthy. In it is an allusion to explaining the reason for lifting its recitation, which is disagreement.

Al-Hakim transmitted through the chain of Kathir ibn al-Salt, who said: "Zayd ibn Thabit and Sa'id ibn al-As were writing in the codex, and they came upon this verse. Zayd said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The elderly man and the elderly woman, stone them absolutely." Umar said: When it was revealed, I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Shall I write it? It seemed that he disliked that. Umar said: Do you not see that the elderly man, if he commits fornication and is not married, is flogged, and the young man, if he commits fornication and is married, is stoned?"

From this hadith is derived the reason for the abrogation of its recitation, since the practice was contrary to its apparent generality. End of the lengthy quotation from *Fath al-Bari*.

In it is the clear evidence for what we mentioned: that the verse of stoning has had its recitation abrogated while its ruling remains, and that it specifies the verse of flogging, according to the view that flogging and stoning are not combined, as has preceded.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 2 (part 2 of 7):

But what Ibn Hajar pointed to, namely deriving the cause of the abrogation of the recitation (naskh al-tilawa, the cancellation of a verse's recitation while its ruling may remain) from some of the mentioned hadiths, is not evident. This is because the Prophet ﷺ specified the generality (takhsis al-'umum, restricting a general wording to some of its referents) of many verses and clarified the intended meaning of them, even where it differed from the apparent meaning that comes to mind first. None of that led to the abrogation of their recitation, as is well known. A Qur'anic verse, at the time of its revelation, carries several rulings, such as: worship through its recitation; acting upon the legal rulings it contains; reciting it in prayer; and similar rulings. When Allah wills to abrogate it in His wisdom, He sometimes abrogates all of its rulings, its recitation, its worship through it, and acting upon the rulings in it, as in the verse of ten known sucklings that make marriage unlawful. At other times He abrogates some of its rulings but not others, such as abrogating the ruling of its recitation and worship through it while the legal rulings it contains remain, or abrogating its ruling but not its recitation and worship through it. The latter is the most common form of abrogation in the Qur'an.

We have explained all of this with its examples in surah "al-Nahl" in the commentary on His saying, ﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], and He has perfect wisdom in all that He does in this regard.

The verse of stoning (ayat al-rajm) is intended for the establishment of its ruling, not for worship through its recitation or for its recitation. It was revealed, the people recited it, and they understood from it the ruling of stoning. When that became fixed in their hearts, Allah abrogated its recitation and worship through it, and He kept its ruling, which is the purpose. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows best.

So stoning is established in the Qur'an. What will come from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said, "I flogged her according to the Book of Allah, and I stoned her according to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," does not contradict this, because the Sunnah is what clarified that the ruling of the verse of stoning remains after its recitation was abrogated, so its ruling in this respect is established by the Sunnah. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: "Abu al-Tahir and Harmala ibn Yahya told me, both saying: Ibn Wahb told us, Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab who said: 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba informed me that he heard 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas say: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab said, while sitting on the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: Indeed Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with the truth and revealed the Book to him. Among what was revealed to him was the verse of stoning. We recited it, memorised it, and understood it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stoned, and we stoned after him. I fear that if a long time passes over people, someone will say, 'We do not find stoning in the Book of Allah,' and they will go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah revealed. Indeed stoning in the Book of Allah is binding upon whoever commits adultery when he is married (ihsan), whether man or woman, if evidence is established, or there is pregnancy, or confession."'" End of quotation.

This hadith, agreed upon by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), from this rightly-guided caliph, Commander of the Faithful 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, is a clear and authentic proof that stoning is established by a verse from the Book of Allah, which was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which the Companions recited, memorised and understood, and that its ruling remains, because the Prophet ﷺ did it and the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did it after him.

Thus we have confirmed the continuation of its ruling, although there is no doubt about the abrogation of its recitation, together with the narrations we mentioned in Ibn Hajar's words, among which is the wording of the verse of stoning mentioned. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

As for the verse whose recitation and ruling both remain, it is His saying, ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, being called to the Book of Allah so that it may judge between them, then a faction of them turns away while they are refusing?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 23], according to the view that it was revealed concerning the stoning of the two Jewish adulterers who were married (muhsan), and the Prophet ﷺ stoned them. The story of his stoning them is famous and established in the Sahih. Upon this view, His saying, ﴿then a faction of them turns away while they are refusing﴾, means: away from what is in the Torah of the ruling of stoning. The censure of one who turns away from stoning in this verse indicates that it is established in our law. Thus the verse, according to this view, shows that stoning is established in our law, and its recitation remains.

* *

Branches related to this question:

First branch: The scholars agreed that stoning applies only to one who commits adultery while being married (muhsan).

The meaning of ihsan is that he has had intercourse during his lifetime, even once, in a valid marriage, and he is adult, sane and free. Men and women are equal in this, and so are Muslims and disbelievers, the rational and the one placed under restraint for foolishness. The evidence that a disbeliever who is married is stoned is the authentic hadith in which it is established that the Prophet ﷺ stoned two Jews who committed adultery after being married. The story of their stoning is famous and authentic, as is well known.

* *

Second branch: The people of knowledge agreed that whoever commits adultery while being married is stoned. We do not know of anyone among the people of the qibla (ahl al-qibla, Muslims who face the Ka'ba in prayer) who disagreed about stoning the married adulterer, male or female, except what al-Qadi 'Iyad and others reported from the Kharijites and some Mu'tazilites like al-Nazzam and his followers, for they did not hold stoning. The falsity of the view of those mentioned from the Kharijites and some Mu'tazilites is clear from the authentic, explicit, established texts from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions after him, as we presented from the hadith of 'Umar that is agreed upon, and as will come, Allah willing.

* *

Third branch: The scholars agreed that a male or female adulterer, if evidence is established against him that they saw him insert his private part into hers like a kohl stick into a kohl pot, must be stoned if he is married (muhsan). The scholars also agreed that testimony (bayyina) for adultery is not accepted with fewer than four just male witnesses. If three just witnesses testify, their testimony is not accepted and they are flogged, because they are false accusers (qadhafa, those who falsely accuse). This is because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. He also says: ﴿And those of your women who commit immorality, call upon four witnesses from among you against them﴾ [al-Nisa': 15]. Both of these verses are explicit that witnesses to adultery must not be fewer than four. He also said: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it? Since they did not bring witnesses, those are the liars in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Nur: 13]. This verse established the requirement of four, as in the two verses before it, and added that the accusers who do not bring four witnesses are the liars in the sight of Allah.

Whoever lies in his claim of adultery against a married man or woman is liable to the hadd for qadhf (the prescribed punishment for false accusation), as will be explained, Allah willing.

What Abu al-Khattab of the Hanbalis reported from Ahmad and al-Shafi'i, that witnesses to adultery who are not complete do not receive the hadd for qadhf because they are witnesses, not accusers, is not to be relied upon. The correct view, Allah willing, is what we have mentioned.

What supports this is the story of 'Umar with those who testified against al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba. When the fourth of them did not explicitly testify to al-Mughira's adultery, 'Umar flogged the three witnesses the flogging for qadhf, eighty lashes. Among them was Abu Bakra, may Allah be pleased with him. The story is well known and famous, and we have explained it in another place.

The majority of the people of knowledge hold that slaves' testimony is not accepted in adultery. We do not know of any disagreement from anyone among the people of knowledge about not accepting slaves' testimony in adultery, except a narration from Ahmad which is not his school's position, and the view of Abu Thawr.

It is required that witnesses to adultery be male. The testimony of women is never valid in it. We do not know of anyone among the people of knowledge who disagreed about this, except something reported from 'Ata' and Hammad that the testimony of three men and two women is accepted in it.

Ibn Qudama said in "al-Mughni": "This is an anomaly (shudhudh) that is not to be relied upon, because the word 'four' is the name of the number of those mentioned, and it requires that four suffice. There is no disagreement that if some of the four are women they are not sufficient, and that the minimum that suffices is five. This contradicts the text. Also, in their testimony there is doubt, because error can reach them, as Allah says: ﴿So that if one of them errs, the other can remind her﴾ [al-Baqara: 282]. And the hadd punishments are averted by doubts." End of quotation.

There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that the testimony of disbelievers, such as dhimmis (non-Muslim subjects under Muslim protection), is not accepted against a Muslim for adultery.

It is disputed whether their testimony is accepted against a disbeliever like them. Some said no, and that the Prophet ﷺ stoned the two Jews only on the basis of their confession of adultery, not on the testimony of Jewish witnesses against them for adultery. Those who held this view claimed that the witnesses in the hadith of Jabir were Muslim witnesses who testified to the confession of the two Jews mentioned of adultery. Among those who held this view is Ibn al-'Arabi the Maliki.

Some people of knowledge said: the testimony of disbelievers against one another is accepted if they come to us for judgment.

Al-Qurtubi said: The majority hold that a disbeliever's testimony is not accepted against a Muslim, nor against a disbeliever, neither in a hadd nor in anything else, and there is no difference between travel and residence in this. A group of the Successors (tabi'un) and some jurists accepted their testimony if no Muslim is found. Ahmad made an exception for travel when no Muslim is found.

Al-Qurtubi answered the majority concerning the incident of the two Jews: the Prophet ﷺ enforced on them what he knew to be the ruling of the Torah, and obliged them to act upon it openly because they had distorted their Book and changed its ruling. Or that was specific to this incident.

Ibn Hajar, after quoting al-Qurtubi's words mentioned above, said: "Thus he said. The second is rejected." Then he said: "al-Nawawi said: The apparent reading is that he stoned them on the basis of confession. If the hadith of Jabir is established, then perhaps the witnesses were Muslims; otherwise their testimony has no weight, and it is necessary that they both confessed to adultery."

Then Ibn Hajar said: "I say: It is not established that they were Muslims. It is possible that the witnesses informed the rest of the Jews of that, and the Prophet ﷺ heard their speech and did not judge concerning them except on the basis of what Allah had shown him, so he judged by revelation and made them bound by their own proof, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And a witness from among her own people testified﴾ [Yusuf: 26]. Their witnesses testified against them when they reported what was mentioned. When the matter was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, he investigated the story in its proper form, and every narrator present mentioned what he had memorised of that. The basis of the Prophet's ruling was only what Allah had shown him." End of the relevant point from Ibn Hajar's words in "Fath al-Bari."

The one who wrote this note, may Allah pardon and forgive him, says: What appears to me to be stronger by evidence is the view of the majority, that the testimony of disbelievers is not accepted in any case. This is because Allah says concerning Muslim transgressors: ﴿And do not ever accept their testimony, and those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has explicitly stated in His clear Book that the testimony of a transgressor is not accepted, then the disbeliever is more deserving of this, as is evident. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has also said concerning the witnesses to adultery, may Allah protect us and our Muslim brothers from it: ﴿And those of your women who commit immorality, call upon four witnesses from among you against them﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], specifying the four as being from among us. The one who objects could answer that the beginning of the verse says ﴿from your women﴾, so it does not include the women of the dhimmis and similar disbelievers. And that the testimony of a disbeliever is not accepted in anything except by a specific proof, such as bequest during travel when no Muslim is found, because Allah explicitly stated this when He said: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 106], and the rest of the verse.

The truth is that its ruling is not abrogated (naskh), because the Qur'an's ruling is not established as abrogated except by an evidence that must be relied upon. As for the verses that whoever claimed abrogation alleged to abrogate it:

• such as His saying: ﴿two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2],
• and His saying: ﴿of those whom you approve as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282],
• and His saying: ﴿and do not ever accept their testimony﴾ [al-Nur: 4].

The majority hold that the more general (al-a'amm) does not abrogate the more specific (al-akhass), contrary to Abu Hanifah.

As for the hadith of Jabir that is referred to, from which it is understood that the testimony of disbelievers against one another in the hadd punishment for fornication is accepted, Abu Dawud, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sunan: "Yahya ibn Musa al-Balkhi narrated to us, Abu Usamah narrated to us, Mujalid said: 'Amir narrated to us, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "The Jews brought a man and a woman from among them who had committed fornication. He said: 'Bring me the two most knowledgeable men among you,'" [the hadith], and in it: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned the witnesses, and they came with four who testified that they saw his member in her private part like the kohl-stick in the kohl-pot. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that they both be stoned."" End of the relevant point.

The apparent meaning that comes immediately to mind is that the witnesses who testified were Jews, as is not hidden. So the apparent meaning of the hadith clearly indicates the acceptance of the testimony of disbelievers against one another in the hadd punishment for fornication, if it is authentic. But the chain of narration (isnad) mentioned, by which Abu Dawud narrated it, is not sound, because in it is Mujalid, and he is (p-376) Mujalid ibn Sa'id ibn Umayr ibn Bisṭam ibn Dhi Miran ibn Shurahbil al-Hamdani, Abu Amr, also called Abu Sa'id al-Kufi. Most scholars of knowledge consider him weak and not a basis for argument. Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj only narrated his hadith in conjunction with others. Therefore no weight is given to the statement of Ya'qub ibn Sufyan that he is "truthful," nor to al-Nasa'i's declaring him trustworthy on one occasion, since he weakened him on another occasion; nor to Ibn Adi's statement that he has some good hadiths from al-Sha'bi, from Jabir, because most scholars of the transmitters consider him weak and not a basis for argument. As for the other transmitters in Abu Dawud's chain besides Mujalid, they are reliable and well known: Yahya ibn Musa al-Balkhi is trustworthy; Abu Usamah mentioned in it is Hammad ibn Usamah al-Qurashi, their mawla, and he is trustworthy and firm, though he sometimes committed tadlis (concealment of defects in a chain), and toward the end of his life he narrated from the books of others; and Amir, who narrated from Mujalid, is the Imam al-Sha'bi, whose eminence is well known.

The conclusion: a chain like this one containing the aforementioned Mujalid cannot be relied upon against the general sound texts that require that the testimony of disbelievers is never accepted under any circumstances. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

Branch Four: Know that the scholars have differed regarding the requirement of the unity of the session (ittihad al-majlis) for the testimony of the witnesses to fornication. On the requirement of this, if they testify in two sessions or in separate sessions, their testimony is void and they receive the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf). On the non-requirement of unity of the session, their testimony is accepted even if they come separately and give their testimony in multiple sessions. Among those who held the requirement of unity of the session are Malik and his companions, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and Ahmad and his companions. Among those who held the non-requirement of unity of the session are al-Shafi'i, Uthman al-Batti, and Ibn al-Mundhir.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: They held the non-requirement of this because of His exalted saying: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ [al-Nur: 13], and He did not mention the session. And He, exalted, said: ﴿Call upon four witnesses from among you against them. And if they testify, then confine them to the houses﴾ [al-Nisa': 15]. Also, every testimony that is accepted, if it agrees, is accepted if it is separated into sessions, like all other testimonies. Our evidence is that Abu Bakrah, Nafi', and Shibl ibn Ma'bad testified before Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, against al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah for fornication, and Ziyad did not testify, so the three were punished with the hadd. Had the session not been a requirement, it would not have been permissible for him to punish them, since they might have completed it with a fourth in another session. Also, if three testified and he punished them, then a fourth came and testified, his testimony would not be accepted; and had the unity of the session not been a requirement, their testimony would have been complete. It is by this that it differs from all other testimonies.

(p-377) As for the verse, it does not address the conditions, and for this reason justice ('adalah) and the description of fornication are not mentioned. Also, His saying: ﴿Then they did not bring four witnesses, so lash them﴾ [al-Nur: 4] either is unrestricted in all time or is restricted. It cannot be unrestricted, because that would prevent the lashing of them, since there is no time in which four witnesses could not come, or the full number could not come if some of them had already testified, and then their lashing commanded would be impossible, which would be a contradiction. And when it is established that it is restricted, the most fitting thing it is restricted by is the session, because the whole session is like a single state; for this reason the option of the session (khiyar al-majlis) applies to it, and possession suffices in what requires possession. When this is established, the gathering of them at the time of their coming is not required; even if they come separated, one after another, in a single session, their testimony is accepted.

Malik and Abu Hanifah said: If they come separated, they are slanderers (qadhafah), because they did not gather at the time of their coming, so their testimony is not accepted, like those who did not testify in a single session. Our evidence is the story of al-Mughirah, for the witnesses came one after another and their testimony was heard, and they were punished only because it was not complete.

In his hadith, that Abu Bakrah said: "Do you see that if another comes to testify, would you stone him?" Umar said: "Yes, by Him in whose hand my soul is." Also, because they gathered in a single session, which is more like if they had come while already gathered. And because the whole session is like its beginning, for the reason we mentioned. And if they separate into multiple sessions, then they incur the hadd, because whoever testifies to fornication and does not complete the testimony is obligated the hadd, by His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not bring four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. End of what is from Ibn Qudamah's al-Mughni.

You have already learned the statements of the scholars regarding the requirement of unity of the session for the testimony of witnesses to fornication, and what each of the two groups argued.

The one who qualifies this (al-muqayyid), may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The stronger of the two views according to my understanding in evidence is the acceptance of their testimony, even if they come separately in multiple sessions. Because Allah, Exalted is He, explicitly stated in His Book the acceptance of the testimony of four in fornication. So voiding it, while they are four, on the claim of non-unity of the session, is voiding the testimony of upright witnesses without a convincing evidence that must be relied upon. And what was argued for the requirement of unity of the session does not fully hold as an argument. If someone says: "The witnesses with us include one who will testify the same as our testimony," the Imam should wait for him and accept his testimony. If no additional witnesses are produced and the judge knows of no further witness, he imposes the hadd on them, because their testimony is not complete (p-378). This is the apparent position for us from the generality of the evidences, even if it contradicts the school of Malik, Abu Hanifah, and Ahmad. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

Note.
Know that Malik and his companions require, in addition to the testimony of the witnesses to fornication being given at one time, that they be witnesses to one act. So if they gather and each one looks after another, their testimony is not valid according to the more correct view of Malik's school, because of the possibility of multiple intercourse, and that the fornicator withdrew his member from her private part after the first saw it, and the second saw a different penetration than the one seen by the one before him; for acts are not combined with one another in testimony in their view. And when their testimony is not accepted, they receive the punishment for slander. The well-known view of Malik's school also is the obligation to separate them, I mean the witnesses to fornication specifically, not the other kinds of witnesses.

Its meaning according to them is that they must come gathered; then when they come gathered, they are separated at the time of giving testimony, so each one of them is questioned out of the presence of the others, and each one testifies that he saw him insert his member into her private part, or penetrate her. And according to them there must be an additional detail, like the kohl-stick in the kohl-pot or the like. It is permissible for the witnesses to look at the private parts of the two fornicators, so that they can give testimony in its proper manner; there is no sin upon them in that, and it does not detract from their testimony, because it is a means of establishing one of the hudud of Allah. This applies if they are four. If they are fewer than four, it is not permissible for them to look at the private parts of the fornicator, since there is no benefit in their testimony, and because they would be lashed with the punishment for slander.

Some of the Malikis said: It is not permissible for them to look at the private parts of the fornicators, even if they are four, because of what the Law has indicated regarding the preference for concealment. According to the Malikis, it is recommended for the judge to question the witnesses to fornication about what is not a condition for the validity of the testimony, such as saying to each witness separately, out of the presence of the others: "In what state did you see the two of them at the time of their fornication? Was the woman on her right side, or her left, or on her stomach, or on her back? And in which parts of the house," and similar things. If they differ, such as one saying she was on her back and another saying she was on her right side, or similar, their testimony is void, because their disagreement indicates their lying. Likewise if they differ about the part of the house where the fornication took place.

There is no doubt that such questioning is more cautious in defending the honor of Muslims, because if they are truthful they will not differ, and if they are lying, their lie is known by their disagreement. We have already presented what may be used as a supporting indication for separating the witnesses to fornication and questioning them separately, in the story of Sulayman and Dawud concerning the woman against whom four had testified that she committed fornication with her dog. Dawud stoned her. Then Sulayman came with the children and made them witnesses, separated them, and questioned them separately about the color of the dog with which she committed fornication. Each one of them reported a color different from the color the other reported. Then Dawud sent for the witnesses, separated them, and questioned them separately about the color of the dog with which she committed fornication, and they differed about its color, as has been previously explained.

Know that whatever establishes stoning (rajm) also establishes flogging (jald); the means of establishing both is one, with no difference between them, as is not hidden.

* *

Branch Five: Know that if two testify that he committed fornication with her in this house, and two that he committed fornication with her in another house, or each pair testifies against him for fornication in a city other than the city in which the other two witnessed, or they differ about the day on which the fornication took place, the scholars have differed as to whether their testimony is accepted, considering that they are four who testified to fornication, or is not accepted, because four did not testify to one single act of fornication; so each act of fornication was testified to by two, and fornication is not established by two.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 2 (part 4 of 7):

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: All of them are slanderers (qadhafah) and the hadd (the prescribed punishment) applies to them. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Bakr chose the view that there is no hadd on them, and this is also the view of al-Nakha'i, Abu Thawr, and the Ashab al-Ra'y (the adherents of opinion), because they completed four witnesses. Our argument is that they did not complete four witnesses for a single act of zina (unlawful sexual intercourse), so the hadd is obligatory on them, just as it would be if two witnesses alone had testified. As for the one who was witnessed against, there is no hadd on him according to all of them. Abu Bakr said that the hadd is on him, and he related it as a view of Ahmad. This is far-fetched, for no single act of zina has been established by the testimony of four witnesses, so the hadd is not obligatory. Furthermore, whatever requires evidence (bayyina) requires that its completeness be present in a single right, so the one who makes the hadd obligatory is preferred, because it is among the matters in which caution is exercised and which are averted by doubts (shubuhat). Abu Bakr also said: If two witnesses testified that he committed zina with a white woman, and two witnesses testified that he committed zina with a black woman, then they are slanderers. This was reported from him by al-Qadi, and this contradicts his own view. End of quotation from him. Then he said: If two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her in a corner of a house, and two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her in another corner of it, and the two corners were far apart, then the ruling regarding them is like the ruling regarding the two houses. If the two corners were close together, their testimony is complete and the one who was witnessed against receives the hadd. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafi'i said: There is no hadd on him, because their testimony is not complete, and because they differed about the place, so it resembles the case where they differed about two houses. According to Abu Bakr's view, their testimony is complete whether the two corners are close or far. Our argument is that when the two corners are close, it is possible for the witnesses to be truthful, by the act beginning in one of them and its completion in the other, or by each pair attributing it to one of the two corners because of its proximity to it. Therefore, their testimony must be accepted, just as it would be if they had agreed. This differs from the case where the two corners are far apart, for then it is not possible that the testified act was a single act.

If it is said: It is possible that the testified act was two acts. Why then do you make the hadd obligatory despite the possibility, when the hadd is averted by doubts?

We say: This is not a doubt, as evidenced by the case where they agreed on one place, for in that case this possibility is admitted and the hadd is obligatory. The same applies to time. Whenever there is a long interval between the two that makes it impossible for a single act to occur throughout it, such as the two ends of the day, their testimony is not complete. Whenever the two are close, their testimony is complete. End of quotation from *al-Mughni*.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: You have seen the statements of the scholars on this branch. The apparent position is that the testimony of the four is not complete unless they testify to a single act in a unified place and a unified time. If they differ regarding the time or the place, they are punished, because these are two acts, and four just witnesses did not testify to either of them, so neither of them is established. The view that their testimony is combined, and that the testimony of some of them is joined to the testimony of others, does not appear sound. You know that Malik and his companions added that the testimony of the four must concern a single act of penetration (iylaj). If they looked at him one after another while the time and place were unified, his testimony would not be accepted by them until they looked at his private part in her private part in a single glance in a single moment. There is a basis for this view.

* *

Sixth branch: If two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her while she wore a white shirt, and two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her while she wore a red shirt, or two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her while she wore a cotton garment, and two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her while she wore a silk (khazz) garment.

The scholars differed on whether their testimony is complete or not. Some said: Their testimony is not complete, because each pair of them contradicts the testimony of the other two. Al-Shafi'i is among those reported to have held this view. Others said: Their testimony is complete, saying: There is no contradiction between the two testimonies, because it is possible that he had two shirts on, and each pair mentioned one of the two shirts and omitted the other. Thus all of them are truthful, because the garment omitted by these two is the one mentioned by those two, and vice versa, so there is no contradiction. It is also possible that she had a red shirt on and he had a white shirt on, the reverse being likewise possible, or that he had a cotton garment on and she had a silk garment on, the reverse being likewise possible. Thus the truthfulness of all of them is possible, and when their truthfulness is possible, there is no basis for rejecting their testimony. The author of *al-Mughni* affirmed this and gave it the basis we have mentioned.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to us in this branch is the obligation to question the witnesses (istifsar). If two of them affirm that he had one red garment on, and the other two affirm that he had one white garment on, their testimony is not complete, because the two testimonies contradict. If they agree that he had two garments, for example, one of which is red and the other white, and each pair mentioned one of the two garments, then there is no difficulty in the completeness of their testimony, because the two testimonies agree. If it is not possible to question the witnesses, because they have died or are absent in a manner that makes questioning them impossible, then what appears to me is that their testimony is not complete, because there is the possibility that their two testimonies contradict. The mere possibility that they agree is not sufficient to establish the hadd, because the hadd is averted by doubts, so it is not enforced on the basis of testimony that is possibly invalid. Rather, the apparent meaning of the wording is that the two testimonies contradict, and acting on the apparent meaning is obligatory unless there is a decisive evidence diverting from it, to which one must return.

What appears is that if their testimony is not complete, they receive the hadd for slander (hadd al-qadhf). As for the testimony that is merely possible, before it is possible to question them, there is no difficulty in not being able to punish them. If it is possible to question them and they explain it in a way that requires the completeness of their testimony, the one witnessed against receives the hadd on the basis of their testimony. If they explain it in a way that requires the invalidity of their testimony, then it appears that they receive the hadd for slander, as we have stated before. And Allah Most High knows best.

* *

Seventh branch: If two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her under coercion (mukrahah), and two witnesses testified that he committed zina with her willingly (mutawi'ah), then there is no hadd on the woman, by consensus (ijma'), because the testimony against her was not complete for an act that requires the hadd. The disagreement concerns the ruling on the man and the witnesses.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: Regarding the man there are two views:

The first: There is no hadd on him. This is the view of Abu Bakr, al-Qadi, and most of the companions, and the view of Abu Hanifa, and one of the two views of the companions of al-Shafi'i, because the evidence was not complete for a single act. The act of willing submission is other than the act of coercion, and the count was not completed for either of the two acts. Also, each pair of them contradicts the other two, and that prevents the acceptance of testimony, or it constitutes a doubt in averting the hadd. The statement of one of them is not contradicting the other except by assuming two acts, in one of which she was willing and in the other coerced. This prevents the testimony from being complete regarding a single act. Also, the two witnesses to her willingness are slanderers of her, and the evidence was not complete against her, so their testimony is not accepted regarding others.

The second view: The hadd is obligatory on him. This was chosen by Abu al-Khattab, and it is the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and a second view of al-Shafi'i, because the testimony was complete regarding the occurrence of zina from him. The disagreement is only about her act, not his act, so it does not prevent the completeness of the testimony against him.

Regarding the witnesses, there are three views:

The first: There is no hadd on them. This is the view of whoever made the hadd obligatory on the man on the basis of their testimony.

The second: The hadd is obligatory on them, because they testified to zina, and their testimony was not complete, so the hadd is obligatory on them, just as it would be if their number had not been completed.

The third: The hadd is obligatory on the two witnesses to her willingness, because they slandered the woman with zina, and their testimony against her was not complete. It is not obligatory on the two witnesses to coercion, because they did not slander the woman, and their testimony against the man was complete. The hadd was dropped from him only because of doubt.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: You have seen the disagreement of the scholars on this branch. The most evident of their views to me regarding it is: There is no hadd on the man or the woman, and the four witnesses receive the hadd for slander. As for the dropping of the hadd from the woman, there is no disagreement about it, and its basis is clear, because the testimony to zina was not complete against her. As for dropping the hadd from the man, it is because the two witnesses to willingness contradict the two witnesses to coercion, and vice versa. When each pair among the four contradicts the other two regarding the state in which the act occurred, their testimony is not complete regarding a single act. Thus the testimony was not complete against the man regarding one act of zina in one state, because coercion and willingness are two contradictory matters. When testimony is not complete against him regarding a single act in a single state, the non-imposition of the hadd on him is the most evident. As for the basis for the hadd on the witnesses: the two witnesses that she committed zina willingly are slanderers of her with zina, and their testimony against her was not complete, so the hadd for their slander of the woman is quite evident. Also, the two witnesses that he committed zina with her under coercion are slanderers of the man, saying that he coerced her and then committed zina with her, and their testimony was not complete, because the two witnesses to willingness contradict them in their claim of coercion. So the hadd for their slander of the man, and the incompleteness of their testimony against him, is evident. As for the claim that the four have agreed in their testimony that he committed zina with her, this is refuted by the fact that each pair of them contradicts the other two in the state in which the zina occurred. This is the most evident view we hold from the statements of the scholars on this branch. And Allah Most High knows best.

[p. 283] It is well known that whatever establishes stoning (rajm) against a married person (muhsan) establishes flogging (jald) against a virgin, so the means of establishing both matters is one.

* *

Eighth branch: Know that if four just witnesses testify against a woman that she committed zina, and their testimony is complete in the required manner, and she says that she is a virgin whose virginity has not been removed, and four women known for their justice look at her and testify that she is a virgin whose virginity has not been removed by anything that removes it, then the scholars have differed on whether the testimony of the women averts the hadd from her or not. Malik and his companions held that the hadd is enforced upon her and the testimony of the women is not taken into account. The wording of *al-Mudawwanah* on this is: If four just witnesses testified against her for zina, and she said that she is a virgin, and women looked at her and confirmed it, their statement is not considered and the hadd is enforced upon her. End of quotation through al-Mawwaq's commentary on the statement of Khalil in his *Mukhtasar*. The evidence (bayyina) of the zina is not annulled by the testimony of four women regarding her virginity. A group of scholars held that the testimony of women regarding her virginity averts the hadd from her. This is the view of Imam Ahmad. Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: This was also the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and the Ashab al-Ra'y. The basis of the view of Malik and his companions, that the hadd is enforced upon her, is that the testimony for her zina was completed by four just witnesses, and the testimony of women has no role in the hudud, so the testimony of men for zina against her is not annulled by their testimony. The basis of the view of the others, that she is not punished, is that her virginity was established by the testimony of women, and the presence of virginity is a barrier to zina apparently, because zina does not occur without penetration into the vagina, and that is not conceivable while virginity remains, for the virgin (bikr) is the one who has not been penetrated in her front passage. When zina is negated, the hadd is not obligatory, just as if evidence had been established that the one witnessed against for zina was castrated (majbub).

Ibn Qudamah also said in *al-Mughni*: It must be sufficient to accept the testimony of one woman, because her testimony is accepted in matters that men do not witness, meaning the aforementioned virginity. End of quotation. As for the four who testified to zina, there is no hadd on them, because their testimony is complete, and it is stronger than the testimony of women regarding virginity.

The commentator of *al-Mughni* said: The hadd was not imposed on them because their number was complete, though their truthfulness is still possible, since it is possible that he had intercourse with her and then her hymen returned, so this would be a doubt (shubhah) that averts the hadd from them. But if a proof (bayyinah) testifies against a man for fornication, and another proof establishes that he is castrated (majbub), or a proof testifies against a woman for fornication and another proof establishes that she is closed (ratqa'), then the apparent ruling is that the hadd for false accusation (qadhf) is obligatory on the witnesses to the fornication, because their falsehood is evident. This is because a castrated man or a closed woman cannot commit fornication with one another, as is well known.

* *

(p. 284) Second issue: Know that the scholars unanimously agreed that fornication is established, and that the hadd is obligatory, whether stoning (rajm) or flogging (jald), by the confession (iqrar) of the male fornicator and female fornicator. However, they differed over whether fornication is established by the male fornicator's confession once, or whether that is not sufficient unless he confesses four times. Imam Ahmad, Abu Hanifah, Ibn Abi Layla and al-Hakam held that it is not established except when he confesses four times. Abu Hanifah and Ibn Abi Layla added that this must occur in four sessions, and that the four confessions in one session are not sufficient according to them. Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Hasan, Hammad, Abu Thawr and Ibn al-Mundhir held that fornication is established by confession once.

As for the proofs of those who said that confession once is sufficient: among them is that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Unays in the famous sound hadith: "Go in the morning, Unays, to this man's wife, and if she confesses, stone her." She confessed, and he stoned her. In another narration in the Sahih: "She confessed, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered her, and she was stoned." They said: This hadith, agreed upon from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani (may Allah be pleased with them both), clearly indicates that fornication is established by confessing it once, because his saying (ﷺ) in it, "If she confesses, stone her," is evidently sufficient with one confession. For if four confessions were a necessary requirement, he (ﷺ) would have said: "If she confesses four times, stone her." Since he did not say that, we know that one time is sufficient, because it is not permissible to delay clarification beyond the time of need, as is well known.

Among their evidences for the sufficiency of confessing fornication once is what is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them both): "A woman from Juhaynah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while she was pregnant from fornication, and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, I have committed a hadd, so establish it upon me.' The Prophet (ﷺ) summoned her guardian and said: 'Treat her well, and when she gives birth, bring her to me.' He did so, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that her clothes be fastened around her, then ordered that she be stoned, then he prayed over her. Umar said to him: 'Will you pray over her, O Prophet of Allah, when she has committed fornication?' He said: 'She has repented a repentance which, if it were divided among seventy of the people of Madinah, would have sufficed them. Have you found a repentance better than that she gave herself up for Allah, the Exalted?'" This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih, and it is a clear text that he (ﷺ) ordered her stoning upon her confession once, because she said: "I have committed a hadd," once; and that the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered her stoning without repetition of confession, because the hadith mentions only her confession once.

Among their evidences for this also: what is established in the Sahih concerning the story of the woman of al-Ghamidiyyah, who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have committed fornication, so purify me." He sent her away. When it was the next day, she said: "O Messenger of Allah, why do you send me away? Perhaps you will send me away as you sent away Ma'iz. By Allah, I am pregnant." He said: "As for that, then go until you give birth." When she gave birth, she came to him with the child wrapped in a cloth and said: "This is the one I have given birth to." He said: "Go and nurse him until you wean him." When she weaned him, she came to him with the child, and in his hand was a piece of bread. She said: "This is him, O Prophet of Allah; I have weaned him, and he has eaten food." So he gave the child to a man from the Muslims. Then he ordered her, and a pit was dug for her up to her chest, and he commanded the people, and they stoned her. Khalid ibn al-Walid came with a stone and struck her head, so blood spattered onto Khalid's face, and he cursed her. The Prophet (ﷺ) heard his cursing of her and said: "Gently, O Khalid! By He in whose hand is my soul, she has repented a repentance which, if a tax collector (sahib maks) had repented it, he would have been forgiven." Then he ordered her, and she was prayed over and buried. This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Buraydah, from his father. It is among the clearest evidences for the sufficiency of the fornicator's confession of fornication once, because when al-Ghamidiyyah said to him (ﷺ): "Perhaps you will send me away as you sent away Ma'iz," he did not reject that from her. Had four confessions been a condition for the obligation of the hadd, he would have said to her: "I only sent him away because he did not confess four times."

Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*, after mentioning this incident: This incident is among the greatest evidences indicating that quadrupling the confession is not a condition, because it is clearly stated in it that it occurred after the case of Ma'iz, and in it he was satisfied with less than four, as will come. End quote.

And in Sahih Muslim also, from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Buraydah from his father, the text is: He said: "Then a woman from Ghamid of the Azd came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, purify me.' He said: 'Woe to you, return, seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him.' She said: 'I see you want to send me away as you sent away Ma'iz ibn Malik.' He said: 'And what is that?' She said: 'She is pregnant from fornication.' He said: 'Is it you?' She said: 'Yes.' He said to her: 'Wait until you deliver what is in your belly.' He said: A man from the Ansar took responsibility for her until she gave birth. He said: He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'The woman of Ghamid has given birth.' He said: 'In that case we will not stone her and leave her child young with no one to nurse him.' A man from the Ansar stood up and said: 'Her nursing is my responsibility, O Prophet of Allah.' He said: So he stoned her." End quote.

This narration is like the previous one in indicating the sufficiency of confession once, and [it is one of] the other evidences indicating that repeating the confession of fornication four times is not a condition. As for the argument of those who said: It is required for the establishment of confession of fornication that he confess it four times, and that the hadd is not obligatory upon him except by four confessions, it is what is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), agreed upon, who said: "A man from the people came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in the mosque, and called out: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have committed fornication,' meaning himself. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned away from him, so he moved to the side of the face toward which the Prophet had turned, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have committed fornication.' He turned away from him again, so he came to the side of the Prophet's face which he had turned away from. When he testified against himself four testimonies, the Prophet (ﷺ) summoned him and said: 'Are you insane?' He said: 'No, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Are you muhsan?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Take him away and stone him.'" The hadith... This is the wording of al-Bukhari in his Sahih. The wording of Muslim: "When he testified against himself four testimonies, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned him and said: 'Are you insane?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Have you been muhsan?' He said: 'Yes.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Take him away and stone him.'" End quote.

They said: This agreed-upon hadith contains the order of stoning upon four testimonies against himself, meaning four confessions, in the form of the arrangement of the consequent upon the condition. Because "lamma" (when) implies the meaning of a condition, and the arrangement of the hadd upon the four is the arrangement of the consequent upon its condition, it is evidence of the requirement of the four mentioned. The man mentioned in this hadith is Ma'iz ibn Malik, and his story is famous and sound. In the wordings of its narrations is what indicates that he (ﷺ) did not stone him until he testified against himself four testimonies, as you saw in the hadith mentioned just above. You have known from what we have mentioned the evidence used by each of the two groups.

My author, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, said: In my view, the more apparent of the two opinions of the people of knowledge on this issue is: combining the hadiths indicating the requirement of four with the hadiths indicating sufficiency of one time. This is because combining the evidences is obligatory whenever possible, since acting upon both evidences is better than nullifying one of them. The way of this combination is to apply the hadiths in which there is a delay in carrying out the hadd after the confession once, to someone whose state of mind is uncertain regarding soundness of intellect, derangement, intoxication, or sobriety after intoxication and the like. And to apply the hadiths of carrying out the hadd after one confession to someone whose soundness of mind and sobriety from intoxication are known, and whose confession is free from invalidating factors. Al-Shawkani preferred this combination in *Nayl al-Awtar*.

Among what supports this is that all the narrations which imply the requirement of four are about the case of Ma'iz, and the narrations of his hadith indicate that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not know whether he was insane or not, whether he was sober or drunk, as shown by his saying to him in the agreed-upon hadith mentioned above: "Are you insane?", and his (ﷺ) asking his people about his intellect, and his (ﷺ) asking: "Did he drink wine?" A man then stood up and smelled him, and found no smell of wine on him. All of that is established in the Sahih, and it is strong evidence for combining the hadiths as we have mentioned. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

Branches related to this issue:

First branch: Know that it is apparent that the confession must explicitly state the cause requiring the hadd, which is fornication, in an explicit manner that excludes every possibility, because some people may apply the name of fornication to what does not require the hadd.

This is indicated by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Ma'iz when he said that he had committed fornication: "Perhaps you kissed, or pressed, or looked?" He said: "No." He said: "Did you then (afnakta-hā) [have intercourse with her]?" — without euphemism — He said: "Yes." He said: At that point he ordered his stoning. This is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and others, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas. From it is derived the allusion (ta'rid) for the fornicator to conceal it upon himself and seek Allah's forgiveness, for He is Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does righteous deeds.

* *

Second branch: Know that when the testimony of the four witnesses to fornication is complete, and the accused fornicator confirms them by confessing that he committed fornication once, the testimony becomes complete, while the confession is not complete according to those who require four.

The more apparent of the two opinions of the people of knowledge according to me is: that the hadd is established against him because the evidence (bayyinah) is complete, contrary to those who claimed that the hadd is not established against him, because a condition for the validity of the evidence is denial, and this one does not deny.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: The cancellation of the hadd by his confessing once is the view of Abu Hanifah. End quote. Likewise, if the testimony of the evidence is complete against him and he confessed against himself four times, then retracted his confession, the retraction does not benefit him, because the hadd is obligatory upon him by the testimony of the evidence. So there is no need for his confession, and no benefit in his retraction of it. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

Third branch: Know that the more apparent of the two opinions of the people of knowledge according to me is: that if he confesses to an old act of fornication, the confession is accepted, and it is not invalidated by the claim that he confessed only after a long time, because the apparent view is to consider the confession absolutely, whether its time has long passed or not. Likewise the testimony of the evidence is accepted, even if it is given only after a long time, because the general wording of the texts requires that, since there is nothing in them distinguishing between prompt and delayed testimony, contrary to Abu Hanifah and those who agree with him in their saying that the confession is accepted after a long time, but testimony is not accepted with delay.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: If they testify to an old act of fornication, or he confesses it, the hadd is obligatory. Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Ishaq and Abu Thawr held this view.

Abu Hanifah said: I do not accept evidence for an old act of fornication, and I impose the hadd by confession of it. This is the view of Ibn Hamid, and Ibn Abi Musa mentioned it as the school (madhhab) of Ahmad. End quote.

**Branch Four:** Know that if a man confesses that he committed fornication (*zina*) with a woman and names her, and she denies it and says that he did not commit it with her:

The most correct opinion of the scholars in my view is that the *hadd* (the fixed prescribed punishment) for fornication is obligatory on him by his confession, and the *hadd* for *qadhf* (false accusation) as well, because he accused the woman of fornication and did not produce four witnesses, so the *hadd* for *qadhf* became obligatory on him.

In *al-Mughni*, he said: Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: there is no *hadd* on him, because we believed her in her denial, so he is judged to be a liar.

The one who restricts this (the author, may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: The obligation of the *hadd* on him by his confession should not be abandoned, and the opposite cannot be correct, for two reasons:

The first: He confessed against himself to fornication with a valid confession. Their statement that "we believed her" is not correct. Rather, we did not believe her, and we did not say that she is truthful. But the absence of the *hadd* for her occurred only because she did not confess, and no evidence was established against her. So the absence of her *hadd* is due to the lack of its requirement, not because she is truthful, as you see.

The second: What Abu Dawud related in his *Sunan*: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Talq ibn Ghannam narrated to us, (p-٣٨٩) Abd al-Salam ibn Hafs narrated to us, Abu Hazim narrated to us, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man came to him and confessed in his presence that he had committed fornication with a woman whom he named to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent for the woman and asked her about it, and she denied that she had committed fornication. So he had the man flogged with the *hadd* and left her alone." End of quote from him. Abd al-Salam mentioned in this chain was declared trustworthy by Ibn Ma'in, and his being declared trustworthy is preferable to the statement of Abu Hatim al-Razi that he is "unknown," because the one who memorized is a proof against the one who did not memorize.

The hadith mentioned is an explicit text that the one who confesses is subjected to the *hadd*, and this is clear, because there is no dispute over the obligation of the *hadd* on one who confesses against himself to fornication. As for his being subjected to the *hadd* for *qadhf* along with it, this is also apparent, and the generality of the Almighty's words supports it: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, flog them with eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. Acting upon the generality of the texts is obligatory unless there is a specifying evidence that must be referred to. The fact that the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi that we mentioned above in Abu Dawud does not state that the Prophet (ﷺ) flogged that man with the *hadd* for *qadhf*, but only with the *hadd* for fornication, does not oppose the generality of the texts.

Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: His being flogged for both fornication and *qadhf* together is the apparent view, for two reasons:

The first: The most that the hadith of Sahl says is that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not flog that man for *qadhf*, and this cannot serve as evidence for its dropping, because it is possible that this was due to the woman not demanding it, or due to the presence of a factor that removes it. Up to his saying: The second reason: The apparent meaning of *qadhf* is general, so nothing is excluded from it except what is excluded by evidence, and it applies to everyone who is in this state as an accuser. End of quote from him. This is the apparent view that should not be abandoned. Likewise, what came in some narrations of the hadith of Ma'iz ibn Malik, that he specified the girl with whom he committed fornication, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not flog him for accusing her, but flogged him only for fornication. The leaving of his *hadd* for *qadhf* cannot be explained by what we mentioned shortly before.

In any case, whoever says: "I committed fornication with so-and-so" undoubtedly confesses against himself to fornication, and is an accuser of her with it. The apparent meaning of the texts is that he is held accountable for his confession against himself, and he is also flogged with the *hadd* for *qadhf*, because he is undoubtedly an accuser, as you see.

What supports this view is what Abu Dawud related in his *Sunan*: Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Faris narrated to us, Musa ibn Harun al-Bardi narrated to us, Hisham ibn Yusuf narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Fayyad al-Abna'i, (p-٣٩٠) from Khallad ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn al-Musayyab, from Ibn Abbas: "A man from the Banu Bakr ibn Layth came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and confessed that he had committed fornication with a woman four times. He flogged him one hundred lashes, and he was unmarried. Then he asked him for evidence against the woman, and she said: 'He lied, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' So he flogged him the *hadd* of slander, eighty lashes." End of quote.

If it is said: This hadith is weak, because in its chain is al-Qasim ibn Fayyad al-Abna'i al-San'ani, of whom Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib*: "unknown," and al-Dhahabi said of him in *al-Mizan*: "Several people weakened him, among them Abbas, from Ibn Ma'in." The answer is in two respects:

The first: Abu Dawud said of al-Qasim mentioned: "trustworthy," as al-Dhahabi quoted from him in *al-Mizan*, and a general declaration of trustworthiness is accepted, while a general declaration of weakness is not accepted, as has already passed.

The second: The hadith of Ibn Abbas in which the combining of the *hadd* for *qadhf* and the *hadd* for fornication is found, if the man said that he committed fornication with a woman whom he specified and she denied it, is strongly supported by the apparent meaning of the texts that show he is held accountable for his confession, and by the texts that show that whoever accuses a woman of fornication, and she denies it, and he does not produce evidence, is flogged with the *hadd* for *qadhf*.

The conclusion: The most apparent of the opinions in our view is that he is flogged with the *hadd* for *qadhf* and the *hadd* for fornication. This is the position of Malik, and he explicitly stated it in *al-Mudawwana*, contrary to those who say he is flogged only with the *hadd* for fornication, such as Ahmad and al-Shafi'i, and to those who say he is flogged only with the *hadd* for *qadhf*. What supports this position that we have chosen in this issue is what Malik and his companions said: that if a man says to a woman, "You committed fornication," and she says to him, "You committed fornication with me," she is flogged for *qadhf* and for fornication together, and the man is not flogged for either of them, because she confirmed his accusation. And Allah knows best.

* *

**Branch Five:** Know that the confession of one who has been coerced is not valid. If a man is coerced by beating or another kind of torture to confess to fornication, and he confesses to it under coercion, his confession does not bind him, so he is not subjected to the *hadd*, and fornication is not established against him. We know of no one among the scholars who disagrees in this, and Allah knows best.

* *

**Issue Three:** Know that we have already mentioned that fornication is established by evidence (*bayyinah*) and by confession, and there is no disagreement that it is established by each of these if it occurs in the required manner. As for the appearance of pregnancy in a woman who is not known to have a husband or a master, the scholars have differed over whether the *hadd* is established by it. Some of the people of knowledge said: pregnancy in a woman who is not known to have a husband or master establishes fornication against her, and the *hadd* becomes obligatory upon her by it. This was established in the hadith of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that we mentioned in his saying: "If evidence is established, or there is pregnancy, (p-٣٩١) or confession." The hadith mentioned is in the two *Sahihs* and others, as mentioned above, and the Commander of the Faithful Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) explicitly stated in it that pregnancy, which is the *hamal*, establishes fornication just as evidence and confession do. Among those who held that pregnancy establishes fornication are Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), as you have seen, and Malik and his companions. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Hanifa, and the majority of the scholars held that fornication is not established and the *hadd* is not obligatory by pregnancy alone, even if the woman is not known to have a husband or master. This opinion was attributed by al-Nawawi in his commentary on Muslim to al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, and the majority of the scholars. Now that the positions of the scholars on this issue are known, these are their evidences.

As for those who said that fornication is established by pregnancy, if she has no husband or master, they argued with the hadith of Umar that is agreed upon and mentioned above, in which Umar explicitly states that pregnancy establishes fornication, like evidence and confession.
