Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: Those who said that the *hadd* is obligatory and fornication is established by pregnancy said so only because of the saying of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and stoning is obligatory on everyone among men and women who commits fornication, if they are married, when evidence is established, or there is pregnancy, or confession. It is related that Uthman was brought a woman who had given birth after six months, so Uthman ordered her to be stoned. Ali said: "You have no authority over her. Allah said: ﴿And its carrying and weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]." This indicates that he was going to stone her because of her pregnancy. And a similar report is related from Umar. It is also related from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "O people, fornication is of two kinds: secret fornication and public fornication. Secret fornication is that the witnesses testify, and the witnesses are the first to cast stones. Public fornication is that pregnancy appears or there is confession, and the Imam is the first to cast stones." This is the saying of the leaders of the Companions, and no dissenter appeared in their era, so it is a consensus. End of the relevant point from *al-Mughni*.

Look at the chains of the reports he mentioned from the Companions. This is the summary of what those who said that fornication is established by pregnancy argued with.

As for those who said that pregnancy alone does not establish fornication, nor is the *hadd* obligatory by it, but evidence or confession is required, Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: Their argument is that it is possible that the pregnancy resulted from intercourse under coercion or by mistake, and the *hadd* is averted by doubts. It has also been said that a woman may conceive without intercourse by semen entering her genital tract, either by her own action or by the action of another. This is why the pregnancy of a virgin has been imagined, and that has occurred.

As for the statements of the Companions, the reports from them differ. Sa'id related: Khalaf ibn Khalifa narrated to us, (p-٣٩٢) Hashim narrated to us, that a woman who had no husband was brought to Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and she was pregnant. Umar asked her, and she said: "I am a woman who sleeps heavily. A man had intercourse with me while I was asleep, and I did not awaken until he had finished." So he averted the *hadd* from her. Al-Bara' ibn Subra related from Umar that a pregnant woman was brought to him, and she claimed that she had been forced. He said: "Release her," and he wrote to the commanders of the armies that no one should be killed except with his permission.

It is also related from Ali and Ibn Abbas that they said: "If there is a 'perhaps' or 'maybe' in a *hadd*, then it is suspended." Al-Daraqutni related with his chain from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and Uqbah ibn Amir (may Allah be pleased with them all) that they said: "If the *hadd* is unclear to you, then avert it as much as you can." There is no disagreement that the *hadd* is averted by doubts, and they are present here. End of his exact words from *al-Mughni*.

Look also at the chains of these reports he mentioned from the Companions. This that he mentioned is the summary of what the majority argued with, who said that pregnancy does not establish fornication.

The one who restricts this (the author, may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: The more apparent of the two opinions of the scholars in my view is that fornication is not established by pregnancy alone, even if the woman is not known to have a husband or master, because pregnancy may occur without doubt without intercourse in the vagina. Indeed, a man may have intercourse with a woman between her thighs, her sexual desire is aroused, her fluid is discharged, and the man ejaculates, and his semen flows and enters her genital tract, so his semen meets her fluid, and she becomes pregnant without intercourse. This is observed and cannot be denied.

For this reason, the more sound view is that if a husband has intercourse with his wife between her thighs without penetrating her vagina, and a pregnancy then appears, he may not perform li'an (the oath of mutual condemnation) to deny that pregnancy. This is because his semen may flow into her vagina, and she may become pregnant from it. As for the statement of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "If the pregnancy or the confession is..." it was an act of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) on his part, because it appeared to him (may Allah be pleased with him) that pregnancy establishes zina (illicit intercourse), as confession and evidence do.

We have said that what appears more correct to us is the opposite of his view (may Allah be pleased with him), because we know that the existence of pregnancy does not necessarily imply penetration of the vagina. Rather, a woman may become pregnant without it. If pregnancy does not necessarily imply penetration of the vagina, there is no basis for establishing zina and enforcing the hadd (prescribed punishment) on the basis of a possibility that does not necessarily entail what requires the hadd, as you can see.

It is well known that hudud (prescribed punishments) are averted by doubts (shubuhat). This is the more correct view according to us, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

Branches related to this issue.

(p-393) The first branch: Know that those who held that the hadd is obligatory on the basis of pregnancy said: if that pregnant woman is a newcomer from other lands, and claims that her pregnancy is from a husband she left in her own country, then there is no hadd upon her according to them, and zina is not established against her by that pregnancy.

The second branch: Know that if a pregnancy appears in a woman and she claims that she was forced (mukrahah), her claim of coercion is not accepted by those who establish zina by pregnancy, unless her claim is supported by evidence that strengthens it, such as her coming forward crying out for help against the one who did this to her, or her coming clinging to a man whom she claims forced her, or her complaining about the one who did this to her before the pregnancy appeared.

Some Maliki scholars said: if her complaint against the man who did this to her is accompanied by the fact that the man she accuses is not known for righteousness, then there is no hadd upon her. But if the man she accuses is known for righteousness, chastity and piety, then it is not accepted from her against him.

Some Malikis said: if she does not name the man she claims forced her, she is subject to ta'zir (discretionary punishment), and she is not subject to hadd if she is known for righteousness and chastity.

* *

The third branch: Shaykh al-Hattab, in his commentary on the words of Khalil in his Maliki Mukhtasar: "or a woman under coercion," said the following text: He said in al-Tiraz, or at the end of the third part, in the chapter on the explanation of divorce and what its expressions entail, Ibn Abd al-Ghafur said: It is said that Abdullah ibn Isa was asked about a virgin girl whose guardian married her off, and her husband consummated the marriage with her, and she bore a child after four months. This was mentioned to her, and she said: "I was sleeping and I woke up to a wetness between my thighs." The husband stated that he had found her a virgin.

He ruled concerning her: she is not subject to hadd if she is known for chastity and good standing, and the marriage is annulled, and she is entitled to the full dowry, unless she knew of the pregnancy and deceived, in which case she is entitled to the amount of what he made lawful of her. End of quotation from al-Istighna. End of the words of al-Tiraz. End of what al-Hattab quoted. It supports that pregnancy may occur without intercourse that entails the hadd, as we have mentioned. Allah the Exalted knows best.

[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicating woman or an polytheist, and the fornicating woman is not married except by a fornicator or a polytheist; and that has been made unlawful for the believers.﴾

We have mentioned many times that among the kinds of clarification (bayan) contained in this blessed Book is that some scholars state an opinion regarding a verse, while within the same verse there is an indicator showing that this opinion is not valid. We mentioned this in the introduction to the book, and we mentioned earlier in the book many examples of this, and among the examples of this is this noble verse.

Its clarification: the scholars differed about what is meant by "nikah" (marriage/intercourse, here "nikah") in this verse. A group said: what is meant by nikah in this verse is the sexual intercourse (al-wat' — the act of intercourse) which is itself fornication (zina). Another group of the people of knowledge said: what is meant by nikah in this verse is the marriage contract ('aqd al-nikah). They said: it is not permissible for a chaste man to marry a fornicating woman, and vice versa. This opinion, that what is meant by nikah in the verse is marriage and not intercourse, has within the verse itself an indicator that shows its invalidity, and that indicator is the mention of the polytheist man and the polytheist woman in the verse; because a Muslim fornicator is not permitted to marry a polytheist woman, due to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10],

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not hold on to the ties of disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. Likewise, a Muslim fornicating woman is not permitted (p-418) to marry a polytheist man;

• due to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry polytheist men until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221].

So the marriage of a polytheist woman or a polytheist man is never lawful in any case. This is an indicator that what is meant by nikah in the verse we are dealing with is the intercourse which is fornication, not the marriage contract; because the marriage contract does not fit with the mention of the polytheist man and the polytheist woman. As for the claim that the marriage of a fornicator to a polytheist woman, and of a fornicating woman to a polytheist man, is abrogated (mansukh), it is manifestly untenable; because Surah "al-Nur" is Medinan, and there is no evidence that this was made lawful in Medina and then abrogated, and abrogation (naskh) necessarily requires evidence to which one must return.

* *

Issue related to this noble verse:

Know that the scholars differed on the permissibility of a chaste man marrying a fornicating woman, and a chaste woman marrying a fornicating man. A group of the people of knowledge, including the four imams (the three imams: Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa — the phrase as stands), held the permissibility of marrying a fornicating woman with makruh tanzihi (a reprehensible but not forbidden disliking) according to Malik and his companions, and those who agreed with them. The proponents of this view argued with evidence:

Among it: the generality of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], which by its generality includes the fornicating woman and the chaste woman; and the generality of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32] and so on, which by its generality also includes the fornicating woman and the chaste woman.

Among their evidence for this: the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: My wife does not turn away the hand of one who touches her. He said: 'Divorce her.' He said: I fear my soul will follow her. He said: 'Then enjoy her.'" Ibn Hajar said in "Bulugh al-Maram," after citing it with the wording we mentioned: it was narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Bazzar, and its men are trustworthy (thiqat); and al-Nasa'i narrated it through another route, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, with the wording: "Divorce her." He said: I cannot be patient without her. He said: "Then keep her." End quote from "Bulugh al-Maram." In this there is Ibn Hajar's explicit statement that its men are trustworthy, and by this you know that Ibn al-Jawzi's mention of this hadith among the fabricated (mawdu'at) hadiths is open to question. He mentioned it among the fabricated ones as mursal (with a missing companion) from Abu al-Zubayr, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: My wife... the hadith; and he also narrated it as mursal from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Hassan ibn 'Atiyya, both from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then he said: Abu Bakr al-Khallal interpreted it as referring to immorality, and this is not permissible; rather it is to be understood as her mismanagement of wealth, if the hadith were authentic.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: this hadith is not established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; it has no basis. End quote from Ibn al-Jawzi's "Mawdu'at." The great disagreement of scholars regarding the authentication and weakening of the said hadith is well known.

Al-Shawkani said in "Nayl al-Awtar": There is no doubt that the Arabs use such an expression to refer to a lack of chastity regarding fornication, meaning by the phrase mentioned the man's saying: "My wife does not turn away the hand of one who touches her." End quote. What al-Shawkani and others said is the apparent meaning; because the phrase "does not turn away the hand of one who touches" is more evident in indicating that she does not refuse anyone who wants from her what is not lawful, as is not hidden. So interpreting it as her mismanagement of wealth is not apparent, because applying the word "touching" (lamis) to taking wealth is not apparent, as you see.

The one who restricts this (its author), may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The hadith mentioned concerns a woman whose lack of chastity became evident while she was under a husband; and our discussion now is about the beginning of marriage, not its continuation, and there is a difference between the two matters, as you will see its clarification, Allah willing.

Then know that those who said that marrying a fornicating woman and a fornicating man is permissible answered the argument from the verse we are dealing with, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicating woman or a polytheist﴾ [al-Nur: 3], in two ways:

The first: that what is meant by nikah in the verse is the intercourse which is precisely fornication. They said: the purpose of the verse is to denounce fornication and to strongly deter from it; because the fornicator is not obeyed in his fornication by any women except one who is at the utmost baseness, either because she is a polytheist who does not regard the prohibition of fornication, or a fornicating woman, wicked and corrupt.

According to this view, the reference in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that has been made unlawful for the believers﴾ is to the intercourse which is fornication, may Allah protect us and our Muslim brothers from it, just as in the reverse; and according to this view there is no difficulty in the mention of the polytheist woman and the polytheist man.

The second way: their statement that what is meant by nikah in the verse is marriage, but this verse, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicating woman﴾ and so on, is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾ and so on [al-Nur: 32]. Among those who held that it was abrogated by it were Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Shafi'i. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this verse, and his words are: This is a report from Allah, may He be exalted, that the fornicator does not have intercourse except with a fornicating woman or a polytheist, i.e., no one obeys him in his desire for fornication except a fornicating woman who is disobedient or a polytheist (p-420) who does not regard that as forbidden; and likewise the fornicating woman is not married except by a fornicator, i.e., one who is disobedient through his fornication, or a polytheist who does not believe in its prohibition.

Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Habib ibn Abi 'Amra, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicating woman or a polytheist﴾ that he said: This is not about marriage; it is only intercourse: no one commits fornication with her except a fornicator or a polytheist. This is a sound chain (isnad) from him, and it has been narrated from him through more than one route; and it has been narrated from Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Dahhak, Makhul, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and others of similar meaning. End of the relevant portion, in its wording.

So you see that he began by stating that what is meant by nikah in the verse is intercourse, not marriage, and he mentioned its soundness from Ibn 'Abbas, whom the Prophet ﷺ prayed that Allah teach the interpretation of the Qur'an; and he attributed it to those among the great exegetes mentioned with him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is among the companions most knowledgeable in the tafsir of the Mighty Qur'an, and there is no doubt of his knowledge of the Arabic language.

So his statement regarding this noble verse that nikah in it is intercourse and not the contract indicates that this runs according to the eloquent Arabic style; so the claim that this interpretation is not valid in Arabic and is ugly is refuted by the statement of the sea of knowledge, Ibn 'Abbas, as you see.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this verse: It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and his companions that nikah in this verse means intercourse.

Know that al-Zajjaj's rejection of this view in this verse, I mean the view that nikah in it is intercourse, and his saying that nikah is not known in the Qur'an except in the sense of marriage, is refuted in two ways:

The first: that the Qur'an uses nikah in the sense of intercourse, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]; and it is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he explained His saying: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ as meaning that her marrying him is his having intercourse with her, when he said: "No, until you taste his honey and he tastes yours," and what is meant by tasting the honey is intercourse, as is well known.

The second way: the Arabs, in whose language the Qur'an was revealed, use nikah for intercourse, and it may also be the contract.

(p-421) They called the marriage contract nikah only because it is the cause of nikah, i.e., intercourse; and naming the effect and meaning its cause is well known in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, and it is what those who speak of metaphor call the metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), as is known to them in its proper place. Among the Arabs' use of nikah for intercourse is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"And a woman with a husband, our spears have made her marry (ankahat-ha) — she is lawful to whoever builds upon her, she was not divorced."

Because the "inkah" in the verse does not mean the marriage contract, since one does not contract marriage over captives; rather what is meant is intercourse by right of possession (milk al-yamin) and captivity along with disbelief. And from it also is his saying:

"And the daughter of a noble man — we have had intercourse with her (nakahna), and she had no suitor except the spear and its wielder."

So what is meant by nikah in this verse is intercourse by right of possession, not the contract, as he made clear by saying: "and she had no suitor except the spear and its wielder."

And his saying:

"When God waters a people with a fertilizing rain, may God not water the people of Kufa with rain — those who leave their wives in purity, and who have intercourse (al-nakihin) with the cattle on the banks of the Tigris."

And it is known that the intercourse of cattle does not mean marriage.

They said: among what indicates that nikah in the verse is other than marriage is that if its meaning in it were marriage, the one who marries a fornicating woman would have to receive the prescribed punishment (hadd), since he is a fornicator, and the fornicator must receive the prescribed punishment; and the scholars have agreed that one who marries a fornicating woman is not subjected to the prescribed punishment for fornication; and had he been a fornicator he would have been subjected to the prescribed punishment for fornication. So understand. This is the essence of the arguments of those who said that nikah in the verse is intercourse, and that marrying a chaste man to a fornicating woman is not forbidden, and the reverse.

* *

Another group of the people of knowledge said: it is not permissible for a fornicator to marry a chaste woman, nor the reverse; this is the view of Imam Ahmad, and it has been narrated from al-Hasan and Qatada. The proponents of this view argued with verses and hadiths.

Among the verses they cited is this verse we are dealing with, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicating woman or a polytheist, and the fornicating woman is not married except by a fornicator or a polytheist; and that has been made unlawful for the believers﴾ [al-Nur: 3]. They said: what is meant by nikah in this verse is marriage, and He has explicitly stated its prohibition in His saying: ﴿and that has been made unlawful for the believers.﴾ They said: the reference in His saying "that" is to the marriage of a fornicator to someone other than a fornicating woman or a polytheist; and this is a Qur'anic text prohibiting the marriage of a fornicator to a chaste woman, and the reverse.

And among the verses they cited as evidence is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [lawfully wed] chaste women from among the believing women, and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their bridal payments, seeking chastity, not unlawful intercourse, nor taking secret lovers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. They said: His saying ﴿seeking chastity, not unlawful intercourse﴾ means: chaste, not fornicators. From the implication of the opposite meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafah, the reasoning by contrast) of the verse, it is understood that it is not permissible to marry a fornicator (al-musafih, the one who is a zani) to a chaste believing woman, nor to a chaste woman of the People of the Book. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their guardians, and give them their bridal payments justly, as chaste women, not unlawful lovers, nor taking secret lovers﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. His saying ﴿as chaste women, not unlawful lovers﴾ means: chaste, not fornicators. From the implication of the opposite meaning of the verse, it is understood that if they were fornicators and not chaste, then their marriage would not be permitted.

Among the evidences of the proponents of this view is that all the narrations concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ are all about the contract of marriage (aqd al-nikah), and none of them is about sexual intercourse (al-wat'). It is established in the principles (al-usul) that the case that is the occasion of revelation is definitive in its inclusion (qat'iyyat al-dukhul). Moreover, the Sunnah has come with what supports the correctness of what they said regarding the verse, namely that nikah in it means marriage (al-tazwij), and that the fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress like himself. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The flogged fornicator does not marry except one like himself." Ibn Hajar said in Bulugh al-Maram regarding this hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "Narrated by Ahmad and Abu Dawud, and its narrators are trustworthy (thiqat)."

As for the narrations concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse:

Among them is what 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As narrated: "A man from among the Muslims asked permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding a woman called Umm Mahzul, who used to commit fornication, and she stipulated for him that she would spend on him. He said: So he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) permission, or mentioned her matter to him, and the Prophet of Allah recited to him: ﴿And the fornicatress, none marries her except a fornicator or an idolater﴾." Narrated by Ahmad.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar in his commentary on this hadith: "The author of al-Muntaqa attributed it to Ahmad alone, and the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr was also reported by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir and al-Awsat." He said in Majma' al-Zawa'id: "The narrators of Ahmad are trustworthy."

(p-423) Among them is the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father, from his grandfather: "That Marthad ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi used to carry prisoners in Makkah, and in Makkah there was a prostitute called 'Anaq, who was his female friend. He said: So I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, may I marry 'Anaq? He said: So he remained silent with me, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿And the fornicatress, none marries her except a fornicator or an idolater﴾. So he called me and recited it to me, and said: Do not marry her." Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar in his remarks on this hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, which was mentioned by the author of al-Muntaqa and attributed by him to Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi: "The hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb was graded hasan by al-Tirmidhi." Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir of this verse, cited the hadiths we have mentioned with their chains, and said regarding this hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb: "al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan gharib hadith, which we do not know except through this route. Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i have narrated it in the Book of Marriage of their Sunan through the hadith of 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Akhnas with it."

They said: These hadiths and others like them indicate that nikah in His saying ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ means marriage (al-tazwij), not intercourse (al-wat'), and the occasion of revelation is definitive in its inclusion, as is established in the principles. They said: And since the meaning intended by it is marriage, the prohibition of marrying a fornicating man or woman is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿And that has been made unlawful to the believers﴾.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Ma'ad, and his exact words are: "As for marrying a fornicatress, Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has explicitly stated its prohibition in Surah al-Nur, and He informed that whoever marries her is either a fornicator or an idolater. For he either commits to His ruling, and believes it to be obligatory upon him, or he does not. If he does not commit to it and does not believe it, then he is an idolater. And if he commits to it and believes it to be obligatory, but opposes it, then he is a fornicator. Then He explicitly stated its prohibition, saying: ﴿And that has been made unlawful to the believers﴾. And it is not hidden that the claim of abrogation (da'wa al-naskh) of the verse by His saying: ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32] is among the weakest things said, and weaker than it is interpreting nikah as zina." 

For the meaning of the verse would become: The fornicator does not commit fornication except with a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress is not committed with except by a fornicator or an idolater. The words of Allah should be safeguarded from such a thing. Likewise, interpreting the verse as referring to an idolatrous prostitute is extremely far from its wording and context. How, when He, Glorified is He, only permitted marrying free women and slave women on condition of ihsan, which is chastity, and said: (p-424) ﴿So marry them with the permission of their guardians, and give them their bridal payments justly, as chaste women, not unlawful lovers, nor taking secret lovers﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. He only permitted marrying them in this state and not in others. And this is not from the indication of implication (dalalat al-mafhum), for private parts (al-abdi') are originally under prohibition, so permission for them is confined to what the Shari'ah has come with, and whatever is beyond that remains under the original prohibition." End of the relevant point from the words of Ibn al-Qayyim.

These are the proofs we have mentioned, which are the arguments of those who prohibit the marriage of a fornicating man to a chaste woman, and likewise the reverse. Now that you know the statements of the scholars and their proofs on the issue of marrying a fornicatress and a fornicator, this is the discussion of their proofs.

As for the statement of Ibn al-Qayyim that interpreting zina in the verse as intercourse should be safeguarded from the Book of Allah, it is refuted by the fact that Ibn 'Abbas, who is among the most knowledgeable in the Arabic language and the meanings of the Qur'an, is authentically reported to have interpreted zina in the verse as intercourse. Had that been something the Book of Allah should be safeguarded from, Ibn 'Abbas would have safeguarded it from that, and would not have said it; and it was not hidden from him that it should be safeguarded from such a thing.

Ibn al-'Arabi said, regarding Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation of zina in the verse as intercourse: "It is a sound meaning," as transmitted by al-Qurtubi quoting him.

As for Ibn al-Qayyim's statement that we quoted: "If he does not commit to it and does not believe it, then he is an idolater," it may be said: Yes, he is an idolater, but an idolater is not permitted to marry a believing fornicatress. Your apparent statement implies that this is permissible, and it is not permissible. So the problem of mentioning the idolater, male and female, remains as an objection to the view that nikah in the verse means marriage, as you see.

As for Ibn al-Qayyim's statement in his words: "And this is not from the category of implication (dalalat al-mafhum), for private parts are originally under prohibition, so permission is confined to what the Shari'ah has come with," it may be said: Texts of general scope have come indicating the permissibility of marrying a fornicatress, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], which by its generality includes the fornicatress and the chaste woman, and the fornicator and the chaste man. And His saying: ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾ [al-Nur: 32], which by its generality also includes all those mentioned. For this reason Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: The verse ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾ abrogates His saying ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress﴾, and al-Shafi'i said: The statement regarding that is as Sa'id said, that it is abrogated by it.

From what we have mentioned, it becomes clear that the indication of His saying ﴿as chaste women, not unlawful lovers﴾ upon the intended point of this discussion is from the category of implication (mafhum), as we explained shortly before, because the general texts mentioned cannot have their generality specified except by an evidence, whether explicit (mantuq) or implicit (mafhum), as was previously clarified.

As for the statement of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Shafi'i that the verse ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾ is abrogated by ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾, it is far-fetched, because what is established in the principles of al-Shafi'i, Malik and Ahmad is that it is not valid to abrogate the specific (khass) by the general ('amm), and that the specific takes precedence over the general absolutely, whether its revelation came before or after. It is known that the verse ﴿And marry the single ones among you﴾ is more general, absolutely, than the verse ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress﴾. So claiming that it abrogates it is impermissible according to the established principles of the three imams mentioned. Abrogation is permitted only according to the established principles of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, as we previously clarified in Surah al-An'am. It may be answered regarding the claim of Sa'id and al-Shafi'i of abrogation, that they understood it from a contextual indicator in the verse: namely, that it did not restrict the free single ones (al-ayama al-ahrar) with righteousness, but restricted with righteousness only the single ones among the slaves and slave-girls. For this reason, after the verse, He said: ﴿And the righteous among your male and female slaves﴾ [al-Nur: 32].

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: This noble verse is among the most difficult of verses to verify. For interpreting nikah in it as marriage does not fit the mention of the idolatress and the idolater, and interpreting nikah in it as intercourse does not fit the related hadiths that are connected with the verse, for they specify that the intended meaning of nikah in the verse is marriage. I know of no clear way out of this difficulty in this verse except with some strain, namely that the most sound of the views among the usulis, as Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah set out in his treatise on the sciences of the Qur'an, attributing it to the great scholars of the four schools, is the permissibility of carrying a homonym (mushtarak) on both of its meanings or its meanings. So you may say: The thieves raided the eye (ayn) of Zayd last night, meaning by that that they blinded his seeing eye, dried up his flowing spring, and stole his eye which is his gold or silver.

Knowing this, be aware that nikah is a homonym between intercourse and marriage, contrary to those who claim it is a literal meaning in one and a metaphor in the other, as we have indicated earlier. If it is permissible to carry a homonym on both of its meanings, then nikah in the verse is carried on both intercourse and marriage together, and the mention of the idolatress and the idolater is in the explanation of nikah as intercourse rather than contract. This is the kind of strain we have pointed to. And Allah knows best.

(p-426) Most scholars hold that marrying a fornicatress is permissible, and those who prohibit it are fewer. You have known the proofs of all of them.

* *

Branches (furu') related to this issue:

The first branch: Know that whoever marries a woman he thinks is chaste, and then she commits fornication while she is under his marital bond, the more apparent of the two opinions is that it is a marriage that is not annulled, and it is not forbidden for him to continue in marriage to her. This was said by some of those who prohibited marrying a fornicatress, distinguishing between continuing in marriage with her and beginning it. Those who said this relied on the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas al-Jushami, may Allah be pleased with him, that he witnessed the Farewell Pilgrimage with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he praised Allah, extolled Him, and reminded and admonished, then said: "Be good to women, for they are with you as captives; you have no authority over them except that, unless they commit a clear immorality. If they do that, then forsake them in their beds and strike them with a light strike that does not leave a mark. If they obey you, then do not seek a way against them."

Al-Shawkani said regarding this hadith of 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas: "Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi narrated it, and al-Tirmidhi declared it sahih." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in al-Isti'ab in the biography of the aforementioned 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas: "And his hadith in the sermon is sahih," end quote. His hadith in the sermon is this hadith, as evidenced by his saying: "He praised Allah and extolled Him, and reminded and admonished," and this reminding and admonishing is the sermon, as is well known.

Among the evidences for the aforementioned hadith is that which says: "A man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Indeed my wife does not turn away the hand of one who touches her. He said: Divorce her. He said: I am attached to her. He said: Keep her." We have explained the discussion regarding its chain, and that it concerns continuing in marriage, not beginning marriage, and that there is a difference between them. By this you know that the view of whoever says that if his wife commits fornication her marriage is annulled and she becomes forbidden to him is contrary to the verification of the matter. And Allah knows best.

**Section Two:** Know that the more correct of the two opinions of the scholars, in my view, is that it is not permissible to marry a pregnant woman who conceived from fornication before she gives birth. Rather, it is not permissible to marry her until she delivers her child. This differs from a group of scholars who said: it is permissible to marry her while she is pregnant. This is related from al-Shafi'i and others, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa. Their reasoning is that a man marrying a woman pregnant by someone else involves watering another's crop with another's water, and that is impermissible. The proof for this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. Nothing is excluded from the generality of this verse except what is excluded by a proof to which one must return. So it is not permissible to marry a pregnant woman until the term of her waiting period (iddah) ends. Allah has explicitly stated that the term of pregnant women is until they deliver their burden. Therefore, this generality must be upheld, and nothing is excluded from it except what is excluded by a proof from the Book or the Sunnah.

**Section Three:** Know that the more correct of the two opinions of the scholars, in my view, is that if the male and female fornicators repent from fornication, regret what occurred between them, and intend not to return to the sin, then their marriage is permissible. So it is permissible for him to marry her after their repentance, and it is permissible for others to marry them after repentance, because the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin. The proof for this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse—and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents and believes and does righteous work; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 68–70]. In this verse, the Exalted has explicitly stated that those who commit fornication, and those mentioned with them, if they repent, believe, and do righteous work, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. This indicates that repentance from fornication removes its effect. Those who said that whoever fornicates with a woman is absolutely forbidden to her, even if they both repent and reform, their view contradicts the careful investigation. Reports have come from the Companions permitting his marriage to the one he fornicated with if they both repent. One of the Companions gave an example of a man who stole something from another man's orchard, and afterwards bought the orchard. What he stole from it was unlawful for him, and what he bought from it is lawful for him. Likewise, what he obtained from the woman unlawfully is unlawful for him, and what he obtains from her after repentance and marriage is lawful for him. And Allah knows best.

And know that the view of one who rejects using the verse ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] as evidence, saying that it was revealed concerning disbelievers and not Muslims, is refuted by the principle that the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the cause (sabab). I have clarified its evidences from the authentic Sunnah many times. And Allah knows best.

**Section Four:** Know that those who said it is permissible for a chaste man to marry a fornicating woman do not necessarily imply that the chaste husband of a fornicating woman is a dayyuth (a man who tolerates immorality among his womenfolk), because he only marries her to protect her, guard her, and prevent her from committing what is not befitting, by firmly watching over her constantly. When he goes out, he locks the doors behind her and entrusts her to someone who will guard her after him. He enjoys her company while being extremely jealous and protective of her against suspicion. If something occurs from her of which he has no knowledge, despite his striving to safeguard and protect her, then there is nothing upon him for it, and he is not a dayyuth, as is well known. You have learned from what has passed that most scholars hold that it is permissible for a chaste man to marry a fornicating woman, as is the reverse, and that a group said this is prohibited.

(p-428) Our view on this issue is that a Muslim should not marry except a chaste, modest woman, due to the verses we have mentioned and the hadiths, and it is supported by the hadith: "Win the one with religion, may your hands be dust." And Allah knows best.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-352) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah an-Nur

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress is not married except by a fornicator or an idolater; and that has been made unlawful to the believers﴾. This noble verse indicates the prohibition of marrying fornicators and fornicatresses to the chaste men and women. The proof for this is His saying: ﴿chaste, not unlawfully fornicating﴾ [an-Nisa: 25], and His saying: ﴿chaste, not unlawfully fornicating﴾ [an-Nisa: 24].

Other verses have come whose generality indicates the opposite, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And marry the unmarried among you﴾ [an-Nur: 32], and His saying: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [an-Nisa: 24].

The answer to this is disputed, a dispute based on the disagreement over the ruling on a chaste man marrying a fornicatress or a chaste woman marrying a fornicator. Whoever says it is forbidden says: this verse specifies the generality of ﴿And marry the unmarried among you﴾ and the generality of ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾.

Those who say there is no prohibition, and they are the majority, answered with several answers:

Among them: it has been abrogated by His saying: ﴿And marry the unmarried among you﴾. The author of al-Itqan (al-Suyuti) limited himself to abrogation (naskh). Among those who said abrogation: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Shafi'i.

Among them: the marriage (nikah) in this verse means intercourse (wati'). Accordingly, the meaning of the verse is that a fornicator is not obeyed in his act and does not share his purpose except by a fornicatress like him, or an idolatress who does not see the prohibition of fornication as unlawful.

Among them: this is particular, because it was about prostitutes, where a man would marry one of them on the condition that she spends on him from what she earned through fornication. This is because that was the cause of the revelation of the verse. So some claimed that it is specific to that cause, based on His saying: ﴿And lawful for you﴾ (the verse), and His saying: ﴿And marry the unmarried﴾ (the verse). This is the weakest of them, and Allah knows best.

(p-353) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women, and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾.

This noble verse was revealed concerning the innocence of the Mother of the Believers, 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from what she was accused of. This supports what 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said, that its meaning is: wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women, and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women. That is, if 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, were not good, Allah would not have made her a wife of the best of the good, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.

On this basis, the noble verse apparently contradicts His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieved: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾ — to His saying — ﴿with those who enter [the Fire]﴾ [at-Tahrim: 10].

And His saying also: ﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believed: the wife of Pharaoh﴾ (the verse) [at-Tahrim: 11].

For the first verse indicates the wickedness of the two disbelieving wives, even though their husbands were among the best of the good, namely Noah and Lot, peace be upon them and upon our Prophet. The second verse indicates the goodness of Pharaoh's wife despite the wickedness of her husband.

The answer is that there are two views of the scholars on the meaning of the verse:

The first: this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and it is related from Mujahid, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Habib ibn Abi Thabit, and al-Dahhak, as transmitted from them by Ibn Kathir, and chosen by Ibn Jarir: that its meaning is wicked words are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked words, and good words are for good men, and good men are for good words. That is, whatever words the hypocrites attributed to 'A'ishah of wicked speech, they are more deserving of it, and she is more deserving of innocence and purity than they are. For this reason Allah said: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾ [an-Nur: 26]. On this view there is no contradiction at all between the verses.

The second view: it is what we previously mentioned from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, and on it the difficulty among the verses is evident. What appears to its compiler, may Allah pardon him, is that His saying ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men﴾ to the end, on this view, is of the general that is specified, by the evidence of the wife of Noah and the wife of Pharaoh.

(p-354) On this basis, it is generally the case that each of the good women, the good men, the wicked women, and the wicked men is paired with its own kind and form which suits it in wickedness or goodness. However, Allah may sometimes pair a wicked woman with a good man, like the wife of Noah and Lot, or a good woman with a wicked man, like the wife of Pharaoh, for a profound wisdom, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieved﴾ and His saying: ﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believed﴾, together with His saying: ﴿And these examples We present to the people, and none understands them except those of knowledge﴾ [al-Ankabut: 43].

This indicates that the pairing of a wicked woman with a good man, or a good woman with a wicked man, contains a wisdom which none understands except the scholars. In the pairing of a wicked woman with a good man, the wisdom is to make clear to the people that kinship with the righteous does not benefit a person; rather, his own deeds benefit him. Do you not see that the greatest thing a person defends is his wife, and the most honored of creation before Allah are His messengers? So the entry of the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot into the Fire, as Allah said: ﴿So they availed them nothing against Allah, and it was said: Enter the Fire with those who enter﴾ [at-Tahrim: 10], contains the greatest admonition and the most powerful warning against being deceived by kinship with the righteous and the eminent, for a person only benefits from his own deeds: ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ (the verse) [an-Nisa: 123].

Likewise, the entry of Pharaoh's wife into Paradise indicates that a person who is compelled by necessity to associate with disbelievers, without his choice, and does his deeds well and is patient in upholding his religion, will enter Paradise, and the wickedness of those he associates with and mixes with will not harm him. Thus the wicked person is wicked even if he associates with the righteous, like the wives of Noah and Lot, and the good person is good even if he associates with the wicked, like the wife of Pharaoh. But associating with the wicked is not permissible by choice, as other evidences indicate.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 4 (part 1 of 7):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever after. And those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, in this verse: "yarmoona" (accuse) means: they accuse chaste women of fornication explicitly, or with what necessarily implies fornication, such as denying the paternity of a chaste woman's child from its father, for if the child is not from its father, it is from fornication. This accusation is the one for which Allah, may He be exalted, has prescribed three rulings:

The first: flogging the accuser eighty lashes.

The second: the non-acceptance of his testimony.

The third: his being judged as defiantly disobedient (fasiq).

If it is said: Where is the evidence from the Qur'an that the meaning of ﴿accuse chaste women﴾ in this verse is accusing them of explicit fornication, or of what necessarily implies it, such as denying lineage?

The answer: Two indicators from the Qur'an point to this:

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then do not produce four witnesses﴾ after His saying ﴿accuse chaste women﴾. It is known that no accusation requires four witnesses to establish it except fornication. Whoever says that sodomy (liwat) has the ruling of fornication applies the rulings of this verse to the one who commits sodomy.

We have already presented the rulings on the one who commits sodomy in full in Surat Hud, as we indicated not far back.

The second indicator: the mention of chaste women after the mention of fornicators, in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The adulterer does not marry except an adulteress﴾ (the verse), and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾. So the mention of chaste women after the mention of fornicators indicates their chastity (ihsan), i.e., their abstinence from fornication, and that those who accuse them accuse them only of fornication. We have already presented all the meanings that are intended by "muhsanat" (chaste women) in the Qur'an, and illustrated all of them from the Qur'an in Surat an-Nisa', in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the chaste women among the women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾ [An-Nisa' 24]. We mentioned there that among the meanings intended by "muhsanat" is that they are chaste and not fornicators, as in His saying: ﴿chaste, not unchaste﴾ [An-Nisa' 24], i.e., chaste women who are not fornicators. Of this meaning is His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾, i.e., the chaste ones. The use of "muhsanat" for chaste women is well known in the speech of the Arabs. Of it is the saying of Jarir:

"So do not feel safe from the tribe of Qays, for they are the sons of chaste women whose wombs were not defiled."

The use of "ramy" (throwing/accusing) for one person's accusing another with his tongue, with ugly speech, is well known in the speech of the Arabs. Of it is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ahmar al-Bahili:

"He accused me of a matter from which I, and my father, were innocent, and out of the well he accused me."

So his saying "ramani bi-amr" means: he accused me with ugly speech. And in the poetry of Imru' al-Qays or another: "And the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand."

Know that this noble verse is, in general, clarified from three aspects:

The first aspect: the two Qur'anic indicators that show that what is meant by "ramy" in His saying ﴿yarmoona al-muhsanat﴾ is accusation of fornication, or what necessarily implies it, such as denying lineage, as we have clarified shortly before.

The second aspect: the general wording of this verse apparently includes a husband who accuses his wife of fornication. But Allah, may He be exalted, has shown that a husband who accuses his wife of fornication is excluded from the generality of this verse, and that if the witnesses do not come, they perform mutual cursing (li'an). This is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who accuse their wives and have no witnesses except themselves﴾ (the verse) [An-Nur: 6].

Its content is that when a husband accuses his wife of fornication and has no witness other than himself, meaning he is unable to produce evidence testifying to the fornication with which he accused her, he testifies four testimonies, saying in each of them: "I testify by Allah that I am truthful regarding what I accused her of, of fornication." Then in the fifth he says: "The curse of Allah be upon me if I am lying concerning her in what I accused her of." The flogging, the non-acceptance of testimony, and the fisq are lifted from him by these testimonies. She testifies four testimonies by Allah, saying in each of them: "I testify by Allah that he is lying regarding what he accused me of, of fornication." Then she says in the fifth: "The wrath of Allah be upon me if he is truthful regarding what he accused me of, of fornication," as is clear from the text of the verse.

The third aspect: Allah has here stated the punishment for one who accuses chaste women in this world, but has not stated what is prepared for him in the Hereafter. However, He has stated in this noble surah what is prepared for him in this world and the Hereafter of Allah's punishment, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unheedless, believing women are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾ ﴿on the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them for what they used to do﴾ ﴿That Day Allah will pay them in full their due reward, and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾ [An-Nur: 23-25]. In this last verse He added that they are believing women, unheedless, to clarify their noble attributes.

His description of the chaste women in this verse as "unheedless" is praise of them, that they are sound of heart, pure of hearts, such that suspicion does not occur to their hearts because of the goodness of their inner selves; there is in them no cunning or deceit, because they have not experienced the matter, so they do not perceive what experienced women full of cunning and guile perceive. This kind of soundness of heart and its clarity from suspicion is among the finest praise. The Arabs call those who possess it by the name "bulh" (naive), praising them, not blaming them. Of it is the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Plump of the bag, its ropes tight, a naive one, not hasty in her divisions."

And the saying of another:

"I have indeed played with a young girl, inclined, naive, who reveals to me her secrets."

And the saying of another:

"I knew her, Hind, and Hind is innocent, far from indecency, naive of evening, sleepy. Plump of forenoon, inclined, swaying, for her speech enchants the forbearing one, gentle."

It is apparent that His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment, on the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them for what they used to do﴾ [An-Nur: 23-24], its place is in the case where they do not repent and reform. If they repent and reform, none of that threat befalls them. What indicates this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Except those who repent﴾ (the verse).

The general wording of the texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicates that whoever turns in repentance to Allah from his sin with sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh), He accepts it from him and expiates his sin, even if it is one of the major sins. By this you know that the saying of a group of eminent exegetes, that the verse: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses﴾, in which Allah made repentance possible by His saying ﴿Except those who repent﴾, is general, and that the verse: ﴿Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unheedless, believing women are cursed in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [An-Nur: 23], is specific to those who accused 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, or others of the specific wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and that whoever accuses them has no repentance, is contrary to the verification. And Allah knows best.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse.

The first issue: It is not hidden that the verse explicitly addresses only the accusation of females by males; for that is the explicit wording of His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾. All Muslims have agreed that the accusation of males against males, or females against females, or females against males, is no different from what the verse explicitly addresses, namely the accusation of females by males, since there is certainty that no distinction exists among all of them.

We have already presented the clarification of this and the refutation of the Zahiri position on it, along with the clarification of many of its parallels in Surat al-Anbiya', in our lengthy discussion of His saying: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field﴾ (the verse) [Al-Anbiya' 78].

* *

The second issue: Know that what is established in the principles of the Malikis, the Shafi'is, and the Hanbalis is that an exception (istithna') that comes after conjoined sentences, or conjoined single terms, returns to all of them, unless there is a proof from transmission or reason that restricts it to some of them, contrary to Abu Hanifa, who holds that the exception returns only to the last sentence. To this issue the author of "Maraqi as-Su'ud" alluded, in his saying:

"Whatever contains conjunction before the exception, all of it follows, without proof from reason or from revelation. And the truth is separation, not joining."

Therefore, if a person says: "This house is a waqf for the poor and the needy, and the Banu Zuhrah, and the Banu Tamim, except the wicked among them," he excludes from the waqf the wicked of all of them, since the exception returns to all. Contrary to Abu Hanifa, who holds that it returns to the last, so according to him only the wicked of the last group is excluded. For this reason, according to him, the exception in this verse returns only to the last sentence, which is: ﴿And those are the defiantly disobedient, except those who repent﴾, for the fisq has left them. He does not say: "And do not accept their testimony ever, except those who repent, so accept their testimony." Rather, he says: the testimony of the accuser is never accepted, even if he repents and reforms, and becomes the most upright person of his time, because the exception returns, according to him, to the last sentence.

Among the scholars who said the same as Abu Hanifa's view are: the judge Shurayh, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Makhul, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Jabir. And al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak said: his testimony is not accepted unless he confesses on himself to lying. Ibn Kathir reported this.

The majority of scholars, including the three Imams, said: the exception in the verse also returns to His saying: ﴿and do not accept their testimony ever,﴾ and that the accuser, if he repents and reforms, his testimony is accepted. As for His saying: ﴿flog them eighty lashes,﴾ the exception does not return to it, because the accuser who repents and reforms does not have the hadd for accusation dropped from him by repentance.

Thus it is established that the last sentence, His saying: ﴿And those are the defiantly disobedient,﴾ is one to which the exception returns without disagreement; that the first sentence, ﴿flog them eighty lashes,﴾ is one to which the exception does not return according to the consensus of the majority of scholars, and none has opposed it except one who deviated; and that the middle sentence, His saying: ﴿and do not accept their testimony ever,﴾ is one to which the exception returns according to the majority of scholars, including the three Imams, contrary to Abu Hanifa. In our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" we mentioned that what appears to us in the issue of the exception after conjoined sentences or conjoined single terms is what some later scholars mentioned, such as Ibn al-Hajib among the Malikis, al-Ghazali among the Shafi'is, and al-Amidi among the Hanbalis: that the ruling regarding an exception that follows conjoined items is suspension (waqf), and it is not judged to return to all, nor to the last, except by a proof.

We said that this is the more apparent view because Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ (the verse) [An-Nisa' 59].

When we refer the dispute in this issue to Allah, we find the Qur'an indicating what we have mentioned as the more apparent according to us, which is suspension. This is because some verses do not have the exception return to the first, and some do not have it return to the last, which shows that its return to what precedes it is not a consistent rule.

Among the examples of this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then freeing a believing slave, and blood-money delivered to his family, except that they forgo it﴾ [An-Nisa' 92]. The exception in this verse returns to the blood-money only, because the demand for it drops by the forgiveness of its rightful recipient, and it does not return to freeing the slave by consensus, because the forgiveness of the recipients of the blood-money does not drop the expiation (kaffarah) for killing by mistake.

Among the examples of this is the verse of "al-Nur" (24:4) before us. The exception in His words, ﴿except those who repent﴾, does not refer back to His words, ﴿flog them eighty lashes﴾, as we mentioned just before.

Another example is His words, exalted is He: ﴿So if they turn away, seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them a friend or a helper, except those who reach a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 89-90]. The exception in His words, ﴿except those who reach a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾, does not refer to the last clause, which is the closest of the clauses mentioned to it, namely His words, exalted is He, ﴿and do not take from among them a friend or a helper﴾ [al-Nisa': 89]. This is because it is not permissible to take a friend or helper from among the disbelievers, even if they have reached a people between you and whom there is a covenant. There is no disagreement about this. Rather, the exception refers to the first two clauses, namely His words, exalted is He, ﴿seize them and kill them﴾ [al-Nisa': 89], meaning: seize them by capture and kill them, except those who reach a people between you and whom there is a covenant. For you may not seize them by capture or kill them, because the covenant that exists for those who have reached those people prevents their capture and killing. This is as Hilal ibn Uwaymir al-Aslami stipulated in his treaty with the Prophet (ﷺ), because this verse was revealed concerning him, and concerning Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji, and concerning the Banu Judhaymah ibn Amir. If the exception sometimes does not refer to the closest clauses to it in the Great Qur'an, which is at the highest level of inimitability, it becomes clear that its reference to all of them is not necessary, nor to the last one. The more apparent position is to pause until one knows, by evidence, which of the preceding coordinated clauses it refers to. It is not far-fetched that if it is stripped of contextual indicators and evidences, it would be apparent that it refers to all of them.

We have expanded the discussion of this issue in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), and so we have summarised it here. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

The third issue: Know that whoever slanders a person with something other than fornication or denial of lineage, such as saying to him, "O corrupt one!" or "O eater of usury!" and similar kinds of abuse, is liable to ta'zir (discretionary punishment, a penalty not fixed by the Shari'ah), and it is determined by what the ruler sees as a deterrent for him and for those like him, from among the punishments, without any specification of a fixed amount from the Shari'ah. Some scholars said: the ta'zir must not reach the measure of the hadd (the prescribed punishment). Some scholars said: the ta'zir is according to the ruler's ijtihad (independent judgement) regarding what he sees as a deterrent, in an unrestricted way. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

(p-434) The fourth issue: Know that the majority of scholars hold that if a slave slanders a free person, he is flogged forty lashes, because it is a hadd that is halved by slavery, like the hadd for fornication. Al-Qurtubi said: It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb that he is flogged eighty lashes. Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad flogged a slave who had slandered a free person eighty lashes, and al-Awza'i also held this view. The majority argued with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if they commit a flagrant immorality, then for them is half the punishment for free married women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. Others said: We understood from that verse that the hadd for fornication is for Allah, and that it may be lighter for the one upon whom Allah's blessings are few, and more severe for the one upon whom Allah's blessings are great.

As for the hadd for slander, it is a right of the human being, which becomes due because of an offence against the honour of the one slandered. An offence does not differ by slavery or freedom. They may say: If it differed, it would have been mentioned, as in the case of fornication.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: What the scholars of the regions hold is the first view, and I say the same. The words of al-Qurtubi end.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The more evidentially sound of the two views in my opinion is that if a slave slanders a free person, he is flogged eighty lashes, not forty, even though this opposes the majority of the scholars. We only preferred flogging him eighty because the slave is included in the generality of His words: ﴿flog them eighty lashes﴾, and it is not possible to exclude him from this generality except by an evidence. No evidence has come to exclude the slave from this generality, neither from the Book, nor the Sunnah, nor analogy. The text was only sent down to halve the hadd for a slave woman in the case of fornication, and the scholars extended it to the male slave by the common cause of slavery. But fornication is not slander. As for slander, no text has come regarding it specifically, nor any analogy.

As for analogising slander to fornication, it is an analogy in the presence of a difference (al-fariq) that distinguishes them: slander is an offence against the honour of a specific person, and deterring offences against honour is a right of the human being, so the slave is deterred just as the free person is deterred. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Caution (tanbih):

We have already mentioned in the discussion of His words, exalted is He, ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾ (the verse) [al-Ma'idah: 32], in Surat al-Ma'idah, that a free person who slanders a slave is not subjected to the hadd for him. This is established in the two Sahihs from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever slanders his slave with fornication, the hadd will be enforced upon him on the Day of Resurrection, unless it is as he said." And his (ﷺ) words in this authentic hadith: "the hadd will be enforced upon him on the Day of Resurrection" indicate that it is not enforced upon him in this world, and this is so. There is no dispute about this among those whose opinion is considered among the people of knowledge.

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: That was only in the Hereafter, because ownership is removed, and the noble and the lowly, the free and the slave are equal, and no one has any superiority except by piety. When that is the case, people are equal in the hadds and in inviolability, and retaliation is exacted for each one from the other, unless the wronged party forgives. The point of the purpose from the words of al-Qurtubi ends.

* *

The fifth issue: Know that the scholars agreed that if he explicitly states fornication in slandering him, it is slander and an accusation that necessitates the hadd. As for if he speaks by allusion (ta'rid) and does not state the slander explicitly, and his allusion is understood from it by indicators to mean that he intends to slander him, such as his saying: "As for me, I am not an adulterer, nor is my mother an adulteress," or "You are not an adulterer, [for] people do not know you for fornication," or "O son of the lawful one (halal)," or similar to that.

The people of knowledge differed: Is slander by allusion that conveys slander necessarily slander, even if he does not state it explicitly, or is he not subjected to the hadd until he states the slander explicitly, in a clear way with no possibility of another meaning? A group of the people of knowledge held that allusion does not necessitate the hadd, even if it is understood from it that slander is intended, unless he admits that he intended slander by it.

Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": This view is the narration of Hanbal from Imam Ahmad, and it is the apparent words of al-Kharaqi, and the preference of Abu Bakr. It was said by Ata', Amr ibn Dinar, Qatadah, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), and Ibn al-Mundhir. The proponents of this view argued with the Book and the Sunnah.

As for the Book, it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you imply of a proposal to women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235]. He, exalted is He, distinguished between explicit statement and allusion for the woman in waiting (iddah). They said: Allah did not distinguish between the two in His Book, except because there is a difference between them. If they were the same, He would not have distinguished between them in His Book.

As for the Sunnah: the hadith agreed upon, which we have mentioned repeatedly, concerning the man who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: "My wife has given birth to a black boy," which is an allusion to denying him (as his son). The Prophet (ﷺ) did not make this slander, nor did he call them to li'an. Rather, he said to the man: "Do you have camels?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What are their colours?" He said: "Red." He said: "Is there any grey (awraq) among them?" He said: "Indeed, there are grey ones among them." He said: "From where did that come to them?" He said: "Perhaps a hereditary trait (irq) pulled it out." He said: "And this black boy, perhaps a hereditary trait pulled him out." They said: Because allusion is open to another meaning besides slander, and every statement that bears two meanings is not slander. This is the essence of the argument of those who said that slander by allusion does not necessitate the hadd, and that the hadd is only necessitated by explicit slander.

Another group of the people of knowledge held that slander by allusion necessitates the hadd, and this is the view of Malik and his companions. Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": al-Athram and others narrated from Imam Ahmad that the one who alludes to slander is subject to the hadd. He said: This was narrated from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Ishaq said so as well. He said: Ma'mar said: Umar used to flog the hadd for allusion. End.

The proponents of this view argued with evidences, among them what al-Qurtubi mentioned. He said: The evidence for what Malik said is that the purpose of the hadd for slander is only to remove the disgrace that the slanderer inflicted on the one slandered. When disgrace is produced by allusion, it must be slander, just as explicit statement is, and reliance is on understanding. Allah, exalted is He, has said, relating about the people of Shu'ayb that they said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾ [Hud: 87], meaning: the foolish, the misguided. So they alluded to him with abuse through words whose apparent meaning is praise, according to one of the interpretations, as passed in Surat Hud. And Allah, exalted is He, said about Abu Jahl: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. And Allah, exalted is He, said about those who slandered Maryam that they said: ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother a prostitute﴾ [Maryam: 28]. They praised her father and negated prostitution (bighà', i.e. fornication) from her mother, and they alluded to Maryam by that. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and for their disbelief and their saying against Maryam a great slander﴾ [al-Nisa': 156]. Their disbelief is well known, and the great slander is their allusion to her. That is: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil, and your mother was not a prostitute﴾, meaning: you are the opposite of both of them, and you have brought this child. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?" Say, "Allah. And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error"﴾ [Saba': 24]. From this statement it was understood that it means that the disbelievers are not upon guidance and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is upon guidance. Thus, from this allusion was understood what is understood from its explicit form. End of the point of purpose from al-Qurtubi's words, with slight rewording for clarity of the intended meaning.

The summary of al-Qurtubi's words mentioned: Among the evidences of those who say that the hadd is necessitated by allusion are Quranic verses, and he explained how they indicate this, as you have seen. He also mentioned that among their evidences is that the disgrace that reaches the one slandered is the same as that from explicit statement, and so the two must be equal. He mentioned that among their evidences is that reliance is on understanding, and allusion is understood as slander, so it must be like the explicit statement.

Among their evidences that the hadd is necessitated by allusion is some of the narrations from some of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": Because Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he consulted them about the one who said to his companion, "I am not an adulterer, nor is my mother an adulteress," they said: "He has praised his father and mother." Umar said: "He has alluded to his companion, and flog him the hadd." Ma'mar said: Umar used to flog the hadd for allusion. Al-Athram narrated that Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, flogged a man who said to another, "O son of the one who smells of meat (shamm al-wadhr)," alluding to his mother's fornication. Al-Wadhr is the rotten pieces of meat, and it alludes to being sodomised by men. Examine the chains of narration (asanid) of these narrations.

Among the evidences of the people of this view is that a kinaya (implicit expression) with an indicator directing it to one of its possible meanings is like an explicit statement which admits only that meaning. For this reason divorce occurs by kinaya. If that was not in a state of dispute, and no indicator directing it to slander exists, there is no doubt that it is not slander. End of the words from "al-Mughni."

Then the author of "al-Mughni" said: Abu Bakr Abd al-Aziz mentioned that Abu Abd Allah retracted from the view of the obligation of the hadd for allusion, meaning Abu Abd Allah, the Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him. Al-Qurtubi said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, imprisoned al-Hutay'ah when he said:

"Leave noble deeds, do not travel in pursuit of them,
and sit, for you are the one who eats and clothes himself."

Because he compared him to women, in that they are fed, given drink, and clothed. Similar examples are many, among them the words of al-Hutay'ah or al-Najashi:

"A tribe that does not break a covenant of protection,
and does not wrong people by even a mustard seed."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 4 (part 3 of 7):

It is related that when ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) heard this satire, he took it as praise and said: "Would that the family of al-Khattab were like that!" When the poet later said:

*"And they come to the water only in the evening, when the drawers of water have turned away from every watering place."*

ʿUmar said again: "Would that the family of al-Khattab were like that!" The outward meaning of this poetry resembles praise, and for this reason they mentioned that ʿUmar wished for the satire it contained to apply to his own household, because to him it was praise, whereas its author intends blame, without any dispute. This is shown by the beginning and the end of the poem. The beginning of the verses is his saying:

*"When Allah has enmity toward a people of baseness and abasement, He has enmity toward the sons of al-ʿAjlan, the kinsmen of Ibn Muqbil."*

*"A tribe that cannot be betrayed..."* (the verse continues).

And at the end of his poem:

*"Al-ʿAjlan was named only for his saying: 'Take the bowl and milk, O slave, and hurry.'"*

That such verses are an allusion to blame is beyond doubt. Likewise the saying of al-Hutay'a:

*"Leave generosity, do not depart seeking its pursuit..."*

with which he satirised al-Zibriqan ibn Badr al-Tamimi, as some historians have mentioned. As for what al-Qurtubi (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned in the passage we quoted from him, that the great slander they uttered against Mary was their allusion to her by saying: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾ [Maryam 19:28], this is not definitively fixed by that alone, because Allah, exalted and majestic, related of them that they said to her something other than that, and it is closer to explicit mention of indecency than what al-Qurtubi mentioned. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said: "O Mary, you have certainly come up with something monstrous."﴾ [Maryam 19:27]. Their saying to her, ﴿you have certainly come up with something monstrous﴾, at the very time she came carrying the child, is very clearly an indication that they intended to accuse her, as you see.
