As for the expression that Ibn Qudamah mentioned, that ʿUthman applied the prescribed penalty (hadd) for it, which is a man's saying to his companion: "O son of the one who sniffs the wadhr," al-Jawhari said in his Sihah: "al-wadhrah, with a sukun, is the lump (ghadrah), and it is a piece of flesh when it is gathered together. From this is their saying: 'O son of the one who sniffs the wadhrah,' and it is an expression of slander, and the Arabs used to revile one another with it, just as they reviled one another with saying: 'O son of the one who throws down the saddles of riders,' or 'O son of the one with banners,' and similar. The plural is wadhr, like tamrah and tamr." End of quotation from al-Jawhari's Sihah.

*Al-shammah*, with the letter mim doubled, is the active participle of *shammahu* (he smelled it). The author of *Lisan al-ʿArab* said: "In the hadith of ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him), that a man was brought before him who had said to another man: 'O son of the one who sniffs the wadhr,' and he applied the hadd to him. It is among the reviling and disparagement of the Arabs. He only meant: 'O son of the one who sniffs the *madhakir*,' meaning fornication, as though she were smelling various penises, so he expressed it allusively. The *dhakar* is a piece of the body of its owner. It is also said that they meant by it the *qulaf*, the plural of *qulfat al-dhakar* (the foreskin), because it is cut off." End of the relevant part of *Lisan al-ʿArab*. This does not clearly show an intention of fornication, and I have not seen anyone explain the meaning of *shammat al-wadhr* in a fully satisfactory way, because smelling men's penises is not a familiar or evident matter.

What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that the speaker of this statement likens the one who alludes to fornication with her to the mating of animals. When the male of most animals wants to mate with the female, he smells her genitals and inhales her scent intensely, and after that he mounts her and covers her. They claim that a woman smells a man's penis as the stallion among animals smells the genitals of his female, and her smelling of men's penises is as though it were a prelude to intercourse. So they used the smelling of penises as an allusion to intercourse, and they described a man's penis as a *wadhrah*, because it is a piece of his body like a piece of flesh. It is also possible that they meant her great involvement in that matter, until she became as though she smelled the scent of that place. Allah knows best.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: You have learned from what we have mentioned the opinions of the scholars and their proofs regarding allusion to qadhf (false accusation of unlawful intercourse): whether the hadd is imposed for it or not.

The more apparent of the two opinions to me is that if the allusion clearly conveys the meaning of qadhf from the surrounding indications, its speaker is subject to the hadd, because an offence against the honour (ʿird) of a Muslim is realised by everything that clearly conveys that, and so that some people do not use the words of allusion from which accusation of fornication is understood as a pretext for accusing others. Apparently, according to the view of those scholars who say that allusion to qadhf does not require the hadd, the speaker of allusive qadhf must be subject to discretionary punishment (taʿzir) for the harm he caused his fellow by the allusion. Allah knows best.

* *

**The sixth issue:** al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: "The majority of scholars hold that there is no hadd upon one who accuses a man or a woman of the People of the Book. Al-Zuhri, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Abi Layla said: he is liable to the hadd if she has a child by a Muslim. There is a third opinion: if he accuses a Christian woman married to a Muslim, he is flogged with the hadd. Ibn al-Mundhir said: most scholars agree on and hold the first opinion. I have not met anyone who disagrees on this. If a Christian accuses a free Muslim, he is subject to what a Muslim is subject to, eighty lashes; I know of no disagreement on this." End of quotation.

* *

**The seventh issue:** Know that the more apparent of the two opinions of the scholars to me regarding the case where one man accuses another, and a third says: "You have spoken the truth," is that the one who confirms the accusation is himself an accuser, and so the hadd must be applied to him, because his confirmation of the accuser is an accusation, contrary to Zufar and those who agree with him.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: "If he said: 'So-and-so informed me that you committed fornication,' he is not an accuser, whether the one he reports it about denies it or confirms it. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y). Abu al-Khattab said: there is another view on this, that he becomes an accuser if the other denies it, and this is the view of Malik and ʿAta', and something similar is reported from al-Zuhri, because he has reported his fornication." End of quotation.

The more apparent of the two opinions to me is that he is not an accuser and is not subject to the hadd, because he is relating what someone else said and did not speak on his own initiative. It is possible that he is truthful, and that the one who informed him later denied it, just as if a witness testified that a man had accused another man, and the accused denied it: the witness is not an accuser. Allah knows best.

* *

**The eighth issue:** The more apparent of the two opinions of the scholars to me regarding one who accused a man of fornication, but the hadd was not applied to him until the accused himself committed fornication, is that the hadd falls from his accuser. This is because, by the fornication of the accused, it is established that he is not muhsan (chaste in the legal sense), and if that had been so it would not have appeared except after the hadd had become binding on the accuser. For it has become evident that he was not chaste before the hadd was applied to the one who accused him, so he is not flogged for one who is not chaste, by analogy with the state in which the hadd is to be applied, since at that time it has been established against him that he is not chaste.

Ibn Qudamah attributed this, which we have preferred, to Abu Hanifa, Malik and al-Shafiʿi. The view that he is flogged is the view of Imam Ahmad.

The author of *al-Mughni* said: This is also the view of al-Thawri, Abu Thawr, al-Muzani and Dawud, and they argued that the hadd had become due and was complete with its conditions, so it does not fall by the removal of a condition of its obligation.

What is more apparent to us is what we have put forward, because it is established that he was not chaste before the hadd was applied to his accuser, and so he is not flogged for one who is established as not chaste.

The hadd became due before this, because the lack of his chastity was concealed, then it became evident before the hadd was applied. Allah knows best.

* *

**The ninth issue:** Know that the more apparent of the two opinions of the scholars with us regarding one who says to a man, "O you who had intercourse between the thighs," is that this is not qadhf, and its speaker is not subject to the hadd, because he has accused him of an act that is not considered zina by consensus (ijma'). This is contrary to Ibn al-Qasim, one of the companions of Malik, who held that the hadd is obligatory, claiming that it is an allusion to him. Allah knows best.

* *

**The tenth issue:** Know that the hadd for qadhf is not applied to the accuser unless the one accused requests that the hadd be imposed on him, because it is his right. And the accuser has no evidence for what he claims regarding the fornication of the accused, because Allah says: ﴿Then they did not bring four witnesses﴾ [al-Nur 24:4]. The implication of the verse is that if the accuser brings four witnesses in the manner accepted by the Sharia, there is no hadd upon him; the hadd for zina is established against the accused by the testimony of the evidence. For this it is also a condition that the accused does not confess. If he confesses to fornication, there is no hadd upon the accuser. If the accuser is a husband, what is considered for the hadd of qadhf is his refusal to perform li'an (the oath-curse between spouses). Ibn Qudamah said: "We know of no disagreement on all of this." Then he said: "The continuation of the demand is required until the hadd is carried out. If he demands it and then pardons the accuser from the hadd, it falls. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi and Abu Thawr. Al-Hasan and the people of opinion said: it does not fall by his pardon, because it is a hadd, and so it does not fall by pardon like the other hadd punishments. Our argument is that it is a hadd that is not carried out except after the human being's demand for its execution, so it falls by his pardon like retaliation (qisas), and it differs from the other hadd punishments, for in carrying them out the demand is not a condition. The hadd for theft requires only a demand for the stolen property, not for carrying out the hadd. Also, they said that his claim is valid, that he may be made to swear an oath concerning it, that the judge may rule on it by his own knowledge, and that his retraction after confession is not accepted. This shows that it is a right of a human being." End of quotation from *al-Mughni*. That it is a right of a human being is one of the opinions concerning it.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Qurtubi said: "The scholars differed concerning the hadd of qadhf: is it one of the rights of Allah, or of human beings, or does it have an element of both?
The first is the view of Abu Hanifa.
The second is the view of Malik and al-Shafiʿi.
The third was held by some later scholars.
The benefit of the disagreement is this: if it is a right of Allah, the imam establishes it when it reaches him, even if the one falsely accused does not demand it, and repentance benefits the accuser between himself and Allah. The hadd is halved for a slave, as with zina. If it is a right of a human being, the imam does not carry it out except upon the demand of the one falsely accused, it falls by his pardon, and repentance does not benefit the accuser until the accused grants him absolution (tahlil)." End of al-Qurtubi's words.

The school of Malik and his companions seems to be based on the third opinion, namely that the hadd falls by the pardon of the one falsely accused before the matter reaches the imam. If it reaches the imam, his pardon does not drop it unless he claims that by pardoning he intends to conceal the matter for himself.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: The apparent position is that qadhf is a right of a human being, and every right of a human being contains a right of Allah.

Its clarification: the hadd for qadhf is a right of a human being insofar as it is legislated to deter its commission and to repel the disgrace of the accusation from the one accused. When the accuser dares to do this, he violates the sanctity of a Muslim's honour, and the Muslim has a right against him because of the violation of his honour. He also violates the prohibition of Allah concerning the commission of this act against the honour of a Muslim, so Allah has a right against the accuser because of his violation of the sanctity of His prohibition and his failure to obey it. He is thus a disobedient person to Allah, deserving His punishment. The right of Allah falls by sincere repentance (tawbah nasuhah), and the right of the Muslim falls by carrying out the hadd or by his absolution.

What appears from this detail is that if the accused pardons and the hadd falls by his pardon, the imam may impose discretionary punishment (taʿzir) on the accuser for the right of Allah. Allah, exalted and majestic, knows best.

* *

**The eleventh issue:** Al-Qurtubi said: "If the testimony against the fornicator for fornication is complete, but the witnesses were not found to be of good character ('udul), then al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Sha'bi held that there is no hadd upon the witnesses, nor upon the one testified against. This is also the view of Ahmad, al-Nuʿman and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan."

[p. 443] Mālik said: if four people testify against him for fornication (zina), and one of them is under censure (maskhūṭan ʿalayhi) or is a slave, then they are all flogged. Sufyān al-Thawrī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq said, regarding four blind men who testify against a woman for fornication: they are flogged. If one of the witnesses retracts after the accused has been stoned for fornication, then one group said: he pays one quarter of the blood money (diyah), and nothing is owed by the others. Qatādah, Ḥammād, ʿIkrimah, Abū Hāshim, Mālik, Aḥmad, and the people of opinion (aṣḥāb al-raʾy) said the same. Al-Shāfiʿī said: if he says, "I intended that he be killed," then the heirs of the victim have the choice: if they wish, they may kill him (qatal), and if they wish, they may pardon him and take one quarter of the blood money, and he is subject to the prescribed punishment (ḥadd). Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: he is killed, and the others owe three quarters of the blood money. Ibn Sīrīn said: if he says, "I made a mistake and meant someone else," then he owes the full blood money; if he says, "I intended it," he is killed. Ibn Shubrumah also said this. End of the quotation from al-Qurṭubī, and we have already quoted part of it.

The most apparent of the opinions to me is that if they are not upright (ʿadl), all of them are subject to the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), because one who brings an unknown witness whose uprightness is not established is like one who brought no witness at all. And if he admits that he deliberately testified against him in order that he be killed, then retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is applied to him. If he claims doubt about his retraction, then he pays his share of the blood money. The view that he pays the full blood money has some basis in reasoning, and God knows best.

* *

**The twelfth issue:** al-Qurṭubī said: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said that whoever slanders (qadhf) someone he assumed to be a slave, and who turns out to be free, is subject to the prescribed punishment. This was also said by al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Whoever slanders an umm walad (a slave woman who has borne her master's child) is subject to the prescribed punishment, and this was reported from Ibn ʿUmar; it is also the analogy of al-Shāfiʿī's view. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: there is no prescribed punishment for him. End of quotation.

The author of these notes, may God pardon and forgive him, says: As for the prescribed punishment for slandering an umm walad, the apparent position is that it applies only after the death of her master and her manumission from the estate of the one who fathered her child. Before that, her freedom has not actually been established, especially according to the view of scholars who permit selling her. The slanderer is not subject to the prescribed punishment for slandering someone who was not fully free, as it appears. Likewise, if it were said that whoever slanders someone he thinks is a slave, who turns out to be free, is not liable to the prescribed punishment because he did not intend to slander a free person but intended to slander a slave, this would have some basis in reasoning, because "actions are by intentions, and every person will have what they intended," and because the disgrace (maʿarrah) is removed from the slandered person by the slanderer's statement: "I did not intend to slander you, nor do I say that you are an adulterer; I only meant the one I believed to be a slave, so in my view you are chaste, and I say nothing about you but good." God knows best.

* *

**The thirteenth issue:** Know that scholars differed regarding one who slanders a group of people with a single word, or with several words, or who slanders one person multiple times. We have already mentioned the disagreement of the scholars regarding one who slanders a group with a single word, in the discussion of the verses of ḥajj (the Qurʾanic passage on the pilgrimage).

Ibn Qudāmah said in *al-Mughnī*, in his commentary on the statement of al-Khiraqī: "If he slanders the group with a single word, then there is one prescribed punishment, if they sue, or if one of them sues." His text reads: This was said by Ṭāwūs, al-Shaʿbī, al-Zuhrī, al-Nakhaʿī, Qatādah, Ḥammād, Mālik, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah and his two companions, Ibn Abī Laylā, and Isḥāq. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir said: each one has a full prescribed punishment. This is also reported from Aḥmad, and al-Shāfiʿī has two views, like the two reports. The basis of this is that he slandered each one of them, so a full prescribed punishment is due to each, just as if he had slandered them with separate words. Our basis is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses — lash them eighty lashes﴾. It does not distinguish between slandering one person or a group. Also, those who testified against al-Mughīrah slandered a woman, and ʿUmar only imposed one prescribed punishment on them. Also, it is a single slander, so only one prescribed punishment is due, as if he had slandered one person. Also, the prescribed punishment is due only because of bringing disgrace upon the slandered person through his slander, and by one prescribed punishment it becomes apparent that this slanderer is lying, and the disgrace is removed, so it is sufficient with it. This differs from the case where he slanders each one with a separate slander: if he is proven a liar in one slander, that does not necessarily mean he is a liar in another, and the disgrace is not removed from one of the slandered persons by the punishment imposed for the other.

Given this, if they demand it collectively, the prescribed punishment is imposed for them all. If one of them demands it, it is carried out, because the right belongs to them as alternatives: whichever of them demands it, he collects it, and it is extinguished, so no one else may demand it, like a woman's right regarding her guardians in marriage: when one of them exercises it, it is dropped for the rest. If one of them waives it, then the others may still demand and collect it, because the disgrace was not removed from him by the pardon of his companion, and the one who pardons has no right to demand it, because he has already waived his right.

It is reported from Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, another report: if they demand it all at once, there is one prescribed punishment. Likewise if they demand it one after another, but it was not carried out until all of them demanded it, then there is one prescribed punishment. If one of them demands it and it is carried out for him, and then another demands it and it is carried out for him, and so on for all of them. This is the view of ʿUrwah, because when they unite in demanding it, its execution is for all of them together, and when one demands it alone, its execution is for him alone, so the rights of the others are not dropped without their execution or waiver. If he slanders a group with several words, then each has a prescribed punishment. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ, al-Shaʿbī, Qatādah, Ibn Abī Laylā, Abū Ḥanīfah, and al-Shāfiʿī. Ḥammād and Mālik said: only one prescribed punishment is due, because it is a crime that entails a prescribed punishment, so when it is repeated one prescribed punishment suffices, just as if he stole from a group or committed fornication with several women, or drank several kinds of intoxicants. Our basis is that these are rights of human beings, so they do not merge, like debts and retaliation. This is unlike what they analogized, because that is a right of God Most High. Then the two said: if he slandered a man several times and was not punished, then there is one prescribed punishment, in one report without dispute, whether he slandered him with one act of fornication or with several. If he slandered him and was punished, and then repeated the slander, you examine: if he slandered him with the same fornication for which he was punished, the prescribed punishment is not repeated against him, according to the consensus of the majority of scholars. It is reported from Ibn al-Qāsim that he required a second prescribed punishment, but this contradicts the consensus of the Companions, because when Abū Bakrah was punished for slandering al-Mughīrah and then repeated the slander, they did not see a second prescribed punishment against him. Al-Athram reported with his chain from Ẓabyān ibn ʿUmārah, who said: three men testified against al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah that he was an adulterer. This reached ʿUmar, and it weighed heavily upon him, and he said: "Three quarters of al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah has been severed." Ziyād came, and he said: "What do you have?" He did not establish it, so he ordered them flogged, and they were flogged, and he said: "False witnesses!" Abū Bakrah said: "Would you not be satisfied if a man came to you saying he saw his stoning?" He said: "Yes, by Him in whose hand is my soul." Abū Bakrah said: "I too testify that he is an adulterer." He wanted to repeat the prescribed punishment against him, but ʿAlī said: "O Commander of the Faithful, if you repeat the prescribed punishment against him, you will impose stoning on him." In another narration: "The slander is not repeated against him by two floggings." Al-Athram said: I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh (Aḥmad), "What is ʿAlī's saying, 'If you flog him, then stone your companion'?" He said: "It seems he regarded his testimony as the testimony of two men." Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: "I used to explain it this way until I saw it in this narration, and it pleased me." Then he said: "He means that if you flog him a second time, it is as if you have made him another witness." As for one who has been punished for him and then slanders him with a second fornication, you examine: if he slanders him after a long interval, then a second prescribed punishment applies, because the sanctity of the slandered person is never removed with respect to the slanderer, such that he can be slandered in every circumstance. If he slanders him right after the punishment, then there are two reports:

The first: he is also punished, because it is a slander whose falsity was not made evident by a prescribed punishment, so a prescribed punishment is due for it, just as if a long interval had passed. Also, all other causes of the prescribed punishment, when repeated after one has been punished for the first, the same ruling applies to the second, such as fornication, theft, and other causes.

The second: he is not punished, because he has already been punished for one instance, so he is not punished for slander immediately after it, just as if he had slandered him with the first fornication. End of the quotation from *al-Mughnī*. I have seen his quotation of the scholars' views regarding one who slanders a group with a single word, or with several words, or who slanders one person multiple times.

The author of these notes, may God pardon and forgive him, says: We have not found in these issues any explicit text from the Book or the Sunnah.

What appears to us on this, and God Most High knows best, is that whoever slanders a group with a single word is subject to one prescribed punishment, because by it his lie becomes evident regarding all of them, the disgrace is removed from all of them, and the satisfaction of the anger is achieved by punishing him for all of them.

The more apparent view to us regarding one who accuses a group with several words is that the prescribed punishment is multiplied according to the number of words with which he slandered them, because he slandered each one with an independent slander in which no one else participated. His punishment for some of them does not make apparent his lie regarding the second, whom he slandered with a different expression, and the disgrace is not removed from that second person by it. This applies if the slander of each one of them was a separate slander not combined with any other. There should be no disagreement about this. The more apparent view is that if he slanders them with different expressions, the prescribed punishment is repeated according to their number, as the author of *al-Mughnī* chose.

The more apparent view to us is that if he repeats the slander against one man before the prescribed punishment is carried out, one prescribed punishment suffices. If he slanders him after being punished for the first slander, after a long interval, then also a prescribed punishment. If he slanders him close to the time of his punishment with the very fornication for which he was punished, the prescribed punishment is not repeated against him, as the author of *al-Mughnī* related in the story of Abū Bakrah and al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah. If the second slander is different from the first, as when he said in the first: "You committed fornication with a white woman," and in the second said: "with a black woman," then the apparent view is that it is repeated. God knows best.

It is reported from Mālik, may God have mercy on him, in *al-Mudawwanah*: if he slandered a man, and when he had been flogged some lashes he slandered him again or slandered another, the prescribed punishment of eighty is begun against him from the moment he slandered him, and the lashes already administered are not counted.

* *

**The fourteenth issue:** The apparent view is that whoever says to a group, "One of you is an adulterer," or "a son of an adulteress," is not subject to the prescribed punishment, because he did not specify one person, so the disgrace did not attach to any one of them. If they demand that the prescribed punishment be imposed on him as a group, he is not punished, because he did not accuse any one of them specifically and did not identify whom he meant by his statement. Al-Mawwāq related this from al-Bājī, from Muḥammad ibn al-Mawwāz, and its basis is evident as you see. Khalīl also limited himself to this in his abridgment, in his statement listing, alongside what carries no prescribed punishment: "or he said to a group, 'One of you is an adulterer.'"

Ibn Qudāmah said in *al-Mughnī*: If someone says, "Whoever slanders me is a son of an adulteress," and a man then slanders him, there is no prescribed punishment for him according to any scholar. Likewise, if two men dispute over something, and one of them says, "The liar is a son of an adulteress," there is no prescribed punishment for him. Aḥmad explicitly stated this, because he did not specify anyone by the slander, and likewise for similar cases. If he slanders a group whose truthfulness in slandering them cannot be imagined, such as slandering all the people of a large town with fornication, there is no prescribed punishment for him, because he did not bring disgrace upon anyone other than himself, since his lie is known. End of quotation.

* *

**Issue 15:** Know that the most apparent of the scholars' opinions, in our view, concerning one who says to a man, "You are more adulterous (*azna*) than so-and-so," is that he has slandered both of them, and he is liable to two prescribed punishments (*hadd*, the fixed penalty for slander, *qadhf*). This is because his saying *azna* is a superlative form (*sigha al-tafdil*), which indicates that the one preferred and the one he is preferred over share the basic act, except that the preferred one surpasses his companion in it. So the meaning of his statement, by the direct indication of the superlative form, is: "You and so-and-so are both adulterers, but you exceed him in adultery." That this constitutes slander against both of them is clear, as you see. From this you know that one of the two views among the Hanbalis, that the punishment applies only to the addressee and not to the named third party, should not be relied upon. The same applies to what Ibn Qudamah attributed to al-Shafi'i and the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*), namely that it is not slander against the first or the second unless he intends slander by it. All of this is incorrect and should not be relied upon, because the phrase "You are more adulterous than so-and-so" is explicit slander against both of them in clear words, with no ambiguity.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*, arguing for the view we mentioned from the Hanbalis, that there is no punishment for the second, and his exact words are: "The second (view) is that it is slander only against the addressee, because the word *af'al* may be used for one who performs the act alone, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted (p-447) ﴿Is one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or one who cannot find guidance unless he is guided? What is wrong with you?﴾ [Yunus: 35] to the end of the verse, and the Exalted said: ﴿Which of the two groups is more worthy of security?﴾ [al-An'am: 81], and Lut said: ﴿These are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾ [Hud: 78], meaning from the posteriors of men, and there is no purity in that." Such an argument should not be relied upon, just as the one who cited it did not rely upon it.

The summary of this argument is that the superlative form may be used to mean the mere attribution of a quality, not the existence of a comparison between two things. He illustrated this with the phrases ﴿more worthy to be followed﴾, ﴿more worthy of security﴾, and ﴿purer for you﴾, since the superlative form in the verses mentioned denotes the mere attribute and not comparison.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: It is not hidden that the superlative form may indeed be used for the mere attribute, as is well known, and among its examples are the verses mentioned by the author of *al-Mughni*. But these cannot be taken to mean other than comparison unless there is an external proof requiring that. And the verses he cited are known not to be capable of being comparative. This is because idols have no share at all in the worthiness of being followed, in His saying ﴿more worthy to be followed, or one who cannot find guidance﴾; and because the disbelievers have no share in being more worthy of security; and because the posteriors of men have no share in purity.

Among the examples of the superlative form used for the mere attribute is also His saying the Exalted: ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], meaning: "it is easy and simple for Him." And the saying of al-Shanfara:

"Even if hands stretched out toward the provision, I would not be the quickest of them; when the greediest of the people is the quickest."

Meaning: I was not hasty among them. And the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mighty and tall."

Meaning: mighty and tall. And the saying of Ma'n ibn Aws:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am indeed very fearful, over which of us death will first run."

Meaning: fearful. And the saying of al-Ahwas ibn Muhammad al-Ansari:

"Indeed I grant you aversion, and indeed I, by oath, with aversion, am very inclined to you."

Meaning: inclined. And the saying of another:

(p-448) "Men wished that I would die, and if I die, that is a path in which I am not unique."

Meaning: not unique. And another said:

"By your life, indeed al-Zibriqan is generous with his kindness in the years of hardship, and is excellent."

Meaning: and excellent. And other than these from the verses. But we have already established that it cannot be taken to mean the mere attribute except by an external proof or a clear indicator showing that.

And his saying to him, "You are more adulterous than so-and-so," has no indicator or proof that diverts the superlative form from its original meaning, so it must be kept in its original sense. The slander punishment applies to each of them. The use of the word *min* (than) in his saying, "You are more adulterous than so-and-so," clearly clarifies the superlative sense. And Allah knows best.

* *

**Issue 16:** Know that it is not permitted to accuse one who has performed mutual imprecation (*li'an*, the oath-exchange between spouses) of adultery, nor to accuse her child of being a child of adultery. Whoever accuses either of them is liable to the prescribed punishment. This should not be disputed, because adultery has not been established against her, nor against her child as being a child of adultery. The child's lineage was only severed from the husband by his *li'an*.

In *Sunan Abi Dawud*: Al-Hasan ibn Ali narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, Abbad ibn Mansur narrated to us, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Hilal ibn Umayya came, and he was one of the three whom Allah forgave. He came from his land in the evening and found a man with his wife, and he saw with his eyes and heard with his ears..." (the hadith), and in it: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ separated them and decided that her child should not be called by a father, and that she should not be accused, nor her child, and whoever accuses her or her child, upon him is the prescribed punishment." ... to the end of the hadith. In this hadith there is explicit statement that whoever accuses her or her child is liable to the prescribed punishment.

Know that what Shaykh al-Hattab (*al-Hattab*) transmitted from some Maliki scholars, that whoever says to the son of one under mutual imprecation, "You are not the son of your father who performed mutual imprecation with your mother," is liable to the prescribed punishment, is contrary to the verified position. This is because the husband who performed mutual imprecation has his lineage to the child negated by the *li'an*, so negating it from him is a truth corresponding to reality. For this reason they do not inherit from each other. And whoever speaks a true statement does not thereby incur the prescribed punishment, just as if he said to him, "O you whom the husband of his mother negated," or "O son of one under mutual imprecation," or "O son of her who was cursed in mutual imprecation." The prescribed punishment is only obligatory on the slanderer when he says, "You are a son of adultery," or similar explicit slander. And Allah knows best.

* *

(p-449) **Issue 17:** Concerning the ruling if someone says to a man, "O adulteress" (*ya zaniyatu*) with the feminine marker (*ta' al-farq*), or says to a woman, "O adulterer" (*ya zani*) without the feminine marker. Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: "It is explicit slander against each of them." He said: "This was chosen by Abu Bakr, and it is the school of al-Shafi'i. Ibn Hamid chose that it is not slander unless he explains it as such, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa, because it is possible that by his saying 'O adulteress' he means 'O expert in adultery' (*'allama fi al-zina*), just as one says to a scholar 'allama' (very learned), to one who narrates much 'rawiya,' and to one who memorizes much 'hafizah.' Our argument is that whatever is slander against one of the two genders is slander against the other, such as saying 'you committed adultery' with the verb pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the *ta'*, addressed to both of them together. Also, this phrase is addressed to them and refers to them by the word 'adultery,' and this suffices without the distinction by the feminine ta' or its omission. For this reason, if he said to a woman, 'O person who is an adulterer,' or to a man, 'O soul who is an adulteress,' he would be a slanderer. Their claim that he means that he is an expert in adultery is not valid, for it is a noun of the act, and when the ta' enters it, it is for intensification, as in their saying 'hafizah' for one who is intense in memorization, and 'rawiyah' for one who is intense in narration, and likewise 'humazah' and 'surakah.' Also, many people masculinize the feminine and feminize the masculine, and this does not take them out of the addressee being meant by the expression that is meant by the correct wording." End of the words of the author of *al-Mughni*.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: The more apparent of the two views in my opinion, concerning one who says to a male, "O adulteress" in the feminine form, or says to a woman, "O adulterer" in the masculine form, is that he is liable to the prescribed punishment.

Its clarification is that the slanderer using these two phrases is in one of two situations. Either he is a common person who does not know Arabic, or he has knowledge of the Arabic language. If he is a common person, he may not know the difference between the two phrases, and his calling the person by the word for adultery is apparent in his intent to slander him.

If he knows the language, then indeed in the language there is frequent use of the masculine description for the feminine, with respect to her being a person (*shakhs*).

We have already mentioned some examples of this in Surat al-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying ﴿and you extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾ [al-Nahl: 14], and among the verses we cited there is the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Worries prevent sleep in the evening, and an imagining when the stars grow jealous (set)."

"Of a beloved who has struck your heart with a sickness, so it is an entering that is hidden."

And he means by the beloved a female, as evidenced by his saying after it:

"The sun of day has not overtaken her in anything, except that youth does not last."

(p-450) And the saying of Kuthayyir:

"If the thirsty, panting one were to come to the water, toward me, a beloved, indeed she is beloved."

Among the examples of this is the saying of Malih ibn al-Hakam al-Hudhali:

"But Layla has destroyed me with her saying, 'Yes,' then Layla, the procrastinating, the shameless."

Meaning: Layla, the person who procrastinates and is shameless.

And the saying of Urwa ibn Hizam al-Udhri:

"And Afra' is the one among people I hope for most in affection, and Afra' turns away from me, the one who is averse and lax."

Meaning: the person who is averse.

And when the masculine description of a female in the sense of a person is frequent in the speech of the Arabs, as you have seen its examples, then there is likewise no obstacle to their describing a male with a feminine form in the sense of a soul (*nasama*) or self (*nafs*). The occurrence of that to feminize the wording while masculinizing the meaning is well known, such as his saying:

"Your father is a caliph whom another woman bore, and you are a caliph; that is perfection."

* *

**Issue 18:** Know that whoever accuses a man who has previously been established as an adulterer, or a woman who has previously been established as an adulteress, by evidence (*bayyina*) or by confession (*iqrar*), there is no prescribed punishment upon him, because he is truthful. Also, the chastity (*ihsan*) of the one accused has been removed by adultery. The proof of this is the opposite implication (*mafhum al-mukhalafa*) in His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾, the verse, for it indicates by its implication that whoever accuses an unchaste woman has no prescribed punishment upon him. This is so, but he is liable to discretionary punishment (*ta'zir*), because he accused him of a grave sin without establishing it, and the honor of one who has previously been established as an adulterer may not be left permissible for everyone who wishes to accuse him of adultery without a deterrent punishment, as you see.

* *

**Issue 19:** Know that if a person was a polytheist and committed adultery while in his polytheism, or was a Magian and married his mother or daughter, for example, while he was a Magian, and then after that he became Muslim, and someone accused him of adultery after his Islam, then he has three situations:

The first: that he says to him, "O you who committed adultery during the days of his polytheism," or "O you who married his mother, for example, during his days as a Magian." In this case there is no prescribed punishment, because the speaker has reported a truth, and Islam erases what came before it.

(p-451) The second: that he says to him, "O you who committed adultery after his Islam," or "who married his mother after his Islam." Then he is liable to the prescribed punishment, as is not hidden.

The third: that he says to him, "O adulterer," without specifying whether that was before his Islam or after it. If he explains it as meaning that he committed adultery after his Islam, then he is liable to the prescribed punishment. If he says, "I meant by it his adultery during the time of his polytheism," is this explanation accepted from him, and the prescribed punishment falls from him? Or is it not accepted from him, and the prescribed punishment is applied to him? The scholars differed on this. Among those who said that he is punished and his explanation is not heeded are Malik and his companions, and al-Khirqi of the Hanbalis stated this explicitly. Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: "There is no prescribed punishment upon him." He differed from al-Khirqi in his commentary on al-Khirqi's statement: "Whoever slanders one who was a polytheist, and says, 'I meant that he committed adultery while he was a polytheist,' his words are not heeded, and the prescribed punishment for the slanderer applies if the one slandered demands it." And likewise for one who was a slave. End of quotation.

* *

**Question Twenty:** Know that whoever accuses a girl who has not reached puberty of fornication (*zina*), or accuses a boy who has not reached puberty of it, the scholars have differed: is the accuser liable to the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) or not? Abu 'Abdullah al-Qurtubi, in his commentary on the verse under discussion, said: If one accuses a young girl who is capable of being penetrated before puberty of fornication, it is slander (*qadhf*) according to Malik. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: it is not slander, because it is not fornication, since no prescribed punishment applies to her, though discretionary punishment (*ta'zir*) does. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The question is open to interpretation and problematic. However, Malik gave priority to protecting the honour of the one accused, while others considered protecting the back of the accuser. Protecting the honour of the accused takes precedence, because the accuser has exposed the accused's concealment with the tip of his tongue, so the prescribed punishment is binding on him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ahmad said concerning a girl of nine, that her accuser is to receive the prescribed punishment; likewise a boy who has reached ten, his accuser is to be flogged. Ishaq said: If one accuses a boy who is capable of being penetrated like that, the prescribed punishment is binding on him, and so is it for a girl once she has passed nine. Ibn al-Mundhir said: No prescribed punishment is applied to one who accuses someone who has not reached puberty, because that is a lie, but he is to receive discretionary punishment for the harm caused. End of quotation; the relevant part is in his own words.

And since you have learned from what we have mentioned the views of the scholars on this question, know that the most apparent of them, in our opinion, is the view of Ibn al-Mundhir: he is not subject to the prescribed punishment but to discretionary punishment. The reasoning is that whoever among males and females has not reached puberty is relieved of the pen (of legal accountability), and no blame attaches to him for a sin, because he is not held accountable. If the accuser of a child brings four witnesses testifying against the child for fornication, there is no prescribed punishment for him, by consensus. Had he slandered him in the true sense, the prescribed punishment would be binding on him by the accuser's establishing evidence of the child's fornication. Although a group of distinguished scholars differed on this, the accuser is to receive discretionary punishment sufficient to deter him and others from accusing one who has not reached puberty. And God knows best.

* *

**Question Twenty-One** [p. 452]: Know that the apparent position regarding a man who says to another, "*zanata*" (you committed fornication) with a hamza, is this: if the accuser is a layman who does not distinguish between the weak-lettered and the hamzated verb, he is subject to the prescribed punishment, because his intention to accuse the other of fornication is evident. But if he knows Arabic and says: "I only meant by my words *zana'ta* with a hamza its linguistic meaning, and the meaning of *zana'ta* with a hamza is: you took refuge in something, or you climbed a mountain," then [the matter is different]. From this is the verse of Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari, who was bouncing his young son Hakim while he was small:

*Resemble your mother's father, or resemble Hamal, and do not be like a clumsy, heavy, lazy oaf,*
*Who in the morning finds himself sprawled in his bed; but climb to the good things, ascending the mountain (zanan'a fi al-jabal).*

The point of evidence in it is his saying *zana'an fi al-jabal*, meaning ascending upon it. *Al-hilawf* is the heavy, rough, large-bearded man, and *al-wakal* is one who entrusts his affairs to others. Al-Jawhari claimed that this rajaz was recited by the child's mother, to whom he sang it, and she was Manfusa daughter of Zayd al-Fawaris. Abu Muhammad ibn Barri refuted this claim of al-Jawhari, and he and others narrated it as we have mentioned. He said: His mother answered his father:

*Resemble my brother, or you will surely resemble your father,*
*But as for my father, you will never reach his (rank); your hands fall short of reaching it.*

Thus it is mentioned in *al-Lisan*.

* *

**Question Twenty-Two**: If someone disavows a man from his grandfather, or from his mother, or attributes him to a people other than his own, or to a tribe other than his tribe, then Malik held: if he disavows him from his mother, there is no prescribed punishment for him, because he has not accused her of fornication, nor has he disowned the child's paternity from his father. If he disavows him from his grandfather, the prescribed punishment is binding on him. According to him there is no prescribed punishment for attributing a person to a different ethnic group, even if the one is white and the other black. In *al-Mudawwana* he said: If he says to a Persian, "O Roman!" or "O Abyssinian!" or something similar, he is not subject to the prescribed punishment. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik's position on this has been reported differently, and I think there is no prescribed punishment for him, unless he says: "O son of the black one!" If none of his forefathers was black, then he is subject to the prescribed punishment. As for attributing him to an Abyssinian, as if he says: "O son of the Abyssinian!" while he is a Berber, then the Abyssinian and the Roman are equal in this, if he is a Berber.

Ibn Yunus said: It is the same whether he says: "O Abyssinian!" or "O son of the Abyssinian!" or "to the Roman" or "O son of the Roman," he is not subject to the prescribed punishment. Likewise was his position in the book of Muhammad. Shaykh al-Mawwaq said: This is what the fatwa should be based on according to the method of Ibn Yunus, so look into it yourself. End of quotation.

This which we have mentioned, that one who attributes a person to a different ethnic group is not subject to the prescribed punishment, is the well-known school of Malik, and he stated it in *al-Mudawwana* [p. 453]. Its application for him is if the person is not of Arab origin.

Malik said in *al-Mudawwana*: Whoever says to an Arab, "O Abyssinian!" or "O Persian!" or "O Roman!", is liable to the prescribed punishment, because the Arabs are attributed to their fathers, and this is a disavowal of them from their fathers.

The compiler of this (may God pardon and forgive him) says: The distinction between the Arab and others as reported from Malik does not hold entirely. The reason that one who says to a Roman, for example, "O Abyssinian!" is not subject to the prescribed punishment is that the apparent meaning is that he means the person resembles the Abyssinian in some of his character traits or actions, which is a well-known usage in Arabic. End of quotation.

The school of Abu Hanifa is that if he disavows him from his grandfather, there is no prescribed punishment on him, namely if he says to him: "You are not the son of your grandfather." He is not subject to the prescribed punishment, because he is truthful, since he is the son of his father, not of his grandfather. Likewise if he attributes an ethnic group to another, such as saying to an Arab, "O Nabatean!", there is no prescribed punishment for him according to Abu Hanifa, by the well-known view. Likewise, according to him, if he attributes him to another tribe other than his own, or disavows him from his tribe, there is no prescribed punishment, because it may be intended as a comparison to that tribe to which he is attributed in character or actions, or in lack of eloquence, and so on. Thus the intention of slander is not specifically determined.

The author of *Tabyin al-Haqaiq* said: It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about a man who said to a man from Quraysh, "O Nabatean!" He said: There is no prescribed punishment for him. End of quotation. Likewise, according to Abu Hanifa, one who says to a man, "O son of rainwater!" is not subject to the prescribed punishment, nor one who attributes him to his paternal or maternal uncle, unlike the Malikis and those who agree with them who hold that one who attributes him to his uncle or the like, or to his mother's husband who is his stepfather, is liable. This is because both the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle are like a father in compassion, and he may intend a comparison to the father in love and compassion. As for his saying "son of rainwater," it may be intended as a comparison in generosity, liberality and purity. They said: 'Amir ibn Harithah was called "Rainwater" for his generosity, and that he would make his wealth in times of drought take the place of rain. They said: The mother of al-Mundhir ibn Imru' al-Qays was called "Rainwater" for her beauty and loveliness, and her children were called "the sons of Rainwater," and they were the kings of Iraq. End of quotation.

If he attributes him to his grandfather, there is no prescribed punishment on him according to Abu Hanifa. There should be no disagreement on this, since the attribution to his grandfather is valid, as it has commonly occurred throughout the ages without objection. End of quotation.

The school of Imam Ahmad is that if he disavows him from his mother, there is no prescribed punishment for him.

There is a divergence from him regarding one who disavows a man from his tribe or attributes an ethnic group to another. Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: If he disavows a man from his father, he is subject to the prescribed punishment; Ahmad stated this explicitly. Likewise if he disavows him from his tribe. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Ishaq, and Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri and Hammad also said so. End of quotation.

You have known the divergence from Abu Hanifa, and the well-known position from him is what we mentioned shortly before. Then Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni* [p. 454]: Analogy requires that the prescribed punishment not be binding for disavowing a man from his tribe, because in that case slander by fornication is not specifically determined. It resembles the case where one says to a non-Arab, "You are an Arab!" If one says to an Arab, "You are a Nabatean or a Persian," then there is no prescribed punishment for him, but he is to receive discretionary punishment, as Ahmad explicitly stated, because it may mean "you are Nabatean in tongue or in nature." A different narration is reported from Ahmad, that he is subject to the prescribed punishment just as if he disavowed him from his father. The first is more sound, and it is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, because it allows for non-slanderous meanings to a great extent, so it is not specifically determined to be slander. Whenever he interprets any of that as slander, he is a slanderer. End of quotation from *al-Mughni*.

Since you have known the views of the scholars on this, know that the question has no texts from revelation, and the apparent position is that whatever allows for a non-slanderous meaning does not bring the prescribed punishment upon its speaker, because prescribed punishments are averted by doubts, and the possibility of a meaning other than slander is no less than a strong doubt. Ibn Qudamah mentioned in *al-Mughni* that al-Ash'ath ibn Qays narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he used to say: "I will not be brought a man who says: 'Quraysh is not from Kinanah,' except that I will flog him." End of quotation. Look into its chain of narration.

* *

**Question Twenty-Three**: On the rulings concerning various scattered words, such as one who says to a man: "O *qarnan*!", or "O *dayyuth*!", or "O *kashkhan*!", or "O *qartaban*!", or "O *mu'fuj*!", or "O *qawwad*!" (pimp), or "O son of the one who lodged the riders!", or "O son of the one with the banners!", or "O *mukhannath*!" (effeminate), or says to a woman: "O *qahba*!" (whore).

Know that the scholars have differed on these expressions mentioned. The school of Malik is that whoever says to a man, "O *qarnan*!", is liable to the prescribed punishment for slander if the wife demands it, because the *qarnan* in the people's usage is the husband of the adulteress. Likewise whoever says to a woman, "O *qahba*!", is liable to the prescribed punishment according to the Malikis. Likewise whoever says, "O son of the one who lodged the riders!" or "O son of the one with the banners!", all of this carries the prescribed punishment for slander according to the Malikis, as the reference to it has already been made. They said: This is because the adulteress in the pre-Islamic era used to lodge riders and place a banner at her door. Likewise, if he says to him, "O *mukhannath*!", he is liable to the prescribed punishment unless he swears that he did not intend slander. If he swears that he did not intend it, he is disciplined but not subject to the prescribed punishment. This is stated in *al-Mudawwana*.

If he says to him, "O son of the immoral woman!", or "O son of the adulteress!", or "O immoral one!", or "O adulterer!", or "O donkey, son of a donkey!", or "O dog!", or "O bull!", or "O pig!", or the like, then there is no prescribed punishment on him, but he is to receive discretionary punishment sufficient to deter, as the ruler sees fit.

The school of Abu Hanifa is that if he says to him: "O sinner!", "O unbeliever!", "O wicked one!", "O thief!", "O adulterer!", "O hypocrite!", "O sodomite!", "O one who plays with boys!", "O consumer of usury!", "O drinker of wine!", "O *dayyuth*!", "O *mukhannath*!", "O traitor!", "O son of the whore!", "O heretic!", "O *qartaban*!", "O haven of whores or thieves!", "O forbidden one!" [p. 455], then there is no prescribed punishment on him for any of these words, but he is to receive discretionary punishment. The most emphasized discretionary punishment according to the Hanafis is thirty-nine lashes.

As for if he says to him: "O dog!", "O billy-goat!", "O donkey!", "O pig!", "O cow!", "O snake!", "O cupper!", "O parrot!", "O hirer-out!", "O son of illegitimacy!", "O rogue!", "O upside-down one!", "O overturned one!", "O object of mockery!", "O laughing-stock!", "O *kashkhan*!", "O fool!", "O one who is rotten!", then according to the Hanafis there is nothing on him for any of these words, and he is not disciplined for them. The author of *Tabyin al-Haqaiq* said: He is not disciplined for all of these words, because it is their custom to use "donkey" and the like to mean dullness, greed, or the like, and they do not intend insult by it. Do you not see that they name people with it and say: "'Iyad ibn Himar," "Sufyan al-Thawri," "Abu Thawr," and "Jamal"? Also, the one accused is not harmed in reputation by this speech; rather the harm falls on the accuser, and everyone knows that he is a human being, not a dog or a donkey, and that the accuser is lying in that. Al-Hindawani related that in our time one is disciplined for words like "O dog!" or "O pig!", because they are used as insults in our custom.

Shams al-A'immah al-Sarakhsi said: The more sound view in my opinion is that he is not disciplined. It was said: If the one addressed is of the noble class, such as jurists or 'Alids, he is to be disciplined, because it is considered a stain on his character and it causes him distress. If he is of the common people, he is not disciplined. This is the best of what has been said on this. Among the words that do not require discretionary punishment is his saying: "O rustic!", "O son of the black one!", "O son of the cupper!", while he is not such. End of quotation from *Tabyin al-Haqaiq Sharh Kanz al-Daqa'iq* in Hanafi jurisprudence.

The author, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, said: As for the expressions that I mentioned from them as requiring discretionary punishment (ta'zir, a non-prescribed punishment set by the judge), the requirement of ta'zir for them, as they mentioned, is clear and there is no difficulty in it. As for the expressions that I mentioned from them as not carrying ta'zir, the more apparent view in my opinion is that ta'zir is required for them, because they are all abuse and defamation. It is not hidden that whoever says to a person, "O dog, O pig, O donkey, O billy-goat, O cow," and so on, this is clear abuse, with no obscurity about it. His intention is not that the person is literally a dog or a pig, but rather to liken the person to the dog and the pig in baseness and blameworthy qualities, as is not hidden. So it is of the type of comparison that the rhetoricians call an eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh). There is no doubt that a sensible person who is told, "O dog," or "O pig," for example, is harmed by it, and there is no doubt that it is abuse. It is clear harm. Accordingly, the apparent ruling is ta'zir for the expressions mentioned. That they call a man a donkey or a dog does not contradict this, because among people there are those who name their son with an ugly name that they would not accept others being disparaged with. The apparent ruling is that if he says to a man, "O son of the black woman," while neither his father nor any of his grandfathers was black, he is liable to the hadd (the fixed prescribed punishment), because it is a denial of his lineage. Likewise, his saying, "O son of the cupper," if neither his father nor any of his grandfathers was a cupper, is qadhf (slander, false accusation of unlawful sex), because it is a denial of his lineage and an attribution of him to a black woman or a cupper with whom he has no kinship. This is the view of the Malikis and those who agree with them.

The author of "Tabyin al-Haqa'iq" said: The interpretation of qartaban (a cuckold who tolerates his wife's infidelity) is one who sees a man with his wife or his mahram (a close relative he is forbidden to marry), and leaves him alone with her. It was also said: he is one who causes two people to be together for an improper purpose. It was also said: he is one who sends his wife with a grown boy or with his farm worker to the estate, or permits the two of them to enter upon her in his absence. End of quotation from him.

Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": If he says to a man, "O dayyuth (a cuckold who allows other men to enter upon his wife)," or "O kashkhan," Ahmad said: he is to be disciplined with ta'zir. Ibrahim al-Harbi said: the dayyuth is one who lets men enter upon his wife. Tha'lab said: the qartaban is one who is content for men to enter upon his wife. He also said: "The qarnan and the kashkhan, I have not seen them in the speech of the Arabs, and their meaning among the common people is like the meaning of the dayyuth or close to it. So the one who slanders with it is liable to ta'zir, by analogy with his ruling on the dayyuth, because he has slandered him with something for which there is no hadd." Khalid ibn Yazid, from his father, said concerning a man who says to another, "O qarnan," if he has sisters or daughters in Islam, he is struck with the hadd, meaning that he is a slanderer of them. Khalid said, from his father: the qarnan among the common people is one who has daughters, and the kashkhan is one who has sisters, meaning, and Allah knows best, if he lets men enter upon them. The qawwad among the common people is the broker in fornication. Slander with all of that requires ta'zir, because it is slander with something that does not require the hadd. End of quotation from "al-Mughni."

He also said in "al-Mughni": The explicit ruling from Ahmad concerning one who says, "O ma'fuj" (a term implying sodomy), is that he is liable to the hadd. The apparent meaning of al-Kharaqi's words requires that one refer to his explanation. If he explains it as other than fornication, such as saying, "I meant O maflaj (paralyzed)," or "O one afflicted below the genitals," and the like, then there is no hadd on him, because he explained it with something for which there is no hadd. If he explains it as the deed of the people of Lot, then he is liable to the hadd, just as if he had stated it explicitly.

The author of "al-Qamus" said: The qarnan is the dayyuth who partners with his wife's companion. End of quotation from him. He also said in "al-Qamus": The qartaban, with a fatha, is the dayyuth, and the one who has no jealousy, or the qawwad. End of quotation from him. He said in "al-Qamus": The tadayyuth is pimping. And in "al-Qamus," under the line (not between brackets), al-kashkhan, with a kasra, is the dayyuth, and he (kashkhahu) made him a kashkhan, that is, he said to him, "O kashkhan." End of quotation from him. This is with the letter kha' (marked with a dot). Al-Jawhari said in his "Sihah": The dayyuth is the qundhu', who is the one who has no jealousy. End of quotation from him.

The author, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, said: What appears is that the correct determination regarding all the expressions mentioned, about which I have quoted the words of the scholars, is that they follow the custom prevailing in the place where they were said. If it is among their customs that the intended meaning is abuse without the kind of slander that requires the hadd, then ta'zir is obligatory because of the harm, and there is no hadd. If their custom is that the expression is intended as abuse by accusing of fornication or denying lineage, and that this is well known as the customary meaning, then the hadd is obligatory, because custom is followed in such matters. And Allah Most High knows best.

[[The author's words have been abridged because of their great length.]]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (*Adwa' al-Bayan*) on surah 24, verse 8 (part 1 of 5):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it shall avert from her the punishment that she bear witness four times by Allah that he is surely among the liars.﴾ His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And it shall avert from her the punishment that she bear witness four times by Allah﴾, to the end of the verse. The meaning of "yadra'" (it averts) is "yadfa'u" (it repels). The intended meaning of "al-'adhab" (the punishment) here is the *hadd* (the prescribed penalty). The verbal noun formed from "an" and its clause in His saying "al-'adhab an tash-hada" is the subject of "yadra'", meaning: her testimony four times repels from her the *hadd*.

The evidence that the intended meaning of "al-'adhab" in ﴿and it shall avert from her the punishment﴾ is the *hadd* comes from several aspects:

The first: the context of the verse, which indicates that the punishment that her testimonies avert from her is the *hadd*.

The second: He has applied the term "punishment" in other places to the *hadd*, with the context in those places indicating that "punishment" means the *hadd*. Such is His saying, exalted is He, in this noble surah: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress: lash each one of them a hundred lashes. And let not pity for them hold you back in the religion of Allah, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. So His saying ﴿let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ means their *hadd*, without dispute. And this is His saying, exalted is He, concerning slave women: ﴿Upon them is half of the punishment imposed on free chaste women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], meaning half of the lashing imposed on free women.

This verse indicates that when a husband accuses his wife and bears his five testimonies mentioned in the verse, the woman becomes liable to the *hadd* on account of his testimonies, and that this *hadd* directed at her on account of the husband's testimonies is averted from her by her own testimonies, which are explained in the verse.

The implied meaning (*mafhum al-mukhalafah*) of the verse indicates that if she refrains from her testimonies, she becomes liable to the *hadd* because of her refusal alongside the husband's testimonies. This is the apparent meaning, from which one should not depart. Thus, the testimonies of the husband who accuses (*al-qadhif*) avert from him the *hadd* of slander (*qadhf*), and direct at her the *hadd* of fornication, which her testimonies repel from her.

The apparent meaning of the Qur'an also is that if he accuses his wife and refrains from *li'an* (mutual imprecation), he is subjected to the *hadd* of slander. Thus, whoever of the spouses refrains from the five testimonies becomes liable to the *hadd*. This is the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verses (p. 465), because the accusing husband is included in the general scope of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]. But Allah has explained that the husband is excluded from this general scope by his testimonies, when He said: ﴿And those who accuse their wives and have no witnesses except themselves, then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah that he is surely of the truthful. And the fifth [testimony] is that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is among the liars.﴾ [al-Nur: 6-7]. Thus He did not provide him an escape from the eighty lashes, from the non-acceptance of testimony, and from the ruling of impiety (*fisq*), except by his testimonies, which stand in his place as the evidence that clears him of the *hadd*. If he refrains from his testimonies, the apparent meaning is that the *hadd* is obligatory upon him, because four upright witnesses who testify to his truthfulness did not avert it from him, nor do testimonies substitute for witnesses. Thus it is established that he is to be punished with the *hadd* because he is a slanderer and has not produced anything that averts from him the *hadd* of slander. Likewise, if the wife refrains from her oaths, she is liable to the *hadd*, because Allah explicitly stated that what averts the *hadd* from her is her testimonies, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it shall avert from her the punishment﴾, to the end of the verse.

Among those who said that the husband incurs the *hadd* if he refrains from the testimonies are the three Imams, in contrast to Abu Hanifa, who said that he is imprisoned until he performs *li'an* or retracts his accusation, whereupon the *hadd* of slander is applied to him. And among those who said that if he testifies and she refrains, she is punished with the *hadd* on account of his testimonies and her refusal are: Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Sha'bi, Makhul, Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Thawr, as transmitted from them by the author of *al-Mughni*.

This position is the more correct in our view, because it is the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿And it shall avert from her the punishment that she bear witness four times by Allah﴾, to the end of the verse. One should not depart from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an except for a proof that must be referred to, from the Book or the Sunnah. Abu Hanifa and Ahmad said: there is no *hadd* upon her for refusing the testimonies, and she is also imprisoned until she performs *li'an* or confesses, whereupon the *hadd* is applied to her.

The author of *al-Mughni* said: this was said by al-Hasan, al-Awza'i, and the companions of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*), and it was narrated from al-Harith al-'Ukli and 'Ata' al-Khurasani. Those who held this view argued with proofs, all of which return to the claim that what prevents the *hadd* upon her is that her fornication has not been established, because the husband's testimonies and her refusal establish neither individually nor together the proof of fornication against her.

The position of al-Shafi'i, Malik, and those who agreed with them on this question is more apparent in our view, because the matter of *li'an* is an independent principle that does not admit analogy with other matters. Therefore one does not depart in it from the apparent meaning of the explicit text toward analogy with another matter. And Allah knows best.

* *

(p. 466) Issues related to this noble verse:

The first issue: know that *li'an* is not obligatory between the spouses except by the husband's slander of his wife with slander that would make him liable to the *hadd* had he said it to someone other than a wife, such as accusing her of fornication or denying paternity of her child. The majority's position here is that for *li'an* to be obligatory it suffices that he accuses her of fornication, without the condition that he say "I saw it with my own eyes." This is more apparent to me than what is reported from Malik, that *li'an* is not obligatory until he explicitly states that he saw it with his own eyes, because accusation of fornication suffices without an explicit statement of seeing with one's own eyes.

As for the statement of the one performing *li'an* in the time of the Prophet ﷺ: "My eye saw and my ear heard," this does not indicate that if he limited himself to saying that she committed fornication, it would not suffice, without the condition of seeing with one's eyes and hearing with one's ears, as is not hidden. And Allah knows best.

* *

The second issue: know that the scholars differed over the testimonies of *li'an* mentioned in His saying: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah﴾ [al-Nur: 6], to the end of the verses, whether they are testimonies (*shahadat*) or oaths (*ayman*), in four positions:

The first: that they are testimonies, because Allah called them testimonies in the verse.

The second: that they are oaths.

The third: that they are oaths emphasized with the wording of testimony.

The fourth: the reverse of this.

The disagreement on this has the following consequence: whoever says they are testimonies holds that *li'an* is valid only from those whose testimony is acceptable, so the one performing *li'an* and the one against whom it is performed must be upright, along with the other conditions for the acceptance of testimony. Whoever says they are oaths holds that *li'an* is valid between any spouses, even if their testimony is not acceptable due to impiety or another factor that disqualifies testimony. The disagreement also has the following consequence: if three upright men testify along with the husband, then on the view that they are testimony, the husband is the fourth witness, and she is liable to the *hadd* for fornication. On the view that they are oaths, the three are subjected to the *hadd* and the husband performs *li'an*. It has been said that they are not subjected to the *hadd*. Among those who said they are testimonies, and that *li'an* is valid only from one whose testimony is accepted, and that she is subjected to the *hadd* on the testimony of the three along with the husband, is Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, and those who followed him. The majority hold that they are oaths emphasized with the wording of testimony.

The author of these notes, may God pardon him and forgive him, said: The most apparent of the positions in my view is that they are oaths emphasized by the word testimony, and that the word testimony is sometimes used in the Qur'an to mean oath, with the context indicating this. We have inclined to the view that they are oaths for several reasons:

The first: the verse explicitly uses the form of an oath in His saying: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah﴾ (p. 467), because the phrase "by Allah" is an oath. His saying "by Allah" indicates that the intended meaning of "testimony" is oath, since the explicit wording of oath is present. Thus "I testify by Allah" means "I swear by Allah."

The second: the Qur'an uses the word testimony to mean oath in His saying: ﴿They swear by Allah: our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 107]. Then He clarified that the intended meaning of that testimony is oath, in His saying: ﴿That is more likely that they would give testimony in its correct form, or fear that oaths would be repeated after their oaths﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 108]. So His saying "or fear that oaths would be repeated after their oaths" is evidence that the intended meaning of the word testimony in the verse is oath, and this is clear as you see.

Al-Qurtubi said: Among that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: We testify that you are surely the Messenger of Allah﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Munafiqun: 1], because His saying: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 2] indicates that the intended meaning of their testimony is oaths. Thus he said. But the inference from this verse is not definitive in my view, and Allah knows best.

The third: what Ibn al-'Arabi said. He said: "The decisive point is that it is an oath, not testimony, since the husband swears for himself to establish his claim and to free himself from the punishment. How could anyone claim in the law that a witness testifies for himself to something that establishes a judgment against another? This is far-fetched in principle and absent in consideration." End of his words, as conveyed through al-Qurtubi's quotation.

The summary of his argument is that inductive survey of the law, a complete *istiqra'* (inductive survey), shows that there is no instance in it of a person testifying for himself to something that establishes a judgment against another. This is a strong argument, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that a complete inductive survey is a valid proof, as we have explained many times. The claim of the Hanafis and those who agree with them, that the husband is not suspected and so his testimony for himself is not permitted, does not hold, since the apparent wording of the texts on the non-acceptance of a person's testimony for himself is absolute.

The fourth: what came in some transmissions of the *hadith* of *li'an*, that when the woman who had been cursed bore a child resembling the man she had been accused of, he ﷺ said: "Had it not been for the oaths, there would have been a matter between me and her." This is in Ahmad and Abu Dawud. In this transmission the Prophet ﷺ called the testimonies of *li'an* oaths. In the chain of this transmission is 'Abbad ibn Mansur, about whom more than one person has spoken, and it is said that he was a Qadari, among other of their proofs.

As for those who said that they are testimonies and not oaths, they argued that Allah called them testimonies in His saying: (p. 468) ﴿And they have no witnesses except themselves﴾, and in His saying: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies﴾, to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿And it shall avert from her the punishment that she bear witness four times﴾, to the end of the verse. They also argued with the *hadith*: "Four [categories] have no *li'an* between them and their husbands: a Jewish or Christian woman under a Muslim husband, a slave woman under a free husband, and a free woman under a slave husband." End of the quotation. They said: *li'an* is prohibited for the Jewish and Christian woman, the slave, and the slave woman only because they are not among those whose testimony is accepted. Had the testimonies of *li'an* been oaths, their *li'an* would have been valid, since their oath is accepted.

Al-Zayla'i said in *Nasb al-Raya*, regarding the *hadith* mentioned: "I say: Ibn Majah transmitted it in his *Sunan* from Ibn 'Ata', from his father 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Four types of women have no *li'an* between them and their husbands: the Christian woman under a Muslim, the Jewish woman under a Muslim, the slave woman under a free man, and the free woman under a slave.'" End of quotation.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 8 (part 2 of 5):**

Al-Daraqutni (may Allah have mercy on him) also narrated it in his *Sunan*, from Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Waqqasi, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb with this chain, and he said, from his grandfather Abdullah ibn Amr, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Four categories have no li'an (the oath of mutual cursing between spouses) between them: there is no li'an between a free person and a slave-woman; there is no li'an between a slave and a free woman; there is no li'an between a Muslim and a Jewish woman; and there is no li'an between a Muslim and a Christian woman." End of quotation. Al-Daraqutni said: "Al-Waqqasi is one whose hadith is abandoned (matruk al-hadith)." Then he narrated it from Uthman ibn Ata al-Khurasani, from his father, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb with this chain. He said: "Uthman ibn Ata al-Khurasani is very weak in hadith." Yazid ibn Zurayʿ followed him, narrating from Ata, and he too is weak. It was also narrated from al-Awza'i and Ibn Jurayj, who are two imams, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, as a statement of his (i.e., of Abdullah ibn Amr), and they did not raise it. Then he narrated it likewise as a mawquf (halted, not attributed to the Prophet). Then he narrated it from Ammar ibn Matar, who said: Hammad ibn Amr narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Rufay', from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Attab ibn Asid, [saying]: There is no li'an among four," and he mentioned something similar. He said: Ammar ibn Matar, Hammad ibn Amr, and Zayd ibn Rufay' are weak. End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi said in *al-Ma'rifa*: This is a hadith narrated by Uthman ibn Ata and Yazid ibn Zurayʿ al-Ramli, from Ata al-Khurasani, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Four categories have no mula'anah (mutual cursing) between them: a Christian woman under a Muslim husband..." to the end. He said: Ata al-Khurasani is known for frequent error, and his son Uthman and Ibn Zurayʿ are weak. It was also narrated by Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Waqqasi, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb with this chain, and he is one whose hadith is abandoned; Yahya ibn Ma'in and other imams declared him weak. It was also narrated by Ammar ibn Matar, from Hammad ibn Amr, from Zayd ibn Rufay', from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, and Ammar ibn Matar, Hammad ibn Amr, and Zayd ibn Rufay' are weak. (p. 469) It was also narrated from Ibn Jurayj and al-Awza'i, who are two imams, from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, as a mawquf.
