This is because all the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, agreed on writing *tasta'nisu* in all copies of the Uthmanic *Mushaf*, and on reciting it with the wording *tasta'nisu*. The consensus (*ijma'*, the agreement of the scholars) of the Muslims in the east and west of the earth in their copies and recitation has continued on this, without any objection. The Mighty Qur'an, Allah the Exalted has undertaken to preserve it from alteration and change, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. He also said about it: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it. It is a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fussilat: 42]. And He said: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16-17].

* *

Issues related to this noble verse.

The first issue: Know that this noble verse indicates, by its apparent meaning, that a person's entering another's house without seeking permission and greeting is not permitted, because His saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your houses﴾ (the verse) [al-Nur: 27] is an explicit prohibition. A prohibition that is free of contextual indicators conveys prohibition (*tahrim*) according to the more correct view, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*).

* *

The second issue: Know that seeking permission is three times. The one seeking permission says at each of them: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" If permission is not given to him at the third time, he should return, and he should not exceed three. This should not be disputed, because it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) with a certainty that has no flaw.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his *Sahih*: "'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, Yazid ibn Khusayfa narrated to us, from Busr ibn Sa'id, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: 'I was in a gathering of the Ansar when Abu Musa came as if he were frightened. He said: I sought permission from 'Umar three times, but permission was not given to me, so I returned. He said: What prevented you? I said: I sought permission three times, but permission was not given to me, so I returned. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If one of you seeks permission three times and permission is not given to him, let him return." He said: By Allah, you must bring evidence for this; is there anyone among you who heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ)? Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: By Allah, none will stand with you except the youngest of the people. I was the youngest of the people, so I stood with him, and I informed 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said that.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "Ibn 'Uyayna informed me: Yazid ibn Khusayfa narrated to me from Busr, I heard Abu Sa'id with this," and this is the wording from the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari. This is an explicit, authentic text from the Prophet (ﷺ) that seeking permission is three times, and if permission is not given after the third, one returns.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his *Sahih*: "'Amr ibn Muhammad ibn Bukayr al-Naqid narrated to me, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated to us, Yazid ibn Khusayfa narrated to us, by Allah, from Busr ibn Sa'id who said: I heard Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, say: 'I was sitting in Madinah in a gathering of the Ansar when Abu Musa came to us, alarmed or frightened. We said: What is your matter? He said: 'Umar sent for me to come to him, so I came to his door and greeted three times, but he did not return my greeting, so I went back. He said: What prevented you from coming to us? I said: I came to you and greeted at your door three times, but they did not return my greeting, so I went back. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If one of you seeks permission three times and permission is not given to him, let him return." 'Umar said: Bring evidence for it, or I will punish you. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: None will stand with him except the youngest of the people. Abu Sa'id said: I said: I am the youngest of the people. He said: Go with him.' Qutayba ibn Sa'id and Ibn Abi 'Umar narrated to us, both saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Khusayfa with this chain, and Ibn Abi 'Umar added in his narration: Abu Sa'id said: So I stood with him and went to 'Umar and testified.'" This is the wording from the *Sahih* of Muslim.

In another wording in Muslim, from the narration of Abu Sa'id, he said: "By Allah, I will surely make your back and belly ache, or you will bring someone who will testify for you on this. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: By Allah, none will stand with you except the youngest of us in age. Stand up, Abu Sa'id. So I stood until I came to 'Umar and said: I have heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say this."

In another wording in Muslim, from the narration of Abu Sa'id, he (Umar) said: "If this is something you memorized from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then produce it; otherwise I will make you an example." Abu Sa'id said: "So he came to us and said: Did you not know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Seeking permission is three times? They began to laugh. I said: Your Muslim brother has come to you, alarmed, and you laugh? Go; I will share this punishment with you. So he went to him and said: This is Abu Sa'id."

In another wording in Muslim, from the narration of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: "Abu Musa sought permission from 'Umar three times," up to his saying: "He said: You must bring evidence for this, or I will do such-and-such. So he left and went to a gathering of the Ansar, and they said: None will testify for you on this except the youngest of us. Abu Sa'id stood up and said: We were commanded with this. 'Umar said: This matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was hidden from me; the trade in the markets distracted me from it."

In another wording in Muslim, from the narration of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "You must come to me with this, or I will do such-and-such. So Abu Musa went. 'Umar said: If he finds evidence, you will find him at the pulpit in the evening; and if he does not find evidence, you will not find him. When evening came, they found him. He said: O Abu Musa, what do you say? Have you found it? He said: Yes, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him. 'Umar said: He is trustworthy. O Abu al-Tufayl, what does this man say? He said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say that, O son of al-Khattab; so do not be a punishment upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Umar said: Glory be to Allah! I only heard something and wished to verify it."

In another wording of Muslim: "'Umar said to Ubayy: O Abu al-Mundhir, did you hear it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? He said: Yes. So, O son of al-Khattab, do not be a punishment upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." This narration does not contain 'Umar's saying "Glory be to Allah" and what follows it.

These authentic narrations from Abu Sa'id, Abu Musa, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with them, clearly and authentically indicate that seeking permission is three times. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: "As for his saying: 'None will stand with him except the youngest of the people,' its meaning is that this is a famous hadith among us, known to our elders and our youngsters, to the extent that our youngest knows it and heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." End of quotation from him. The apparent meaning is as he said. These authentic, explicit narrations show that this seeking of permission, which the verse expresses by *istinas*, and the greeting mentioned in it, are not to be increased beyond three times, and that the *istinas* mentioned in the verse is seeking permission repeated three times. This is because the best way to explain the Book of Allah after the Book of Allah is the established Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

By this you know that what Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari*, that the meaning of *istinas* in His saying: ﴿until you have asked permission﴾ is seeking permission by clearing the throat or similar gestures, according to the majority, is contrary to careful verification. What he cited as evidence for it, from the narration of al-Tabari through Mujahid explaining the verse with what was mentioned, is not to be relied upon, along with the other evidences mentioned. The truth is what the authentic narrations have brought of seeking permission and greeting three times, as you have seen.

The correct view in this matter is what Ibn Hajar transmitted from al-Tabari through Qatada, who said: "*Istinas* is seeking permission three times," and so on to its end. The authentic narration from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Seeking permission is three times" is supported by the fact that he (ﷺ) used to act in this way.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 27 (part 2 of 4):

Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: In the narration of ʿUbayd ibn Ḥunayn, which I pointed to in al-Adab al-Mufrad, there is a useful addition, namely that Abu Saʿid, or Abu (p-496) Masʿud, said to ʿUmar: "We went out with the Prophet ﷺ, and he intended Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah, until he came to him and gave the greeting of peace, but he was not given permission. Then he gave the greeting a second time, and he was not given permission. Then he gave the greeting a third time, and he was not given permission. So he said: 'We have done what is incumbent upon us.' Then he returned, and Saʿd gave him permission." (The hadith continues.) Thus this is established from his saying ﷺ and from his action. The story of Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah was narrated by Abu Dawud in a lengthy form, with the same meaning, from the hadith of Qays ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah, and by Ahmad through the route of Thabit, from Anas or another, as it stands there. Al-Bazzar narrated it from Anas without any hesitation, and al-Tabarani narrated it from the hadith of Umm Tariq, the freed woman of Saʿd. End of the relevant point.

His statement "Thus this is established from his saying ﷺ and from his action" indicates that the account of his ﷺ seeking permission to enter upon Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah is sound and established.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this verse: Imam Ahmad said: ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated to us, ʿUmar informed us, from Thabit, from Anas or another, that "the Prophet ﷺ sought permission to enter upon Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah, and said: 'As-salamu ʿalayka wa-rahmatullah.' Saʿd said: 'Wa-ʿalaykas-salam wa-rahmatullah,' but he did not let the Prophet ﷺ hear it until he had given the greeting three times, and Saʿd returned the greeting to him three times without him hearing it. So the Prophet ﷺ returned, and Saʿd followed him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, may my father and mother be ransomed for you, every greeting you gave was in my ear, and I returned it to you without making you hear it, for I wished to increase your greetings and the blessing.' Then he brought him into the house, and set before him raisins, and the Prophet ﷺ ate. When he finished, he said: 'The righteous have eaten your food, the angels have sent blessings upon you, and the fasting ones have broken their fast with you.'"

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Abu ʿAmr al-Awza'i: I heard Yahya ibn Abi Kathir say: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Asʿad ibn Zurarah narrated to me, from Qays ibn Saʿd (that is, Ibn ʿUbadah), who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited us in our dwelling and said: 'As-salamu ʿalaykum wa-rahmatullah.' Saʿd returned it in a low voice. I said: 'Will you not give permission to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?' He said: 'Leave him, let him increase the greetings upon us.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'As-salamu ʿalaykum wa-rahmatullah,' and Saʿd returned it in a low voice. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'As-salamu ʿalaykum wa-rahmatullah.' Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned, and Saʿd followed him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I was hearing your greeting and returning it in a low voice so that you would increase the greetings upon us.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned back with him."

Ibn Kathir mentioned the story to its end, then said: This has been narrated through other routes, so it is a good and strong hadith, and Allah knows best.

From what we have mentioned, you know that the "istiʾnas" (seeking familiarity) in the verse means seeking permission three times, and that it does not mean clearing the throat or the like, as he attributed in Fath al-Bari to the majority (al-jumhur). It has been disputed whether the greeting is to be given first or the seeking of permission. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: The scholars agreed that seeking permission is prescribed, and the proofs of the Qur'an and the Sunnah and the consensus (ijma') of the Ummah support it. The Sunnah is that one gives the greeting and seeks permission three times, thus combining the greeting with seeking permission, as stated in the Qur'an. They differed as to whether it is recommended to give the greeting first and then seek permission, or to seek permission first and then give the greeting. The correct view, which the Sunnah brought and which the researchers (al-muhaqqiqun) affirmed, is that one gives the greeting first, saying: "As-salamu ʿalaykum, may I enter?" A second view is that one seeks permission first. A third view, which is the choice of al-Mawardi from among our companions, is that if the eye of the one seeking permission falls upon the owner of the house before he enters, he gives the greeting first; otherwise he seeks permission first. Two hadiths have been authentically related from the Prophet ﷺ regarding giving the greeting first." End of the relevant point in his wording.

It is not hidden that what has two authentic hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ takes precedence over other views, so one should not depart from giving the greeting before seeking permission. The phrase "tastaʾnisu" (seek familiarity), which means seeking permission, is mentioned before the greeting in His saying: ﴿until you seek permission and greet their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. This does not indicate that seeking permission is to be placed first, because conjunction with "wa" (and) does not necessarily imply sequence; it only implies general association. Thus it is permissible to conjoin the first with the last using "wa," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Mary, be devoted to your Lord, prostrate and bow with those who bow﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 43], where bowing (ruku') is mentioned before prostration (sujud), and His saying: ﴿And from you and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], where Noah came before our Prophet ﷺ. This is well known. What we have mentioned does not contradict the fact that "wa" is sometimes used for conjunction while intending sequence, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "I begin with what Allah began with," and in another narration: "Begin with what Allah began with," in the imperative form, and as the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

"You satirized Muhammad, and I answered on his behalf, and with Allah is the reward for that."

This is according to the narration with "wa" in this verse.

The clarification of this is that "wa," when stripped of contextual and external indicators, only implies general association between the conjoined and the conjoined-to. It does not preclude that if there is a proof for intending sequence in the conjunction, such as the hadith mentioned about beginning with al-Safa, or if a context indicates it, such as the verse mentioned, since the response to satire can only come after it, then it indicates sequence because a proof or context exists for that. The verse we are dealing with has no strong proof or context indicating that sequence is intended by "wa" in it. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his tafsir of this verse hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ in the Sunan and elsewhere, which indicate that the Prophet ﷺ repeatedly taught the manner of seeking permission to those who did not know it, by saying: "As-salamu ʿalaykum, may I enter?" So look into it. We have already mentioned that al-Nawawi stated that two authentic hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ support this. The preferred formula for seeking permission, from which one should not depart, is that the one seeking permission says: "As-salamu ʿalaykum, may I enter?" If permission is not given after the third time, he leaves, as the proofs indicate.

Know that the hadiths related about the story of ʿUmar with Abu Musa in the Sahih differ in their context. In some of them, ʿUmar sent for Abu Musa after he had departed, and he returned at once. In others, he did not come to him until the next day. Ibn Hajar reconciled them in al-Fath, saying: The apparent meaning of these two contexts is contradictory, for the first implies that he did not return to ʿUmar until the next day, while the second implies that ʿUmar sent for him immediately. Ibn Hajar continued: They may be reconciled thus: when ʿUmar finished the business that occupied him, he remembered him and asked about him, and was informed that he had returned, so he sent for him, but the messenger did not find him at that time, and he himself came to ʿUmar the next day. End of quotation. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

Points related to this issue.

First: Know that if the one seeking permission is certain that the people of the house heard him, he must leave after the third time, because when they heard him and did not give permission, this indicates non-permission. The authentic Sunnah has made clear that one should not exceed three times, contrary to those scholars who said he may exceed three absolutely. Likewise, if he does not know whether they heard him or not, he must leave after the third time, as we have explained with their proofs, and none of those proofs was restricted by his knowing that they heard him.

Second: Know that what appears to us to be the stronger view from the proofs is that if he knows that the people of the house did not hear his seeking permission, he should not exceed the third time, but should leave after it, due to the general applicability of the proofs and because none of them is restricted by their not having heard him. This is contrary to those who allowed him to increase, and those who made distinctions in this matter. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: As for when he seeks permission three times, is not given permission, and thinks that they did not hear him, there are three positions, the most well known of which is that he leaves and does not repeat seeking permission. The second is that he repeats it. The third is that if it was with the same wording as the earlier seeking of permission, he does not repeat it, and if it was with other wording, he repeats it. Whoever holds the more apparent view has as his proof the Prophet's saying ﷺ: "If he is not given permission, let him return." Whoever holds the second view interprets the hadith as referring to one who knows or thinks that they heard him and did not give permission. And Allah knows best.

The correct view, if Allah the Exalted wills, is what we have already put forward: not exceeding three times, because this is the apparent meaning of the texts, and it is not permissible to depart from the apparent meaning of a text except by a proof that must be followed, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul).

(p-499) Third: Some scholars said: The one seeking permission should not stand in front of the door, facing it directly, but should stand with the door to his right or left, and seek permission in that position. Ibn Kathir said: Then know that the one seeking permission upon the people of a house should not stand facing the door directly, but the door should be on his right or left, due to what Abu Dawud related: Mu'ammal ibn al-Fadl al-Harrani narrated to us along with others, they said: Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid narrated to us, Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Bishr, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to the door of a people, he did not face the door directly, but from its right or left corner, and he would say: 'As-salamu ʿalaykum, as-salamu ʿalaykum.' That was because the houses did not have curtains (sutur) over their doors at that time." Abu Dawud alone narrated it. Abu Dawud also said: ʿUthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Jarir narrated to us (with a transition, ḥ), and Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Hafs narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Talhah, from Hudhayl, who said: "A man came" (ʿUthman said: Saʿd [ibn Abi Waqqas]), "and stood at the door of the Prophet ﷺ seeking permission, and he stood facing the door," (ʿUthman said: facing the door), "so the Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'Move aside, or like this, for seeking permission is for avoiding gazing.'" Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it from Sufyan al-Thawri, from al-Aʿmash, from Talhah ibn Musarrif, from a man, from Saʿd, from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Dawud narrated it, from his hadith. End of Ibn Kathir's quotation. The two hadiths which he attributed to Abu Dawud we have taken from the Sunan of Abu Dawud, because the copy of Ibn Kathir available to us contains distortions in them.

What we have mentioned indicates what we mentioned: that the one seeking permission should not stand facing the door, for fear that when the door opens he will see something of the household that they do not want him to see. This is unlike when the door is to his right or left, for at the moment the door opens he does not see what is inside the house. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

Third issue: Know that if the owner of the house says to the one seeking permission, "Who are you?", it is not permissible for him to say, "I," but he should state his name and kunyah (honorific by-name) if he is known by it, because the word "I" is used by everyone to refer to himself, so the identity of the one seeking permission is not established by it. The meaning of this has been established from the Prophet ﷺ with an authenticity that cannot be challenged.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Abu al-Walid Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik narrated to us, Shu'bah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: I heard Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "I came to the Prophet ﷺ regarding a debt that was owed by my father, and I knocked on the door. He said: 'Who is it?' I said: 'I.' He said: 'I, I!' as if he disliked it." End of quotation. His ﷺ repetition of the word "I" is evidence that he did not approve of it from Jabir, because it does not identify the one seeking permission. So it is an answer to him ﷺ that does not correspond to his question. The apparent meaning of the hadith is that answering the one seeking permission with "I" is not permissible, because of the Prophet's ﷺ disapproval and his lack of acceptance of it. This is contrary to those who said it is disliked (makruh) in the sense of reprehensible but not forbidden (karahat tanzih), which is the view of the majority.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 27 (part 3 of 4):

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his Sahih: Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Numayr narrated to us, Abdullah ibn Idris narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "I came to the Prophet ﷺ and called out (to him). The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Who is it?' I said: 'I.' He came out saying: 'I, I.'"

Yahya ibn Yahya and Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, and the wording is that of Abu Bakr. He said: Yahya said: "Akhbarana" (informed us), and Abu Bakr said: "Haddathana" (narrated to us): Waki' narrated to us from Shu'bah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "I asked permission to enter upon the Prophet ﷺ. He said: 'Who is it?' I said: 'I.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'I, I.'"

Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and Abu Amir al-Aqadi narrated to us ("ḥ"), and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, Wahb ibn Jarir narrated to me ("ḥ"), and Abd al-Rahman ibn Bishr narrated to me, Bahz narrated to us, all of them from Shu'bah with this isnad. In their narration is: "It is as if he disliked that," the end of his quotation. The statement of Jabir, "as if he disliked that," indicates that it is not hidden that his repeating the word "I" was disliked by him, and that he did not approve of it. This hadith of Jabir was narrated by others than the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the rest of the (six) collections.

* *

The fourth issue: Know that the most evident view, from which one should not depart, is that a man must ask permission before entering upon his mother, his sister, and his adult sons and daughters, because if he enters upon any of those mentioned without permission, his eye may fall upon the private parts (awrat) of those mentioned, and that is not permissible for him.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, in his commentary on the hadith: "Indeed the permission was prescribed only because of the sight," the following text: "It is derived from it that seeking permission is prescribed upon everyone, even mahrams, so that one's private parts are not uncovered." Al-Bukhari also narrated in al-Adab al-Mufrad from Nafi': "When some of Ibn Umar's children reached puberty, he would not enter upon them except with permission." And by way of Alqamah: a man came to Ibn Mas'ud and said: "Shall I ask permission before entering upon my mother?" He said: "Yes, at all times, you want to see her." And by way of Muslim ibn Nudhayr (with the letter nun, diminutive): a man asked Hudhayfah: "Shall I ask permission before entering upon my mother?" He said: "If you do not ask permission upon her, you will see what you dislike." And by way of Musa ibn Talhah: "I entered with my father upon my mother, and he entered, and I followed him, and he pushed me in the chest and said: 'You enter without permission?'" And by way of Ata': "I asked Ibn Abbas: 'Shall I ask permission before entering upon my sister?'" He said: "Yes." I said: "She is in my care (hijr)?" He said: "Would you like to see her naked?" The chains of all these narrations are sound, the end of his quotation from Fath al-Bari.

These narrations from these Companions support what we have mentioned about asking permission before entering upon those we have mentioned. It is understood from the authentic hadith: "Indeed the permission was prescribed only because of the sight," so the sight falling upon the private parts of those mentioned is not permissible, as you see. Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his tafsir of the verse under discussion: Hushaym said: Ash'ath ibn Sawwar informed us, from Kurdus, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "It is incumbent upon you to ask permission before entering upon your mothers and sisters." Ash'ath said, from Adi ibn Thabit: "A woman from the Ansar said: 'O Messenger of Allah ﷺ, I am in my house in a state that I do not like anyone to see me in, neither a father nor a son, and a man from my household keeps entering upon me while I am in that state.' So there was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses...﴾ the verse." Ibn Jurayj said: I heard Ata' ibn Abi Rabah report from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "Three verses have been denied by people." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you with Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. He said: "And they say: 'Indeed the most honourable of you with Allah is the one with the greatest house.'" Up to his saying: "And all of the etiquette has been denied by people." He said: I said: "Shall I ask permission before entering upon my sisters, orphans in my care, who are with me in one house?" He said: "Yes." I repeated to him so that he would grant me a concession, but he refused, and said: "Would you like to see her naked?" I said: "No." He said: "Then ask permission." I returned to him, and he said: "Would you like to obey Allah?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then ask permission." Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn Tawus informed me from his father, who said: "There is no woman more hateful to me to see her private part than a non-mahram." He said: "And he was strict about that." Ibn Jurayj said, from al-Zuhri: I heard Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil al-Awdi, the blind, that he heard Ibn Mas'ud say: "It is incumbent upon you to ask permission before entering upon your mothers." End of the relevant point of his quotation. It indicates what we have mentioned about asking permission before entering upon those we have mentioned. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

The fifth issue: Know that if there is no one with a man in his house except his wife, the more evident view is that he does not ask permission upon her. This is understood from the apparent meaning of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own houses﴾. Also because there is no modesty (hishmah) between a man and his wife, and between them there are circumstances and intimacies that are not permissible for anyone else, even if it were a father, a mother, or a son, as is not hidden. And the narration we mentioned just above from Musa ibn Talhah supports this: that he entered with his father Talhah upon his mother, and Talhah rebuked him from entering upon his mother without permission, although Talhah, her husband, had entered without permission.

Ibn Kathir said in his "Tafsir": Ibn Jurayj said: "I said to Ata': 'Does a man ask permission before entering upon his wife?' He said: 'No.'" Then Ibn Kathir said: "This is to be understood as not obligatory; otherwise, it is better that he informs her of his entry and does not surprise her with it, since she may be in a state in which she does not like him to see her." Then Ibn Kathir quoted from Ibn Jarir, with his chain, from Zaynab, the wife of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When Abdullah came from some need and reached the door, he would clear his throat and spit, out of dislike that he should surprise us in something he disliked." He said: "Its chain is sound." End of the relevant point of his quotation. The first view is more evident, especially according to those who permit a husband to look at his wife's private part, such as Malik and his companions and those who agree with them. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

The sixth issue: If the people of the house say to the one seeking permission: "Go back," it is obligatory upon him to return, because of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back; it is purer for you﴾ [al-Nur: 28]. Some scholars used to wish, when they sought permission upon some of their friends, that they would say to him: "Go back," so that he would return, and thereby attain the virtue of returning mentioned in His words: ﴿it is purer for you﴾, because what Allah has said is purer for us undoubtedly contains good and reward for us. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

The seventh issue: Know that the strongest of the views in evidence and the most preponderant, concerning one who looks through an opening (kuwwah) into the inside of a people's house, so that they gouge out the eye with which he looked, in order to spy upon their private parts, is that there is no sin upon them in that, nor any liability for the blood-money of the eye, nor retaliation. This should not be departed from, since it is established from the Prophet ﷺ with an establishment that has no flaw; and for this reason we have not mentioned here the views of those scholars who disagreed on this, since they are discarded in our view, for they contradict the established text from him ﷺ. Al-Bukhari (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his "Sahih": "Chapter: Whoever looks into a people's house and they gouge out his eye, there is no blood-money for him." Then he mentioned among the hadiths of this chapter: Ali ibn Abdullah narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, Abu al-Zinad narrated to us, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah who said: Abu al-Qasim ﷺ said: "If a man looked at you without permission, and you struck him with a pebble and gouged out his eye, there would be no sin upon you." End of his quotation. Al-junah means sin (haraj). The Prophet's ﷺ saying in this sound hadith: "there would be no sin upon you" — the word junah is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it generalises the lifting of every liability, whether sin, blood-money or retaliation, as you see.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his "Sahih": Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to me, Jarir narrated to us, from Suhayl, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever looks into a people's house without their permission, it is lawful for them to gouge out his eye." End of his quotation.

This sound hadith explicitly states from him ﷺ that it is lawful for them to gouge out his eye, and that this being lawful for them necessarily implies that there is no sin upon them in it, nor blood-money, nor retaliation; for whatever Allah has made lawful through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, there is absolutely no accountability for doing it in any kind of accountability, as is not hidden.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (may Allah have mercy on him), in his "Sahih," immediately connected to this statement of his that we have quoted from him, said: Ibn Abi Umar narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu al-Zinad, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If a man looked at you without permission, and you struck him with a pebble and gouged out his eye, there would be no sin upon you." End of his quotation.

We have explained the aspect of its indication that there is nothing for the eye of the mentioned person, and the establishment of this from the Prophet ﷺ, as you have seen, indicates that when he transgressed and violated the sanctity, and looked into another's house without permission, Allah permitted, through the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ, the taking of his treacherous eye, and that it is waste (hadr), with no blood-money, no retaliation, and no sin. What we have mentioned is further confirmed and clarified by what came from him ﷺ, that he intended to do that.

Al-Bukhari (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his Sahih under the chapter mentioned just above, which is his saying: "Chapter: Whoever looks into a people's house and they gouge out his eye, there is no blood-money for him": Abu al-Yaman narrated to us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Anas, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "A man looked into one of the holes of the Prophet's ﷺ (dwellings), so he went towards him with an arrowhead (mishqas) or arrowheads, and began to stalk him in order to stab him."

Qutaybah ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Layth narrated to us, from Ibn Shihab, that Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi informed him "that a man looked through a hole in the door of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was a comb with which he was scratching his head. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw him, he said: 'If I knew that you were watching me, I would have stabbed you in your eyes with it.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Indeed the permission was prescribed only because of the sight.'" End of his quotation. Al-Bukhari mentioned these hadiths that we have mentioned from him here in the Book of Blood-Money (Diyat).

He also said in the Book of Seeking Permission (Isti'dhan): "Chapter: Seeking permission because of the sight": Ali ibn Abdullah narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us. Al-Zuhri said: "I memorised it just as you are here from Sahl ibn Sa'd," who said: "A man looked through a hole into the rooms of the Prophet ﷺ, and with the Prophet ﷺ was a comb with which he was scratching his head. He said: 'If I knew that you were looking, I would have stabbed you in your eye. Indeed the permission was prescribed only because of the sight.'"

Musaddad narrated to us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him): "A man looked from one of the rooms of the Prophet ﷺ, so the Prophet ﷺ went towards him with an arrowhead or arrowheads, and it is as if I see him stalking the man in order to stab him."

These sound texts support what we have mentioned, so no attention is to be paid to those scholars who opposed them, nor to those who interpreted them away; for a clear text may not be departed from except by a proof that obligates returning to it.

Know that al-mishqas, with a kasra on its first letter, a sukun on its second, and a fatha on its third, is the blade of an arrow when it is long and not broad. The word in the mentioned hadith, "from a hole in the rooms of the Prophet ﷺ": the first "juhr" (hole), with a damma on the jim and sukun on the unpointed ha, is every round opening in ground or wall; the second, with a damma on the unpointed ha and fatha on the jim, is the plural of hujrah, which is a section of the house.

And the Prophet's (ﷺ) hadith: Imam Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his Sahih: Yahya ibn Yahya, Abu Kamil Fudayl ibn al-Husayn and Qutaybah ibn Sa'id narrated to us, and the wording is that of Yahya and Abu Kamil. Yahya said: "Akhbarana (he informed us)," and the other two said: "Hadathana (he narrated to us)," Hammad ibn Zayd, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him): "A man looked into one of the rooms of the Prophet (ﷺ), so he came toward him with a mishqas or mashaqis (a broad arrowhead or arrowheads). I seem to see the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stalking him in order to stab him." And in a wording in Muslim, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi: "A man looked through a hole in the door of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a comb with which he was scratching his head. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him, he said: 'If I had known that you were looking at me, I would have thrust it into your eye.' And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Permission to enter was only prescribed because of the sight.'" Muslim has other narrations with this same meaning, but we have sufficed with what we have mentioned.

These authentic texts that we have mentioned should not be departed from, nor should they be interpreted without a sound basis from the Book or the Sunnah. For this reason we have chosen what has come in them, that the eye of that treacherous person may be lawfully taken and its loss is unrecompensed (hadr), and we have not paid attention to any opinion of those who opposed that, nor to their interpretation of the texts without a basis to which one must return. And Allah knows best.

* *

The eighth issue: Know that when the owner of a house sends a messenger to a person asking him to come to him, the scholars have differed: Does sending to him count as permission, because he has requested his presence by sending to him? According to this view, if he comes to the house of the one who sent for him, he may enter without a new permission, relying on the sending. Or must he seek permission when he comes to the house, asking for permission anew, and not rely on the sending? Each of the two opinions has been held by some of the scholars. Those who said that sending to him is permission that suffices instead of seeking permission upon arriving at the house argued with what Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan: Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Hammad narrated to us, from Habib and Hisham, from Muhammad, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The messenger of a man to a man is his permission." Husayn ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, Abd al-A'la narrated to us, Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you is invited to a meal and comes with the messenger, that is permission for him." Abu Ali al-Lu'lu'i said: I heard Abu Dawud say: "Qatadah did not hear anything from Abu Rafi'." End of quote from Abu Dawud.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: Qatadah's hearing from him has been established in the hadith that will come in al-Bukhari in the Book of Tawhid, through the narration of Sulayman al-Taymi, from Qatadah: "That Abu Rafi' narrated to him." End of quote.

What supports the soundness of what Abu Dawud narrated, and what al-Bukhari narrated as a suspended (mu'allaq) report, is his chapter heading: "Chapter: If a man is invited and comes, does he seek permission?" Sa'id narrated from Qatadah, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It is his permission." End of quote. It is well known that al-Bukhari does not state a report in the definitive form (with a firm attribution) unless it is sound in his view, as we have mentioned repeatedly. Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath, regarding the hadith that "the messenger of a man to a man is his permission": it has a supporting narration (mutabi') that al-Bukhari recorded in al-Adab al-Mufrad through the route of Muhammad ibn Sirin from Abu Hurayrah, with the wording "The messenger of a man to a man is his permission." He also cited a supporting report (shahid) stopping at Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "If a man is invited, then that is his permission," and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet). End of the point relevant to the subject.

This is the body of evidence of those who said that the one who is invited does not seek permission when he arrives.

As for those who said that he seeks permission when he arrives at the house of the one who sent for him, and does not rely on the sending of the messenger, they argued with what al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, Umar ibn Dharr narrated to us; and Muhammad ibn Muqatil narrated to me, Abdullah informed us, Umar ibn Dharr informed us, Mujahid informed us, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I entered with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he found milk in a bowl, so he said: 'Abu Hirr, go and call the people of the Suffah (Ahl al-Suffah) to me.' He said: So I went to them and invited them, and they came and sought permission, and he gave them permission, and they entered." End of quote from it. He said: This sound hadith is explicit that he (ﷺ) sent Abu Hirr to the people of the Suffah, and they did not rely on the sending instead of seeking permission. Had it sufficed in place of it, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have explained that, because he does not delay explanation past the time of need.

Among the evidence of the proponents of this view is the apparent generality of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked for permission and greeted their occupants﴾, the verse, because its apparent meaning includes the one who was sent for and others. Some scholars have reconciled the evidence of both views. Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: Al-Muhallab and others reconciled by applying these rulings to two different circumstances: if a long time passes between the invitation and the coming, he needs to renew the seeking of permission; likewise if little time passes but the one who invited is in a place where, customarily, permission is needed; otherwise he does not need to renew the permission. Ibn al-Tin said: Perhaps the first ruling applies to one who knows that there is no one with him for whose sake he must ask permission, and the second is the opposite. He said: Seeking permission in every circumstance is more cautious. Others said: If he arrives in the company of the messenger, the messenger's seeking permission suffices for him, and the greeting of meeting is enough for him; but if he lags behind the messenger, he needs to seek permission. Al-Tahawi reconciled in this way, and argued with the words in the hadith, "they came and sought permission," which indicates that Abu Hurayrah was not with them; otherwise it would have said "we came." Thus he said. End of Ibn Hajar's words.

The closest of these to me is the last reconciliation, and the hadith mentioned in it supports it, as does the statement in the hadith of Abu Dawud mentioned above: "came with the messenger, then that is permission for him." And Allah knows best.

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ ﴿And say to the believing women that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts.﴾

Allah, Exalted and Most High, commanded the believing men and women to lower their gaze and to guard their private parts. Included in guarding the private parts is guarding them from unlawful intercourse (zina), from sodomy (liwat, the act of the people of Lut), and from sexual activity between women (musahaqa), and guarding them from being exposed to people and uncovered before them. Other verses have shown that guarding it from the physical contact implied by this verse is required in every case except with one's wife and one's concubine (sariyya, a slave woman owned by the master). This is in the saying of Allah, the Exalted, in Surat al-Mu'minun and Surat Sa'ala sa'il: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their spouses or what their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5-6] and [al-Ma'arij: 29-30].

This verse has clarified that guarding the private parts from unlawful intercourse and sodomy is obligatory, and that guarding it is not required with regard to one's wife or the woman one owns as a concubine.

We have explained in Surat al-Baqara that a man is obligated to guard his private part from having intercourse with his wife in the anus, and we mentioned many proofs for that. We have also clarified the discussion of the verse ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5] in Surat Qad aflaha al-mu'minun. Allah, the Exalted, has promised those men and women who obey His command in this verse forgiveness and a great reward, provided they also do the qualities mentioned with it in Surat al-Ahzab. This is in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ up to (p-507) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the men and women who guard their private parts, and the men and women who remember Allah often, Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35].

He also emphasized the obligation of guarding the private part from fornication in other verses:

- such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not approach fornication. Indeed, it is ever an immorality and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra': 32];
- and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse. And whoever does that will meet a penalty. The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein humiliated, except one who repents﴾ [al-Furqan: 68-70], and other verses.

He also clarified the obligation of guarding the private part from sodomy and stated that it is transgression in several verses about the people of Lut:

- such as His saying: ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds, and leave what your Lord has created for you of your wives? Rather, you are a transgressing people﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 165-166];
- and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Lut, when he said to his people, "Indeed, you commit an immorality no one in the worlds has preceded you in. Do you approach men and cut off the road and commit wrong in your gatherings?"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 28-29],

and other verses.

We have explained the words of the scholars and their proofs regarding the punishment of the one who commits the immorality of sodomy in Surat Hud, and the punishment of the adulterer at the beginning of this noble surah.

Know that the command to guard the private part includes guarding it from being exposed to people. Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: "Guarding the private part is sometimes by preventing it from fornication, as Allah said: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5], and sometimes by guarding it from being looked at, as came in the hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad and the Sunan: 'Guard your 'awra except from your wife or what your right hand possesses.'" End of quote from him.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze﴾, al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Min (from) is for partitive emphasis, and the intended meaning is lowering the gaze from what is forbidden and restricting it to what is permitted. Al-Akhfash allowed that it could be extra (zaida), but Sibawayh rejected that. If you ask: How did it enter 'lowering the gaze' and not 'guarding the private part'? I say: To show that the matter of looking is broader. Do you not see that there is no harm in looking at the hair, chests, breasts, upper arms, shins and feet of unmarriageable relatives (mahram), and likewise at slave girls being displayed, and that a non-mahram woman's face, palms and feet may be looked at according to one of the two narrations? As for the matter of the private part, it is restricted. It is enough to show the difference that looking is permitted except for what is excluded from it, while intercourse is forbidden except for what is excluded from it. It is also possible that, along with guarding it from leading to what is not lawful, it means guarding it from being exposed."

And from Ibn Zayd: "Everything in the Qur'an about guarding the private part is about fornication, except this, for he meant by it concealment." End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

What is transmitted from Ibn Zayd, that the intended meaning of guarding the private part in this verse is concealment, is questionable. Rather, it enters primarily to include guarding it from fornication and sodomy. Among the proofs for this is that the command to lower the gaze is mentioned before the command to guard the private part, because looking is the messenger of fornication, as its explanation will come shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills. As for what was mentioned about the permissibility of looking at unmarriageable relatives, some of it is not free from looking, and its verification and details will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in Surat al-Ahzab, as we promised in the introduction to this blessed book, that we will clarify the issue of hijab in Surat al-Ahzab.

Al-Zamakhshari's statement that min in His saying ﴿lower their gaze﴾ is for partitive emphasis was said by others. Al-Qurtubi strengthened it with the hadiths reported that a glance by surprise (nazrat al-fuja'a) carries no blame, but one must then lower his gaze afterward and not deliberately look at what is not lawful. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned from al-Akhfash, and what al-Qurtubi and others mentioned, that min is extra, is not to be relied upon. Al-Qurtubi said: "It was said that ghadd means decrease. It is said: Fulan ghadda min Fulan, meaning he diminished him. So when the gaze is not allowed to do its function, it is diminished and reduced. Thus min is connected to ghadd, and it is neither partitive nor extra." End of his words.

Our view is that the root ghadd transitively takes its object directly and also takes it with the particle min, and similar to that is common in Arabic speech. Among the examples of ghadd taking an object directly is the saying of Jarir:

*So lower the glance, for you are from Numayr; you have not reached Ka'b, nor Kilab.*

And the saying of 'Antara:

*And I lower my glance whenever my neighbor appears to me, until my neighbor's dwelling covers her.*

And the saying of another:

*Lowering the glance was not our nature, but we among Mudhhij are ravens.*

Because His saying "ghadd al-tarf" is a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its object without a particle.

Among the examples of ghadd taking min is His saying: ﴿lower from their gaze﴾ and ﴿lower from their gaze﴾. What is mentioned here about the command to lower the gaze has also been accompanied in another verse by a warning to those who do not comply and do not lower their gaze from the forbidden. It is His saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ [Ghafir: 19].

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan said to al-Hasan: Indeed, the women of the non-Arabs uncover their chests and heads. He said: Turn your gaze away from them. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze from their sights and guard their private parts﴾. Qatada said: from what is not lawful for them. ﴿And say to the believing women that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾. The treachery of the eyes is looking at what one has been forbidden." End of the relevant part of his words verbatim.

From this you know that His saying ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ contains a threat to whoever betrays with his eye by looking at what is not lawful for him. What the two verses indicate of the prohibition against looking at what is not lawful has been explained in many hadiths.

Among them is what is established in the Sahih, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of sitting on the roadsides." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have no choice but to sit in our gatherings where we talk." He said: "If you insist on sitting, then give the road its right." They said: "And what is the right of the road, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Lowering the gaze, removing harm, returning the greeting, commanding good, and forbidding evil." End of quote. This is the wording of al-Bukhari in his Sahih.

Among them is what is established in the Sahih from Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) let al-Fadl ibn Abbas ride behind him on the day of sacrifice, on the back of his mount. Al-Fadl was a handsome man. The Prophet (ﷺ) stopped for the people to give them rulings. A woman from Khath'am, who was beautiful, came asking the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a ruling. Al-Fadl began to look at her, her beauty impressing him. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned while al-Fadl was looking at her, so he put his hand and took hold of al-Fadl's chin and turned his face away from looking at her." The hadith continues.

The point of evidence in it is that he (ﷺ) turned al-Fadl's face away from looking at her, which shows that looking at her was not permissible. The argument of those who hold that a woman may uncover her face in the presence of non-mahram men, based on the Khath'ami woman uncovering her face in this hadith, will be answered, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the discussion of the issue of hijab in Surat al-Ahzab. (p-510)

Among them is what is established in the two Sahihs and others: that the looking of the eye at what is not lawful for it is that by which she becomes an adulteress. It is established in the Sahih from Ibn Abbas that he said: "I have not seen anything more resembling minor sins (lamam) than what Abu Hurayra said from the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Allah has prescribed for the son of Adam his share of fornication, he will inevitably encounter it. The fornication of the eye is looking, the fornication of the tongue is speech, the soul wishes and desires, and the private part either confirms all that or denies it.'" End of quote. This is the wording of al-Bukhari, and the hadith is agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayhi), and in some of its narrations there is an addition to what we have mentioned here.

The point of evidence in it is his (ﷺ) saying: "The fornication of the eye is looking." Calling looking at what is not lawful by the name of fornication is clear evidence of its prohibition and of warning against it. Hadiths of this kind are many and well known.

It is well known that looking is the cause of fornication. Whoever looks often at the beauty of a woman, for example, may through it have her love take root in his heart to such an extent that it becomes the cause of his ruin, and we seek refuge in Allah. Thus looking is the messenger of fornication. Muslim ibn al-Walid al-Ansari said:

*A glance earned my heart, to please it; my eye became misery and ruin.*

*Nothing has passed over me that is harder than desire; glory be to Him who created desire and is exalted.*

Another said:

*Do you not see that the eye is a scout for the heart? The two eyes do not become familiar with anything unless the heart becomes familiar with it.*

Another said:

*And when you send your glance out as a scout for your heart one day, the sights will exhaust you.*

*You see what you are not able to have all of, nor are you patient with part of it.*

Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi said:

*I am the one whose glance brought about death for himself; so who is the pursuer, and who is the slain and the slayer?*

Ibn al-Jawzi, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his book Dhamm al-Hawa good, beneficial sections in which he explained the harms that looking causes and warned against it. He mentioned many poems of the poets and prose wisdom sayings concerning that, and all of it is known. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾. Know first that the statements of the scholars concerning this verse all go back to three opinions:

The first: that "adornment" here refers to a part of the woman's body itself, such as her face and her palms.

The second: that "adornment" is what one adorns oneself with, external to her body.

According to this second opinion, there are two views regarding the adornment mentioned, which is external to the woman's body:

One of them: that it is the adornment whose display does not involve the seeing of any part of the body, such as the outer garment (mulaya) a woman wears over the shirt, the headcover (khimar), and the wrapper (izar).

The second: that it is the adornment whose display does involve the seeing of a part of the body, such as kohl (antimony) in the eye, for it involves seeing the face or part of it; and dye (khidab) and the ring, for seeing them necessarily entails seeing the hand; and earrings, necklaces and bracelets, for seeing these necessarily entails seeing the part of the body where they are placed, as is not hidden.

We will mention some of the statements of the people of knowledge on this, then we will explain which of what is understood from the verses of the Qur'an is preponderant.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾: That is, they should not display any of their adornment to non-mahram men, except what cannot be concealed. Ibn Mas'ud said: such as the outer garment and clothing, meaning in accordance with what the women of the Arabs used to do with the veil (miqna'a) that covers their garments, and what appears of the lower parts of garments; there is no blame upon her for this, because she cannot conceal it. Its parallel in women's dress is what shows of her izar and what cannot be concealed. Al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Abu al-Jawza', Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others said the same as Ibn Mas'ud. Al-A'mash related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾, that he said: her face, her palms and the ring. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Sha'tha', al-Dahhak, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others something similar. This may be an explanation of the adornment which they were forbidden to display, as Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i related from Abu al-Ahwas, from 'Abd Allah, who said regarding His saying: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment﴾: the adornment is the earring, the armlet, the anklet and the necklace. In another narration from him with this chain, he said: The adornment is of two kinds: an adornment that no one sees except the husband, the ring and the bracelet; and an adornment that is seen by non-mahram men, which is what is apparent of the garments. (p-512) Al-Zuhri said: What appears to those whom Allah has named, to whom it is permissible [for her to reveal it], is only the bracelets, the head-coverings (akhmira) and the earrings, without uncovering; as for the common people, only the rings appear of it. Malik related from al-Zuhri regarding ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾: the ring and the anklet. It is possible that Ibn 'Abbas and those who followed him intended by "what appears thereof" the face and the two palms, and this is the well-known view of the majority, and it is supported by the hadith which Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan:

Ya'qub ibn Ka'b al-Antaki and Mu'ammal ibn al-Fadl al-Harrani related to us, both saying: al-Walid related to us, from Sa'id ibn Bashir, from Qatada, from Khalid ibn Duraik, from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "That Asma' bint Abi Bakr entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) wearing thin garments, and he turned away from her and said: 'O Asma', when a woman reaches menstruation, it is not proper that anything of her be seen except this,' and he pointed to his face and his palms." But Abu Dawud and Abu Hatim al-Razi said: it is mursal; Khalid ibn Duraik did not hear from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and Allah knows best. End of Ibn Kathir's words.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾: People differed about the extent of that. Ibn Mas'ud said: the apparent adornment is the garments. Ibn Jubayr added: the face. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also, and 'Ata' and al-Awza'i said: the face, the two palms and the garments. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Miswar ibn Makhrama said: the apparent adornment is kohl, the bracelet, dye up to half the forearm, earrings, rings and the like; it is permissible for the woman to display this to every person who enters upon her. Al-Tabari related from Qatada, regarding the meaning of half the forearm, a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), and related another from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day, when she has reached maturity, to display anything except her face and her hands up to here," and he grasped half the forearm.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It appears to me from the wording of the verse that the woman is commanded not to display, and to strive in concealing everything that is adornment, and the exception occurs in what appears by necessity of movement in what is unavoidable, or for the sake of a matter that needs attending to, and the like. So what appears in this manner, of what necessity brings about for women, is what is pardoned.

I say: This is a good opinion, except that since the majority of the face and the two palms usually and customarily appear, and in worship, namely in prayer and Hajj, it is suitable that the exception refers to these two; what supports this is what Abu Dawud related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, then al-Qurtubi mentioned the hadith of 'A'isha mentioned above, which we have already presented shortly before, then he said: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad, one of our scholars, said: if a woman is beautiful and there is fear of temptation from her face and palms, then it is obligatory upon her to cover that; and if she is an old woman or unattractive, it is permissible for her to uncover her face and palms. End of the relevant part of al-Qurtubi's words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The adornment is what a woman adorns herself with of jewelry, kohl or dye. What is apparent of it, such as the ring, the fat'a (a ring/bezel), kohl and dye, there is no harm in it; and what is hidden of it, such as the bracelet, the anklet, the armlet, the necklace, the crown, the shawl (wishah), and the earring, she should not display except to those mentioned. He mentioned the adornment without its places, for the sake of emphasis on the command to guard and to conceal; because this adornment falls upon places of the body which it is not lawful to look at for anyone other than these, namely the forearm, the shin, the upper arm, the neck, the head, the chest and the ear. So He forbade the display of the adornment itself, so that it would be known that if looking at it is not lawful because it accompanies those places, then, since looking at it apart from its accompanying those places is not disputed as to its permissibility, looking at the places themselves is all the more firmly forbidden, firmly established in prohibition, a witness that women ought to be careful about covering them and fear Allah regarding uncovering them. End of his words.

The author of "al-Durr al-Manthur" said: 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding His saying: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment﴾ he said: The adornment is the bracelet, the armlet, the anklet, the earring and the necklace; ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the garments and the jilbab.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The adornment is of two kinds: an apparent adornment and a hidden adornment that no one sees except the husband. As for the apparent adornment: the garments; and as for the hidden adornment: the kohl, the bracelet and the ring. The wording of Ibn Jarir: "As for what is apparent of it: the garments; and what is hidden: the two anklets, the two earrings and the two bracelets."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Anas regarding His saying: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the kohl and the ring.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the kohl, the ring, the earring and the necklace.

(p-514) 'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: it is the dye of the palm and the ring.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: her face, her palms and the ring.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the area of the face and the inner part of the palm.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she was asked about the apparent adornment, and she said: the qulb and the fataKh, and she gathered the end of her sleeve.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from 'Ikrima regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the face and the hollow of the throat.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the face and the palm.

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ata' regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the two palms and the face.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, regarding ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the two anklets (or bracelets), the ring and the kohl.

Qatada said: It has reached me that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day, except up to here," and he grasped half the forearm. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama regarding His saying: ﴿except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the two bracelets (qulbayn), meaning the bracelet, the ring and the kohl.

Sa'id and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except that which [necessarily] appears thereof﴾ he said: the ring and the masaka (a type of bangle). Ibn Jurayj said: 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: the qulb and the fatkha. "'A'isha said: My brother's daughter, the daughter of my maternal sister 'Abd Allah ibn al-Tufayl, came in to me adorned, and she entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and he turned away. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: She is my brother's daughter and a young girl. He said: 'When a woman has reached maturity, it is not lawful for her to display anything except her face and what is below (p-515) this,' and he grasped his own forearm, leaving between his grip and the palm the width of another grip." End of the relevant part of the words of the author of "al-Durr al-Manthur."

You have seen in these reported statements from the early generation the views of the scholars concerning the apparent adornment and the hidden adornment, and that all of them go back, in general, to three opinions, as we have mentioned:

The first: that what is meant by adornment is what a woman adorns herself with, external to the original form of her creation, and looking at it does not necessitate seeing any part of her body; such as the statement of Ibn Mas'ud and those who agree with him: that it is the outer garments, because garments are an adornment for her external to the original form of her creation, and they are apparent by necessity, as you see.

This opinion is the most apparent of the opinions in our view, and the most cautious, and the furthest from suspicion and causes of temptation.

The second opinion: that what is meant by adornment is also what a woman adorns herself with, and is not from the original form of her creation, but looking at that adornment necessitates seeing some part of the woman's body, such as dye and kohl and the like; because looking at that necessitates seeing the place of the body adjoining it, as is not hidden.

The third opinion: that what is meant by the apparent adornment is some part of the woman's body which is from the original form of her creation; such as the statement of one who said that what is meant by "what appears thereof" is the face and the two palms, and what was mentioned earlier from some of the people of knowledge.

Now that you understand this, know that we mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that among the types of clarification it contains is that some scholars state an opinion concerning a verse, while within the same verse there is an indicator showing that this opinion is not sound. We also mentioned in its introduction that among the types of clarification it contains is that the most frequent usage in the Qur'an is for a particular meaning to be intended by a word, with that word repeated in the Qur'an. That this meaning is most often the one intended by the word indicates that it is the one intended in the disputed place, because of the indication that its frequent intention with that word in the Qur'an is dominant. We mentioned some examples of this in the introduction.

Now that you know this, know that these two types of clarification, which we mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book and illustrated with several examples, are both present in this verse that we are addressing.

As for the first, its clarification is that the saying of whoever says, regarding ﴿and not to show their adornment except what [necessarily] appears thereof﴾, that what is meant by the adornment is the face and the palms, for example, there is in the verse an indicator showing that this opinion is not sound (p-516). This is because adornment in the language of the Arabs is what a woman adorns herself with that is external to her original creation, such as jewelry and fine garments. Therefore, explaining adornment as part of a woman's body is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it is not permissible to interpret it that way except with an evidence to which one must return. By this you know that the saying of whoever says "the apparent adornment is the face and the palms" is contrary to the apparent meaning of the verse's wording, and this is an indicator against the soundness of this opinion. So it is not permissible to interpret it that way except with a separate evidence to which one must return.

As for the second type of clarification mentioned, its explanation is that the word "adornment" occurs very frequently in the Glorious Qur'an meaning the adornment external to the original of the thing adorned with it, and not meaning some parts of that adorned thing itself:

• such as the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O Children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer﴾ [al-A'raf: 31],
• and His words: ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 32],
• and His words: ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ [al-Kahf: 7],
• and His words: ﴿And whatever you have been given of a thing – it is but the enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment﴾ [al-Qasas: 60],
• and His words: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars﴾ [as-Saffat: 6],
• and His words: ﴿And horses and mules and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [an-Nahl: 8], and the verse continues,
• and His words: ﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment﴾ [al-Qasas: 79], and the verse continues,
• and His words: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], and the verse continues,
• and His words: ﴿Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], and the verse continues,
• and His words: ﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59],
• and His words about the people of Moses: ﴿But we were made to carry loads of the adornment of the people﴾ [Ta-Ha: 87],
• and His words: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet to make known what they conceal of their adornment﴾ [an-Nur: 31].

So the word "adornment" in all these verses means that with which a thing is adorned, which is not part of its original creation, as you see. The fact that this meaning is the most frequent for the word "adornment" in the Qur'an indicates that the word "adornment" in the disputed place is intended with this meaning, the one whose intention predominates in the Glorious Qur'an, and which is well known in the speech of the Arabs, such as the words of the poet:

"They take their adornment, the finest of what you see,
and when they go without it, they are the best of the unadorned."

By this you know that explaining "adornment" in the verse as the face and the two palms is open to scrutiny.

Since you know that what is meant by "adornment" in the Qur'an is that with which one adorns oneself, which is external to the original creation, and that the scholars who explained it this way disagreed into two opinions: some said it is an adornment whose looking at does not necessarily entail seeing any part of a woman's body, such as outer garments. Others said it is an adornment whose looking at necessarily entails seeing its place on a woman's body, such as kohl, henna dye, and the like (p-517).

The author of these notes – may Allah pardon him and forgive him – says: The more preferable of the two opinions mentioned, in my view, is the opinion of Ibn Mas'ud – may Allah be pleased with him – that the apparent adornment is that whose looking at does not necessarily entail seeing any part of the body of a non-related woman. We only said that this opinion is the more preferable because it is the most cautious of the opinions and the furthest from causes of temptation (fitna), and the purest for the hearts of men and women. It is not hidden that the face of a woman is the essence of her beauty, and seeing it is among the greatest causes of being tempted by her, as is known. What is customary according to the rules of the Noble Shari'a is complete safeguarding and keeping far from falling into what is not fitting.

Know that the matter of the veil, and clarifying that it is not permissible for a man to look at any part of the body of a non-related woman, whether the face and palms or other than them, is something we promised in the introduction to this blessed book and elsewhere, that we will clarify in the surah of "al-Ahzab," in the discussion of the verse of the veil. Allah willing, we will fulfil this promise with what makes clear to the fair-minded person what we have mentioned.

Know that the hadith we mentioned in the words of Ibn Kathir in [the collection of] Abu Dawud, which is the hadith of Aisha concerning Asma' entering upon the Prophet ﷺ in thin garments, and he said to her: "When a woman reaches menstruation, it is not proper that anything of her be seen except this," and he pointed to his face and his two palms – is a weak hadith according to the people of knowledge of hadith, as we previously quoted from Ibn Kathir that he said about it: Abu Dawud and Abu Hatim al-Razi said: it is mursal (broken in its chain), and Khalid ibn Duraik did not hear from Aisha.

The matter is as he said. In any case, Allah willing, we will explain this issue with a thorough explanation, together with discussing the evidences of all parties, in the surah of "al-Ahzab." For this reason we have not lengthened the discussion of it here.

* *

Note.
We have mentioned in the words of the people of knowledge concerning adornment the names of many types of adornment. Perhaps some of those who look into this book do not know the meaning of those types of adornment, so we wished to explain them here to complete the benefit.

As for kohl and dye, they are well known. The most famous type of women's dye is henna. The earring (qurt) is what is hung from the lobe of the ear, and its plural is qirata, like qiradah, qirat, qurut, and aqrat. From it is the saying of the poet:

"May I eat blood if I do not make you [the enemy] feel [my wrath] with a co-wife,
far from the place where the earring hangs, fragrant in her scent."

The ring (khatam) is well known; it is an ornament of the fingers. The fatakh is the plural of fatkha, with fatakhat, and it is a silver ring without a bezel (stone). If it has a bezel, then it is a khatam. It was said: the fatkha may have a bezel, and in that case it is a type of ring. Women wear the fatkha on the fingers of their hands, and sometimes a woman places it on the toes of her feet. From this is the saying of the female reciter, who was al-Dahna' daughter of Mishal, wife of al-'Ajjaj:

"By Allah, you will not deceive me with embracing, nor with kissing, nor with smelling,
except with a jolt that relieves my worry, from which my fatkha falls into my sleeve."

The anklet (khalkhal), which is also called "al-khulkhul," is a well-known ornament that women wear on their feet, like the bracelet on the wrist. The mukhalkhal is the place of the anklet on the shin. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"When I say, 'Come, give me [your hand],' she sways over me, slender-waisted, full-buttocked at the anklet place."
