The armlet (dumluj), which is also called "al-dumludj," is what is tied on the upper arm of a woman, of beads and other things. The 'adud (upper arm) is from the elbow to the shoulder. From it is the saying of the poet:

"No mount, nor riding horses, pleases me
like a mount between an armlet and an anklet."

The bracelet (siwar) is an ornament of gold or silver, round like a ring, that a woman wears on her wrist, and it is the area between the joint of the hand and the elbow; it is the qulb, with the qaf vowelled with a damma. Some lexicographers said: the qulb is the bracelet twisted from one strand, not from two or more strands. From it is the saying of Khalid ibn Yazid ibn Mu'awiya concerning his wife Ramla daughter of al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam – may Allah be pleased with him:

"The anklets of women jingle, but I see
no anklet of Ramla jingling, nor a qulb."
"I love the sons of al-Awwam for the sake of her love,
and for her sake I have loved her maternal uncles, a dog."

The masaka, with fatha on both letters, is a bracelet of ivory or dhabl. Ivory is elephant tusk, and dhabl with a fatha is something like ivory, which is the back of the sea turtle, from which a bracelet is made. From it is the saying of Jarir describing a woman:

"You see the one-year-old [the arm], with its wrist fair-hued, with bracelets of masak
not of ivory nor of dhabl."

Al-Jawhari said this in his "Sihah." Masak with two fathas is the plural of masaka.

Some lexicographers said: masak are bracelets of ivory, horn, or dhabl, and what their speech implies is that they are not of gold or silver. We have already mentioned in the surah of "al-Tawba," in the discussion of Allah's words: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾ [at-Tawba: 34], in the topic of zakat on permissible jewelry, from the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, in [the collections of] Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i: "A woman came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with her daughter, and on her daughter's hand were two thick masakat of gold," the hadith. This is evidence that the masaka may be of gold, just as it may be of ivory, horn, and dhabl, and this is the more apparent view, contrary to the words of many linguists who said that the masak is not of gold or silver. The necklace (qilada) is well known. And Allah knows best.

* *

Allah's words: ﴿And turn in repentance to Allah all together, O believers, that you may succeed﴾.

When Allah the Exalted commanded these mentioned etiquettes in the preceding verses, and shortcomings in carrying out those commands may occur, He taught His creatures what they could use to make up for what shortcomings occurred from them in carrying out the command and avoiding the prohibition. He made clear to them that this is achieved by repentance (tawba), which is turning back from sin and returning to Allah by seeking His forgiveness. It has three pillars:

The first: giving up the sin if one is engaged in it.
The second: regret over the disobedience that has been committed.
The third: the intention never to return to the sin, ever.

The command in His words in this verse: ﴿And turn in repentance to Allah all together﴾ is apparently for obligation, and it is so. Repentance is therefore obligatory on every responsible person, for every sin he has committed, and delaying it is not permissible, so repentance from that delay is also obligatory.

His words: ﴿that you may succeed﴾: we have mentioned many times that the most famous meanings of "la'alla" (perhaps/so that) in the Qur'an are two:

The first: that it retains its original meaning of hope, i.e., "turn in repentance to Allah in hope that you will succeed." On this view, the hope is in relation to the servant. As for Allah – exalted is He – He knows everything, so it is not permissible to attribute hope to Him. On this basis, His words to Moses and Aaron when addressing Pharaoh: ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44] (p-520), while He – exalted is He – knows what has already preceded in eternity, that he will neither remember nor fear. Its meaning is: speak to him gentle speech, hoping from you both, according to your lack of knowledge of the unseen, that he will remember or fear.

The second: what some scholars of tafsir said, that every "la'alla" in the Qur'an is for causation, except the one in the surah of "al-Shu'ara'," which is in His words: ﴿And you take fortresses, perhaps you will abide forever﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 129]. They said: it there means "as if you." We have already mentioned that the use of "la'alla" for causation is known in Arabic, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"You said to us, 'Stop the wars, so that we may stop,'
and you gave us a firm covenant of every pledge."

That is: stop the wars, for the sake of our stopping, as has preceded.

On this view, the meaning is: "And turn in repentance to Allah all together, O believers, for the sake of your succeeding," that is, that you may attain success. In the Arabic language, "falah" (success) is used in two meanings:

The first: winning the greatest desired thing. From this meaning is the saying of Labid:

"Then understand, if you are one who understands, though you have not understood;
and indeed the one who has understood has succeeded."

*Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 3 of 4):*

[p. 520] That is, whoever Allah has granted intellect has attained the greatest objective.

The second meaning is lasting remaining in bliss and joy. From it is the saying of al-Adba' ibn Quray', though it is also said to be Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*"For every worry among the worries there is a respite,*
*but in morning and evening there is no success with it."*

He means that no one remains in this world, given that evening and morning succeed one another over him. There is also the saying of Labid ibn Rabi'ah:

*"Had a living being been one who could attain success,*
*he would have obtained the one who plays with spears."*

He means: had anyone been able to attain permanence and not die, the one who plays with spears would have attained it. This is his paternal uncle 'Amir ibn Malik ibn Ja'far, known as "the one who plays with the spear-points." A poet composed about him, praising him and disparaging his brother al-Tufayl, the father of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, the well-known one:

*"You fled and abandoned your mother's son 'Amir,*
*who plays with the tips of the swaying spear-shafts."*

With each of the two meanings we have mentioned for *al-falah* (success), the hadith of the adhan and the iqamah is explained: *"Hasten to success"* (*hayya 'ala al-falah*), as is well known. Whoever repents to Allah, as Allah has commanded him, attains success in both of its meanings, for he wins the greatest objective, which is Paradise and the pleasure of Allah the Exalted. Likewise he attains lasting permanence in bliss and joy. What this noble verse contains of His command, glorified and exalted is He, to all the Muslims to repent, indicating that it leads to their success, is in His saying: ﴿so that you may succeed﴾. He explained this in another place, and made clear that the repentance by which Allah erases sins and expiates misdeeds is the sincere repentance (*tawbah nasuh*). He made clear that there follows from it the expiation of misdeeds and entry into Paradise. This is especially so according to those among the people of knowledge who say that *'asa* (perhaps) from Allah is binding, and this has a basis in reasoning: He, Mighty and Majestic, is generous and bountiful, merciful and forgiving. So when He makes His servant hope for something of His bounty, His generosity, His kindness, and the vastness of His mercy make that person whom his Lord has made hopeful for that bounty trust that He has made him hope for it only so that He may bestow it upon him.

Among the verses that clarify this meaning here is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8]. His saying in the verse of *al-Tahrim*, ﴿That is because those who disbelieved﴾, is like His saying in the verse of *al-Nur*, ﴿O believers﴾, because whoever has his misdeeds expiated and is admitted into Paradise has attained success in both of its meanings. His saying in the verse of *al-Tahrim*, ﴿repent to Allah with sincere repentance﴾, clarifies His saying in *al-Nur*: ﴿And repent to Allah all together﴾. His addressing them with the description of faith in the two verses stirs them and urges them to comply with the command, because being characterized by the attribute of faith in its correct meaning requires hastening to comply with the command of Allah and avoiding His prohibition. The hope understood from the word *'asa* in the verse of *al-Tahrim* is the same as that understood from the word *la'alla* (so that) in the verse of *al-Nur*, as is not hidden.

**Clarifications.**

**The first:** Sincere repentance (*al-tawbah al-nasuh*) is truthful repentance.

Its essence is that one fulfils its three pillars correctly: one abandons the sin if one was engaged in it, one regrets what proceeded from one of opposing the command of one's Lord, glorified and exalted, and one forms a firm intention never to return to disobedience to Allah.

The most evident of the opinions of the people of knowledge is that if he repents sincere repentance and Allah expiates his misdeeds by that sincere repentance, and then he later returns to the sin, his first repentance, which occurred in the required manner, is not nullified by his return to the sin. Rather, he must repent anew for his new sin. This is contrary to those who say that his returning to the sin is a breaking of his first repentance.

**The second:** Know that there is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that repentance from a sin is not valid except with regret for committing the sin and abandoning it, if one was engaged in it, as we have previously mentioned that these two are among the pillars of repentance. Each of them has a well-known difficulty. Its clarification regarding the first, which is regret, is that regret is not an act; rather, it is an affect (*infi'al*). There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that Allah does not impose obligation (*taklif*) on anyone except by an act that occurs by the choice of the one obligated, and He does not impose on anyone anything except what is within his capacity, as He said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and He said: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16].

Knowing this, know that regret is an affect that does not fall under the power of the servant. Thus it is not an act at all, and it is not within the capacity of the one obligated to do it. Obligation does not occur without an act, nor with what cannot be borne, as we have explained. He said in *Maraqi al-Su'ud*:

*"And He does not impose obligation except by act, the Sender of the prophets and Lord of grace."*

He also said:

*"Knowledge and capacity, according to the known view,*
*are a condition that encompasses every bearer of obligation."*

Know that the statements of the scholars of legal theory (*al-usuliyyun*) on the question of obligation with what cannot be borne, and their disagreement on it, concern only rational possibility (*al-jiwar al-'aqli*). The meaning is: does reason permit it or prohibit it?

As for its actual occurrence, they are all agreed on prohibiting it, as the verses of the Qur'an and the prophetic hadiths indicate. Some of the scholars of legal theory express this question as obligation with the impossible: is it rationally permissible or not? As for the occurrence of obligation with the rationally or customarily impossible, they all agree on prohibiting it, provided the impossibility is not due to Allah's prior knowledge that it will not occur. An example of the rationally impossible is being obligated to combine two opposites, such as whiteness and blackness, or two contradictories, such as nonexistence and existence. An example of the customarily impossible is obligating the lame [p. 523] to walk, or obligating a human to fly, and the like. Obligation with such things does not occur, by consensus.

As for what is impossible because of Allah's eternal knowledge that it will not occur, it is rationally permissible, and there is no disagreement about obligation with it. For example, the faith of Abu Lahab: Allah knew from eternity that it would not occur, as He said about him: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame﴾ [Hud: 3]. Its occurrence is rationally impossible because of Allah's eternal knowledge that it will not exist, for if it existed, His knowledge of its non-existence would become ignorance, and that is impossible with respect to Him, the Exalted. But this impossibility resulting from the knowledge of its non-occurrence is rationally permissible, for reason does not prevent the faith of Abu Lahab. Had it been impossible, Allah would not have obligated him to believe through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ. Thus possibility is general, the call is general, and success (*tawfiq*) is specific.

The clarification of the question of the rational judgment is that, according to the majority of the rational theologians (*nuzzar*), it has three divisions:

The first: the rationally necessary (*wajib 'aqlan*).
The second: the rationally impossible (*mustahil 'aqlan*).
The third: the rationally permissible (*jaiz 'aqlan*).

The proof of this restriction of the rational judgment to these three is that a thing, insofar as it is a thing, cannot be free of one of three states. Either reason accepts its existence and never accepts its non-existence; or reason accepts its non-existence and never accepts its existence; or reason accepts both its existence and its non-existence. If reason accepts its existence but not its non-existence, it is the rationally necessary, such as the existence of Allah, the Exalted, characterized by the attributes of perfection and majesty. For if sound reason is presented with the existence of the Creator of these creatures, it accepts it, but if it is presented with its non-existence, and that these were created without a creator, it does not accept it. Thus it is rationally necessary. If it accepts its non-existence but not its existence, it is the rationally impossible, such as a partner of Allah, glorified and exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation. If sound reason is presented with the non-existence of a partner of Allah in His dominion and worship, it accepts it, but if it is presented with its existence, it never accepts it, as He said: ﴿Had there been within them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22], and He said: ﴿Then each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overpowered others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]. Thus it is rationally impossible. If reason accepts both its existence and its non-existence, it is the rationally permissible, which is also called the essentially permissible (*al-jaiz al-dhati*). Such is the faith of Abu Lahab. If its existence is presented to sound reason, it accepts it, and if its non-existence is presented instead of its existence, it also accepts it, as is not hidden. So it is rationally permissible with essential permissibility, and there is no disagreement about obligation with this type, which is the essentially rationally permissible.

[p. 524] Groups from among the people of desires (*ahl al-ahwa'*) said: the rational judgment has only two divisions, namely the rationally necessary and the rationally impossible. They said: the rationally permissible has no existence at all. They claimed that the proof of the restriction to the necessary and the impossible is that the matter either is one that Allah, in His eternal past, knows will exist, so it is necessary to exist, because its non-existence is impossible given the prior eternal knowledge of its existence, such as the faith of Abu Bakr. So it is rationally necessary according to them, because Allah knows it will occur, for if it did not occur, His knowledge would be ignorance, glorified and exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation, and that is impossible.

Or the matter is one that Allah, in His eternal past, knows will not exist, such as the faith of Abu Lahab. So it is rationally impossible, for if it existed, knowledge would turn into ignorance, glorified and exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation. The invalidity of this view is not hidden. It is also not hidden that the faith of Abu Lahab and the faith of Abu Bakr are both such that reason permits their existence and their non-existence. Thus both are permissible, except that Allah, the Exalted, willed the existence of one of these two permissible things, so He brought it into existence, and willed the non-existence of the other, so He did not bring it into existence.

The conclusion is that what is impossible for other than Allah's prior knowledge that it will not exist, because it is impossible in an essential way, such as combining two contradictories, is not subject to obligation, by consensus. Likewise what is customarily impossible, as is not hidden.

As for the essentially permissible, obligation with it is permissible and occurs by consensus, such as the faith of Abu Lahab. For it is rationally permissible, even if its occurrence is impossible because of Allah's knowledge that it will not occur. They call this essentially permissible "impossible accidentally" (*mustahil 'aradi*). We, however, exalt the attribute of Allah's knowledge from saying that the impossibility due to it is accidental.

Knowing this, know that the scholars of legal theory (*'ulama' al-usul*) and all the people of knowledge are agreed on the occurrence of obligation with the essentially rationally permissible, such as the faith of Abu Lahab, even though its occurrence is impossible because of Allah's knowledge that it will not occur.

As for what is rationally impossible in its essence, such as combining two contradictories, and what is customarily impossible, such as the lame man walking or a human flying without an instrument, there is no disagreement among the people of knowledge in prohibiting obligation with either of them. As He said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and He said: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "If I command you with something, then do of it what you are able."

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (*Adwa' al-Bayan*) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 4 of 4):**

As for the rationally impossible (*al-mustahil al-'aqli*), a group of the scholars of *usul* (the principles of jurisprudence) said: it is permissible to impose obligations to do what is impossible in its essence, both rationally and customarily, and to do what is customarily impossible. Some of them said: it is not permissible rationally, while they all agree that its occurrence in fact is not valid. The argument of those who prohibit it rationally is that it is futile (*'abath*), with no benefit in it, because the one charged cannot possibly be able to do it in any circumstance. So imposing on him what he is definitely unable to do is futile, with no benefit. They said: therefore it is impossible, because Allah is All-Wise, All-Aware. The argument of those who permit it is that its benefit is the testing (*imtihan*) of the one charged: whether he feels regret at his lack of ability and shows that, had he been able, he would have complied. Testing is one of the causes of imposing obligation, just as Allah charged Ibrahim to slaughter his son, while He knew that he would not slaughter him. He made clear that the wisdom of this charge was the trial (*ibtila'*) of Ibrahim, that is, testing him, whether he would comply. When he began to comply, Allah ransomed him with a great sacrifice, as Allah, exalted is He, said about him: ﴿So when they had both submitted and he laid him down upon his brow, and We called to him, "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good. Indeed, this was the clear trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–107].

The author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud* has alluded to the issue of imposing the impossible and the views of the scholars of *usul* on it. It is their disagreement over whether this is permissible rationally, while they agree on prohibiting it if the impossibility is due to other than Allah's knowledge, by non-occurrence, as in essential impossibility. He said:

> He permitted imposing the impossible, in all of it, in three conditions.
> It was said: prohibited, for what is impossible, for other than Allah's knowledge that it will not occur.
> It does not occur when it is impossible, for other than the knowledge of our Lord, exalted is He.

His saying "permitted imposing" means: rational permissibility. His saying "it was said: prohibited" means: rationally. By "the three conditions" he means: what is rationally and customarily impossible, such as combining two contradictories; what is customarily impossible, such as the paralytic walking, a human flying, or the blind seeing; and what is impossible due to Allah's knowledge that it will not occur.

Now that you know the statements of the scholars of *usul* on this question, know that repentance (*tawbah*) is obligatory by the Book, the Sunnah and consensus, from every sin a person commits, immediately. Regret (*nadam*) is one of its pillars, and the pillar of an obligation is obligatory. Regret is not an act, nor is it within the capacity of the one charged, because it is an affect (*infi'al*), not an act, and affects are not by choice. So what is the basis for charging someone with regret, when it is not an act of the one charged, nor something he is able to do?

The answer to this difficulty is that what is meant by charging with regret is charging with its causes through which it is produced, and these are within the power of the one charged. If the one who committed sin reflects on himself in a sound reflection, and does not favour it over the disobedience of Allah, he will know that the pleasure of sins is like the pleasure of a sweet drink in which there is deadly poison. No sensible person enjoys a drink containing deadly poison because of the great harm that follows its pleasure. The sweetness of sins contains something worse than deadly poison: what disobedience to Allah, exalted is He, entails of His wrath upon the sinner and His punishing him with the most severe punishment. And the punishment for sins may come to him in this world, destroying him and spoiling for him the pleasure of life. There is no doubt that whoever makes the causes of regret for sin a means to regret, he reaches the attainment of regret for sin through using the causes by which it is attained.

The result is that he is charged with the causes that necessitate regret, and if he uses them, regret will be attained for him. In this sense he is charged with regret, even though it is an affect and not an act.

Among examples of using the causes that lead to regret for sin is the saying of the poet al-Husayn ibn Mutayr:

> So do not approach the forbidden matter, for its sweetness perishes while its bitterness remains.

It is related of Sufyan al-Thawri, may Allah have mercy on him, that he often recited the saying of the poet:

> The pleasure of one who attains its purity from the forbidden perishes, while the sin and the shame remain.
> The consequences of evil remain in its outcome; there is no good in a pleasure after which is the Fire.

As for the difficulty concerning abandoning sin (*al-iqla' 'an al-dhanb*), its summary is this: whoever repents of a sin in which he is currently engaged, while the corruption of that sin remains, i.e. its evil effect, is his repentance valid? This is based on the view that he has done in his repentance everything he is able to do, even though abandoning the sin has not been realized because he is unable to remove its corruption at that time. Or is his repentance not valid, because abandoning the sin, which is the pillar of repentance, has not been realized?

Among examples of this is one who holds an evil innovation (*bid'ah*) that contradicts the Law and entails punishment: when he spreads his innovation and it spreads throughout the lands of the world, then he repents of committing that innovation, regrets it, and intends never to return to it ever. Yet his abandoning of his innovation is beyond his power, because it has spread throughout the lands of the world. Also, whoever establishes an evil practice bears its burden and the burden of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection. So the corruption of his innovation remains.

Among its examples: one who usurped land, then settled in its midst, then repented of that usurpation, regretting it and intending not to return to it, and left the usurped land quickly, taking the nearest route out of it. Is his repentance valid during his walking in the usurped land before leaving it, because he has done in his repentance everything he is able to do? Or is it not valid, because his abandoning of usurpation is not complete as long as he is present in the usurped land, even if he is walking through it to leave it?

Among its examples: one who shot an arrow at a Muslim, then repented, regretted that, and intended not to return, before the arrow struck the person he shot at, such that the repentance occurred while the arrow was still in the air on its way to the target. Is his repentance valid, because he has done what he is able to do? Or is it not valid, because his abandoning of the sin was not realized at the time of repentance, since his arrow was on its way to striking a Muslim? The majority of the scholars of *usul* hold that his repentance is valid in all these examples, because repentance is obligatory for him, and he has done of this obligation all that he is able to do, and what is beyond his ability is excused for him, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], along with the rest of the evidence we presented earlier.

Abu Hashim, who was among the great figures of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school), as was his son Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, said: the repentant one who exits the usurped land is committing a prohibited act, because what he does by leaving is a disposal of another's property without permission, like staying there. Repentance is realized only at the end of his stay, since there is no abandoning except then. Abandoning is leaving what is forbidden. So departing is, in his view, ugly, because it is a disposal of another's property without his permission, and this contradicts abandonment. So it is forbidden. Yet the said departure is also commanded in his view, because it is separation from staying in the usurped land. He built this on his corrupt principle, which is rational ugliness (*al-qubh al-'aqli*). But he undermined another of his principles, which is the prohibition of imposing the impossible, for he said: if he leaves he disobeys, and if he stays he disobeys. So he has forbidden him both opposites together. End of quote, as stated in *Nashr al-Bunud*.

On this question, the author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud* alluded, limiting himself to the view of the majority, saying:

> Whoever repents after engaging in the cause has fulfilled what was obligatory upon him.
> And if its corruption remains, like one who returns from spreading an innovation that is followed,
> Or repents while outside the place of usurpation, or repents after shooting and before striking.

[p. 528] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And marry off the unmarried among you, and the righteous among your male servants and your female servants. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty.﴾ Here *al-inkah* (إنكاح) means *al-tazwij* (marriage, giving in marriage). ﴿And marry off﴾ means: marry them off. *Al-ayama* (الأيامى) is the plural of *ayyim* (أيِّم), with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the kasra-vowelled yaa. The *ayyim* is the one who has no spouse, whether male or female, whether he or she had married before or never married at all. One says: *rajulun ayyim* (a man who is an ayyim) and *imra'atun ayyim* (a woman who is an ayyim). The poet al-Shammakh ibn Dirar, in his verse, explained the female *ayyim* as the one who is not married in her present state, in his saying:

؎ يُقِرُّ بِعَيْنِي أنْ أُنَبَّأ أنَّها وإنْ لَمْ أنَلْها أيِّمٌ لَمْ تَزَوَّجِ

*It gladdens my eye to be told that she, though I have not attained her, is an unmarried woman who has not been wed.*

So his saying "lam tazawwaj" (she has not been married) is an explanation of his saying "annaha ayyim" (that she is an ayyim). From the application of *ayyim* to the male who has no spouse is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi:

؎ لِلَّهِ دَرُّ بَنِي عَلِيٍّ ∗∗∗ أيِّمٌ مِنهم وناكِحْ

*By God, the excellence of the sons of Ali! Among them is one who is unmarried, and one who is married.*

From its application to the female is the saying of a poet:

؎ أُحِبُّ الأيامى إذْ بُثَيْنَةُ أيِّمُ ∗∗∗ وأحْبَبْتُ لَمّا أنْ غَنِيتُ الغَوانِيا

*I love the unmarried ones since Buthayna is unmarried, and I came to love the singing maidens when I sang to them.*

The Arabs say: *amma al-rajulu ya'iimu* (the man became an ayyim) and *amati al-mar'atu ta'iimu* (the woman became an ayyim), when either of them becomes an ayyim. Likewise they say: *ta'ayyama* (he became an ayyim) if he was an ayyim.

An example of the first (*amma yaImu*) is the poet's saying:

؎ لَقَدْ إمْتُ حَتّى لامَنِي كُلُّ صاحِبِ ∗∗∗ رَجاءَ بِسَلْمى أنْ تَئِيمَ كَما إمْتُ

*I became an ayyim, until every companion blamed me, hoping that Salma would become an ayyim as I did.*

And from the second is his saying:

؎ فَإنْ تَنْكِحِي أنْكِحْ وإنْ تَتَأيَّمِي ∗∗∗ وإنْ كُنْتُ أفْتى مِنكُمُ أتَأيَّمُ

*If you marry, I will marry; and if you remain unmarried, I too will remain unmarried, though I am more youthful than you.*

Also from the first (*ya'iimu* meaning to become unmarried) is the saying of Yazid ibn al-Hakam al-Thaqafi:

؎ كُلُّ امْرِئٍ سَتَئِيمُ مِنهُ ∗∗∗ العُرْسُ أوْ مِنها يَئِيمُ

*Every man from whom the wedding will make a widower, or from whom she will become a widow...*

And the saying of another:

؎ نَجَوْتَ بِقَوْفِ نَفْسِكَ غَيْرَ أنِّي ∗∗∗ إخالُ بِأنْ سَيَيْتِمُ أوْ تَئِيمُ

*You have escaped with the pride of your own self, but I think that your son will be an orphan, or your wife will be a widow.*

He means: your son will become an orphan (*yaytimu*) and your wife will become a widow (*ta'iimu*).

Having known this, know that His saying in this verse, ﴿And marry off the unmarried﴾, includes both males and females. His saying in this verse, "among you" (*minkum*), means: among the Muslims. And it is understood from the argument from implication (*dalil al-khitab*), that is the inverse implication (*mafhum al-mukhalafa*) in His saying "among you", that the unmarried ones from others, that is, from other than the Muslims, namely the disbelievers, are not so.

This implication understood from this verse is stated explicitly in other verses, such as His saying, exalted is He, concerning the unmarried disbelieving men: ﴿And do not marry the polytheists until they believe﴾ [al-Baqara: 221], and His saying concerning their unmarried women: ﴿And do not marry the polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqara: 221], and His saying concerning both together: ﴿So if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahana: 10].

By these explicit Qur'anic texts clarifying the implication of this verse, you know that it is not permissible to marry a Muslim woman to a disbeliever in any way, and that it is not permissible to marry a Muslim man to a disbelieving woman, except that the generality of these verses has been specified by the verse of "al-Ma'ida", which made clear that a Muslim man may marry a chaste woman from the People of the Book specifically. That is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them; and [lawful are] the chaste women from among the believers and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5]. So His saying, exalted is He, coordinated with what is lawful for the Muslims: ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ is explicit in permitting a Muslim to marry a chaste woman from the People of the Book. The apparent meaning is that she is a free, chaste woman.

The conclusion is that marriage between disbelievers and Muslims is prohibited in all cases, except one case: the marriage of a Muslim man to a chaste woman from the People of the Book. The texts indicating that are Qur'anic, as you have seen.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾, it indicates the obligation to marry off the unmarried among the righteous male slaves and the female slaves owned. The apparent meaning of this command is obligation, because of what has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (*al-usul*).

[p. 529–530] We have explained many times that the bare form of the command, free of any indicators, requires obligation. By this you know that an unmarried woman whom a suitable match (*kafu'*) proposes to, and she is pleased with him, it becomes obligatory upon her guardian (*waliyyuha*) to marry her to him. And what some scholars of the Malikis and those who agree with them say, that the master has the right to prevent his male slave and female slave from marriage absolutely, is not correct, because it contradicts the text of the Qur'an in this noble verse.

Know that His saying in this noble verse, "and your female servants", the verse of "al-Nisa'" clarified that a female slave may not be married to a free man except under the conditions indicated by that verse. So the verse of "al-Nisa'" mentioned is specifying the generality of this verse of "al-Nur" regarding the female slaves. The verse of "al-Nisa'" mentioned is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free, believing women, then [he may marry] from what your right hands possess of your believing young women...﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for whoever fears sin among you; but to be patient is better for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. So this verse of "al-Nisa'" indicates that a free man may not marry a believing female slave, except when he is unable to marry a free woman due to lacking the means (*al-tawl*), and he fears fornication. Then he may marry the slave with the permission of her owners, and he must pay her dowry. She must be a believing, chaste woman, not one of the adulteresses nor one who takes secret lovers. And despite all of this, his patience in not marrying her is better for him. If patience in not marrying her, along with what we have mentioned of necessity, is better for him, then in the absence of necessity it is even more deserving of prohibition. By what we have mentioned, you know that the correct view is the opinion of the majority (*al-jumhur*) prohibiting a free man from marrying a female slave, except under the conditions mentioned in the Qur'an, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and His saying: ﴿That is for whoever fears sin among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], i.e., fornication, to the end of what is mentioned in the verse. This is in opposition to Abu Hanifa, who says that it is permissible to marry her absolutely, except if he marries her in addition to a free woman.

The conclusion is that His saying, exalted is He, in this verse of "al-Nur", "and your female servants", its generality has been specified by the verse of "al-Nisa'", as we have explained just above. The scholars say that the reason for prohibiting a free man from marrying a female slave is that if she bears a child from him, the child would be a slave; for every womb-possessor, her offspring is in her position. So it is incumbent upon him not to cause the enslavement of his children as far as he is able. Its reasoning is clear, as you see.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ contains a promise from Allah to the poor married person, whether free or slave, that Allah will enrich him, and Allah does not break His promise. Allah promised the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who were poor ease after that hardship, and fulfilled that for them. That is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not charge a soul except [according to] what He has given it. Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]; that is, his provision was constricted, up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. This promise from Him, glorified and exalted, is a promise He made to whoever fears Him, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 2–3], to the end of the verse. He also promised provision to whoever commands his family to pray and perseveres in it, as in His saying: ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast therein. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you, and the best outcome is for righteousness﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132]. He also promised abundant provision to those who seek forgiveness, through the tongue of His Prophet Nuh, in His saying, exalted is He, concerning him: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness of your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in showers, and provide you with wealth and children and make for you gardens and make for you rivers﴾ [Nuh: 10–12]; and through the tongue of His Prophet Hud, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in showers and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ [Hud: 52], to the end of the verse; and through the tongue of our Prophet (ﷺ), may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and upon them all: ﴿And that you seek forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term﴾ [Hud: 3].

Among the verses indicating that obedience to Allah, exalted is He, is a cause of provision is His saying: ﴿And if the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96], to the end of the verse. Among the blessings of the sky is rain, and among the blessings of the earth is vegetation of which people and livestock eat. And His saying: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 66], to the end of the verse. And His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], that is, in this world, as we have previously explained in surah "al-Nahl", and as His saying after it indicates concerning its reward in the Hereafter: ﴿And We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. We have previously mentioned that He, glorified and exalted, promised wealth at marriage and at divorce.

As for marriage, it is in His saying here: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾.

As for divorce, it is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisa': 130], to the end of the verse.

The apparent meaning is that the married person whom Allah promised wealth is the one who intends by his marriage to help himself obey Allah by lowering the gaze and guarding the chastity, as the Prophet (ﷺ) explained in the authentic hadith: "O assembly of youth, whoever among you is able to marry, let him marry, for it lowers the gaze and guards the chastity." And if his intention in marriage is obedience to Allah by lowering the gaze and guarding the chastity, then the promise of wealth is only upon obedience to Allah in that.

[p. 532] You have seen what we have mentioned of verses indicating Allah's promise of provision to whoever obeys Him, glorified and exalted is He; how generous He is! He recompenses good deeds in this world and the Hereafter. As for what the Zahiris (*Ahl al-Zahir*) said, that this noble verse indicates that the slave owns his property, because His saying: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ after His saying: ﴿And the righteous among your male servants and your female servants﴾ indicates the attribution of poverty and wealth to slaves, and wealth is only applied to one who owns the property by which he becomes rich, the argument is strong, and it does not contradict the fact that his master may take from them that property which they own. And Allah knows best.

**Verse 24:33:** ﴿And let those who cannot find marriage keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty.﴾

The chastity (al-istiʿfaf) commanded in this noble verse is the same as that mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ [An-Nur: 30], and His saying: ﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. Indeed, it is ever an immorality and evil as a way.﴾ [Al-Isra: 32], and similar verses.

His saying, Exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And whoever compels them - indeed, Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ It has been said: "Forgiving toward them (the women)." It has been said: "Forgiving toward them (the compellers)." And it has been said: "Forgiving toward them (the women) and toward them (the compellers)."

The most apparent of these views is that the meaning is "Forgiving toward them (the women)," because the one who is compelled is not held accountable for what he was compelled to do; rather, Allah forgives him for his excuse of compulsion. This is clarified by His saying: ﴿except one who has been forced while his heart is secure in faith﴾ [An-Nahl: 106]. It is supported by the recitation (qiraʾah) of Ibn Masʿud, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, and Ibn Jubayr: "Indeed, Allah, after their compulsion, for them (the women) is Forgiving and Merciful." Al-Qurtubi reported this from him, and al-Zamakhshari reported it from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them all.

We have already stated in the introduction to this blessed book that we do not explain the Qur'an by an irregular recitation (qiraʾah shadhdhah, a non-canonical reading). Sometimes we mention an irregular recitation as evidence for a canonical (sabʿiyyah, one of the seven recognized) recitation, as here. The addition of the word "lahunna" (for them) in the recitation of those we mentioned is cited as evidence from an irregular recitation, to clarify by a non-irregular recitation that the one promised forgiveness and mercy is the one excused by compulsion, not the compeller; because he is not excused for his ugly act. This clarifies what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿except one who has been forced while his heart is secure in faith﴾ [An-Nahl: 106].

(p-533) Al-Zamakhshari said in explaining this noble verse: "If you say there is no need to tie the forgiveness to them, because the woman compelled to fornication, unlike the one compelled to do it, is not sinful."

I say: Perhaps the compulsion was less than what the Sharia considers as compulsion by killing, or by what fear of death or loss of a limb from severe beating or otherwise, so that she is spared sin. And perhaps it fell short of the limit at which it is impossible to resist, so she would be sinful. End of his words.

What appears is that there is no need for this, because the removal of accountability for compulsion truly constitutes forgiveness and mercy from Allah toward His servant. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 34:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing (the truth), and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾ In this noble verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions that He sent down to us, through the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ), clear verses. Primarily included in these are the verses that were made clear in this noble surah and that explained the meanings of the rulings (ahkam) and the prescribed limits (hudud). The evidence from the Qur'an for what has been mentioned is His saying, the Exalted:

﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear verses that you may remember.﴾ [al-Nur: 1] There is no doubt that these clear verses, whose sending down is explicitly stated in this noble surah, are included in His saying here: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing (the truth)﴾, and so on.

By this you know that His saying here, ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing (the truth)﴾, means: We sent them down to you so that you may remember, i.e., that you may take admonition from what they contain of commands, prohibitions and admonitions. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And We sent down in it clear verses that you may remember.﴾ In this noble verse He has explicitly stated that among the wisdoms of their being sent down is that people may remember and take admonition from what is in them. The generality of His saying also indicates this: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may ponder its verses and that those of understanding may remember.﴾ [Sad: 29], and His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. A Book revealed to you, so let there be no discomfort in your breast concerning it, that you may warn thereby and as a reminder for the believers.﴾ [al-A'raf: 1-2], as well as other verses. His saying in this noble verse, ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾, is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "verses", i.e., We sent down to you verses, and We sent down to you an example from those who passed away before you.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr al-Muhit: "Mathalan (an example) is coordinated with ayat (verses), so it is possible that the meaning is 'an example from the likes of those who came before you', i.e., a strange story from their stories, like the story of Yusuf and Maryam in their innocence."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Mathalan from the likes of those before you, i.e., a wondrous story from their stories, like the story of Yusuf and Maryam", meaning the story of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. What we have quoted from Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari has been mentioned by others besides them.

Its clarification: the meaning is: and We sent down to you an example, i.e., a wondrous, strange story in this noble surah, and that wondrous story is among the likes of "those who passed away before you", i.e., of the kind of their wondrous stories. According to what we have mentioned, the wondrous story that was sent down to us, and which He expressed by His saying "an example", is the innocence of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from what the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk) accused her of. This is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander are a group among you﴾ [al-Nur: 11], up to His saying: ﴿Those are cleared of what they say﴾ [al-Nur: 26]. In the ten verses referred to, He made clear that the people of the slander accused 'A'ishah, and that Allah cleared her in His Book of what they accused her of. On this basis:

Among the verses that make clear some of the examples of those before us is His saying, concerning the wife of the Aziz accusing Yusuf of intending evil with her, meaning fornication: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your wife except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾ [Yusuf: 25], and His saying: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time﴾ [Yusuf: 35]; because they imprisoned him for several years, on the claim that he had intended fornication with the wife of the Aziz. Allah cleared him of that slander which was fabricated against him, by the admission of the women and the wife of the Aziz herself. This is in His saying: ﴿So when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him about the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾ ﴿He said, "What was your condition when you sought to seduce Yusuf from himself?" They said, "Perfect is Allah! We know of him no evil." The wife of the Aziz said, "Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful."﴾ [Yusuf: 50-51]. He also said, the Exalted, concerning the wife of the Aziz in her speech with the women who cut their hands: ﴿She said, "That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I did seek to seduce him, but he refused.﴾ up to the end of the verse [Yusuf: 32].

So the story of Yusuf is an example from the likes of those before us, because he was accused of intending fornication, and Allah cleared him of that. The example that He sent down to us in this surah is similar to the story of Yusuf, because both he and 'A'ishah were accused of what was not fitting, and both were cleared by Allah, the Exalted, and the innocence of each of them was revealed in this great Qur'an. Although the innocence of Yusuf occurred before the revelation of the Qur'an, through the admission of the wife of the Aziz and the women, as has been mentioned shortly before, and by the testimony of a witness from her family: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said, "Indeed, it is from your plotting. Indeed, your plotting is great."﴾ [Yusuf: 26-28].

Among the verses that make clear some of the examples of those before us is what Allah the Exalted mentioned about the people of Maryam, that they accused her of fornication when she bore 'Isa without a husband, as in His saying: ﴿and for their disbelief and their saying against Maryam a great slander﴾ [al-Nisa': 156], meaning the sin of adultery; and His saying: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Maryam, you have certainly come with something unprecedented."﴾ [Maryam: 27], meaning fornication. Then Allah made clear her innocence of what they accused her of in several places in His Book, such as His saying: ﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.﴾ ﴿And He has made me blessed...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And the day I am raised alive.﴾ [Maryam: 29-33]. So the speech of 'Isa, while still an infant, in her defense indicates that she is innocent. Allah has also made clear her innocence along with the explanation of the cause of her conceiving 'Isa without a husband, in His saying: ﴿And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place.﴾ ﴿And she took a screen from them, and We sent to her Our Spirit, and it presented itself to her as a perfect man.﴾ ﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing of Allah."﴾ ﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord to give you a pure boy."﴾ ﴿She said, "How will I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ ﴿He said, "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me. And We will make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us, and it is a matter decreed.'"﴾ ﴿So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ [Maryam: 16-22] up to the end of the verses.

Among the verses in which Allah made clear her innocence is His saying concerning the Prophets: ﴿And [mention] she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our Spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], and His saying in al-Tahrim: ﴿And Maryam, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into it of Our Spirit, and she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was of the devoutly obedient.﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the example of 'Isa with Allah is like the example of Adam. He created him from dust.﴾

These verses we have mentioned, which indicate the accusation against Yusuf and his innocence, and the accusation against Maryam and her innocence (p-536), are of the examples of those before us, and they are what make clear some of what His saying indicates: ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾.

The verses that indicate the accusation against 'A'ishah and her innocence made clear the example that was sent down to us, and that it is of the type of the examples of those before us is evident, because each of 'A'ishah, Maryam and Yusuf was accused of what was not fitting, each was cleared by Allah, and the story of each of them is wondrous. Therefore the name "example" was applied to them in His saying: ﴿and an example from those who passed away before you﴾, and His saying in this noble verse: ﴿and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Mawi'zah' (admonition) is what is admonished with in the verses and the example, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And let not pity for them detain you in the religion of Allah﴾ [al-Nur: 2], ﴿Why, when you heard it...﴾ [al-Nur: 12], ﴿And why, when you heard it...﴾ [al-Nur: 16], ﴿Allah admonishes you never to return to the likes of it again﴾ [al-Nur: 17]." End of al-Zamakhshari's words. The apparent reason for specifying the admonition to the God-fearing rather than others is that they are the ones who benefit from it.

A parallel in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18], and His saying: ﴿You are only a warner for one who fears it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45]. He restricted the warning to those mentioned in the verses, because they are the ones who benefit from it, although he (ﷺ) is in reality a warner to all people, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. A similar parallel is His saying: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45], and similar verses.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses clearly showing (the truth)﴾, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Shu'bah ibn 'Asim read mubayyanat with a fatha on the ya' and a shaddah, in the form of the passive participle. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read mubayyinat with a kasrah on the shaddah ya', in the form of the active participle. On the reading of one who reads it with a fatha on the ya', there is no difficulty in the verse, because Allah made them clear and explained them. On the reading of one who reads mubayyinat with a kasrah on the ya', in the form of the active participle, there are two well-known interpretations of the verse.

The first: His saying mubayyinat is the active participle of bayyana, which is transitive (muta'addiyah), and on this basis the object is omitted, i.e., mubayyinat al-ahkam wa'l-hudud (verses making clear the rulings and the limits).

The second: His saying mubayyinat is an adjective from bayyana, which is intransitive (lazimah), and it is then an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah), and on this basis (p-537) the meaning is "verses that are mubayyinat", i.e., clear, evident verses. The last interpretation is indicated by His saying: ﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and sent down [in it]...﴾ [al-Nur: 1]. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and others mentioned both interpretations, and they illustrated the intransitive bayyana with the well-known proverb of the Arabs: "qad bayyana al-subhu li-dhi 'aynayn" (the dawn has become clear to one with two eyes).

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon and forgive him, says: It is well known in Arabic that bayyana (doubled) and abana are both used transitively and intransitively. The transitive use of bayyana with an object is well known and clear, as in His saying: ﴿We have certainly made the verses clear to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]. The transitive use of abana with an object is also well witnessed and clear, as in the saying: abana lahu al-tariq, i.e., he made the way clear for him and explained it. As for the intransitive use of bayyana meaning "become manifest and clear", it comes from the proverb mentioned: "qad bayyana al-subhu li-dhi 'aynayn", i.e., it became manifest and appeared. From it is the verse of Jarir:

"The faces of Mujashi' were smeared with baseness; it appears (yubayyinu) on the necklace and the cheek-piece."

So His saying yubayyinu, with a kasrah on the ya', means: appears and becomes evident. Also Jarir's verse:

"The people saw the insight and went straight, and the sick became distinguished from the healthy."

Also from it is the verse of Qays ibn Dhurayh:

"And for love there are signs that become manifest (tubayyinu) in the young man: paleness, and the bones of his hands showing through."

According to the well-known narration, with the raising of "shuhubun" (paleness).

The meaning: for love there are signs which become manifest (tubayyinu, with kasrah) in the young man, and they are paleness, etc. Tha'lab recited this verse with "shuhuban" in the accusative, and according to that there is no evidence in the verse, because shuhuban in that case is the object of tubayyinu, so it is then from transitive bayyana. As for the intransitive use of abana meaning "bana and zahara" (became evident), it is also common in Arabic speech, and from it is Jarir's verse:

"When our fathers and your father are counted, the mixed-breed (al-muqrafat) among the purebred camels become evident."

I.e., the mixed-breed camels became evident and distinguished. And the verse of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi:

"Were an ant to crawl upon the surface of her skin, the traces of its marks (hudud) would become evident on her from its traces, i.e., a swelling."

I.e., it would become evident and clear from their traces, i.e., a swelling. And the verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"A she-camel with a curved nose, in her two reddish flanks, for one who sees her clearly there is a noble lineage (itq mubin), and in her cheeks is ease."

So His saying mubin is an adjective from the intransitive abanat, i.e., a clear, evident noble lineage, meaning evident generosity.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 24, verse 36 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised up and in which His name is mentioned. Therein He is glorified by men (rijal) in the mornings and the evenings﴾ ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah and establishing prayer and giving zakat. They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about, that Allah may reward them﴾.

All the Seven Readers recited this letter (word) except Ibn 'Amir, Shu'bah from 'Asim: yusabbihu lahu fiha, with a kasra on the single, doubled letter ba' (yusabbihu), in the active voice, its subject being rijal (men), and the meaning is clear according to this reading. Ibn 'Amir, Shu'bah from 'Asim recited it: yusabbahu lahu fiha, with a fatha on the single, doubled letter ba' (yusabbahu), in the passive voice. According to this reading, the omitted subject has been indicated by the first reading, that its implied subject is rijal. It is as if, when He said "yusabbahu lahu fiha" (He is glorified therein for Him), it was asked: "And who glorifies Him therein?" He said: "Rijal (men)", meaning: "Men glorify Him therein."

We have already mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book words to the effect that we are committed to explaining the Qur'an only by a Seven-fold reading, whether the other reading is in the same verse being explained or in another verse, and so on to its end. We only said that a verse may be explained by some readings giving the meaning of others, because it is established among the scholars that two readings in one verse are like two verses.

Knowing this, know that the reading of the majority, yusabbihu with a kasra and its subject rijal, makes clear that the omitted subject in the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Shu'bah from 'Asim, yusabbahu with a fatha in the passive voice, by the omission of the subject, is rijal, as is not hidden. The verse according to this reading has the subject of "yusabbihu" omitted, and the verb that raises the subject, which is rijal, is also omitted, in line with his saying in the Khulasah (Alfiyya):
"A verb is hidden which raises the subject, like Zayd in answer to 'Who read?'"
A parallel in Arabic speech is the saying of Dirar ibn Nahshal, lamenting his brother Yazid or another:
"Let Yazid be wept for by one humbled by litigation, and one dazed by what the calamities have struck down."
So his saying "Liyubka Yazid" (let Yazid be wept for), with a damma on the first letter (ya') and a fatha on the kaf, is passive, as if it were said: "And who weeps for him?" He said: "He is wept for by one humbled by litigation," etc. The reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah here is like the reading of Ibn Kathir: "Kadhalika yuha ilaykа" (thus is it revealed to you) with a fatha on the ha', in the passive voice; so his saying "Allah" is the subject of the omitted "yuha" (is revealed).

His description of these men who glorify Him in the mornings and evenings, as those whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah, from establishing prayer and giving zakat, is in the manner of praising them and commending them, and indicates that these qualities must never be neglected in any way; because Allah's commendation of one who possesses them shows that whoever falls short in them deserves blame, which is the opposite of commendation. This is made clear by His forbidding neglect of them with a categorical prohibition in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, let not your wealth or your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah. Whoever does that, those are the losers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 9], and His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], and other verses.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse.

The first issue: Know that according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah, yusabbahu, it is sunnah to pause at His saying "bil-asal" (in the evenings). As for the reading of the majority, yusabbihu with a kasra, it is not proper to pause at His saying "bil-asal", because the subject of yusabbihu is rijal, and pausing before the subject is not proper, as is not hidden.

The second issue: Know that the feminine pronoun in His saying "yusabbihu lahu fiha" refers to the mosques, described as "houses" in His saying "In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised up and in which His name is mentioned." The correct view is that the houses mentioned are the mosques.

Knowing this, know that His restricting those who glorify Him therein to men, in His saying "Therein He is glorified by men in the mornings and evenings", indicates by its implied meaning (mafhum) that women glorify Him in their houses, not in the mosques. It may appear to the observer that the implied meaning of His saying "rijal" is a mafhum of title (mafhum laqab), and the correct view among the scholars of legal theory is that it is not used as evidence.

Its author (may Allah pardon and forgive him) says: There is no doubt that the implied meaning of the word rijal, considered merely as a word, is a mafhum of title, and that the mafhum of title is not a proof according to the correct view, as we have clarified elsewhere. However, the implied meaning of rijal here is taken into account, and it is not a mafhum of title according to the correct view, because the word rijal, although considered merely as a word it is a solid generic noun and is a title without dispute, entails attributes of maleness that are suitable for attaching the ruling to it, and the difference between it and women is that men are not feared for temptation and are not 'awrah, unlike women. It is known that the attribute of maleness is an attribute suitable for attaching to it the ruling which is the glorification in mosques and going out to them, rather than the attribute of femaleness.

The conclusion: the word rijal in the verse, although by terminology it is a title, what it includes of male attributes suitable for distinguishing males from females requires taking into account the mafhum of opposition in the word rijal. So it is in reality a mafhum of attribute, not a mafhum of title, because the word rijal entails attributes suitable for attaching the ruling to it, and the difference in this between men and women is not hidden.

* *

The third issue: Once you know that the correct view is that the mafhum of His saying "rijal" is a mafhum of attribute, by reason of the male attributes it entails that are suitable for distinguishing males from females, regarding the ruling of going out to mosques, and not a mafhum of title, and that the mafhum of attribute is taken into account by the majority, unlike Abu Hanifah, then know that the implied meaning of His saying here, "rijal", is general, because the most that is understood from it is that women are not like men in going out to mosques. We have already mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that when the Qur'anic explanation is not sufficient to achieve the complete meaning, we complete the explanation from the Sunnah, insofar as it is an explanation of what is explained by the active participle, and examples of this have preceded.

Knowing this, know that the prophetic Sunnah explained the implied meaning of opposition in His saying in this noble verse, "rijal". It made clear that the stated implied meaning is taken into account, and that women are not like men in the ruling on going out to mosques. It also made clear that their prayer in their houses is better for them than going out to mosques and praying there in congregation, unlike men. It further made clear that they may go out to mosques under conditions that will be explained, if Allah the Exalted wills, and that when they ask their husbands for permission to go out to mosques, the husbands are commanded by the Law to grant them permission, provided they observe the stated conditions.

As for the command to husbands to permit their wives to go out to mosques when they request it, it has been authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Bukhari (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his Sahih, in the Book of Marriage: "'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, al-Zuhri narrated to us from Salim, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ: 'When the wife of one of you asks permission to go to the mosque, let him not prevent her.'" Al-Bukhari also said in his Sahih, in the Book of Prayer, chapter: "The wife's asking her husband's permission to go out to the mosque": "Musaddad narrated to us, Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ: 'When the wife of one of you asks permission, let him not prevent her.'" Al-Bukhari (may Allah have mercy on him) also said in his Sahih: "'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, from Handhalah, from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet ﷺ who said: 'When your women ask your permission to go to the mosque at night, grant them permission.'" Shu'bah followed him, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his Sahih: "'Amr al-Naqid and Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to me together, from Ibn 'Uyaynah. Zuhayr said: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from al-Zuhri, who heard Salim narrating from his father, raising it to the Prophet ﷺ: 'When the wife of one of you asks your permission to go to the mosque, let him not prevent her.'" In a wording in Muslim, from Ibn 'Umar who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Do not prevent your women from the mosques when they ask your permission to go there.'" In another wording in Muslim, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah." In another wording of his from him as well: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'When your women ask your permission to go to the mosque, grant them permission.'" In another wording from him as well: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not prevent women from going out to the mosques at night." In a narration of his from him as well, he said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Grant women permission to go to the mosques at night." In another wording of his from him as well, he said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not prevent women their portions of the mosques when they ask your permission." In a narration: "when they ask your permission." An-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: "It is sahih, and they were treated like men because of their request to go out to the men's assembly." This hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) which we have mentioned from the two Shaykhs with multiple narrations, was also reported by others, and it is clear that husbands of women are commanded, on the Prophet's ﷺ tongue, to grant them permission to go out to the mosques when they request it, and are forbidden to prevent them from going out to it.

Some scholars have mentioned that the command to husbands to grant them permission in the narrations mentioned is not an obligation but a recommendation, and likewise his ﷺ prohibition against preventing them is for reprehension of tanzih, not prohibition.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: "In it is an indication that the mentioned permission is not obligatory; because if it were obligatory, the meaning of asking permission would vanish, since that is realized only when the one asked is free to grant or refuse."

An-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: "If he prevents her, it is not unlawful for him. This is our school. Al-Bayhaqi said: 'This is the view of the general body of scholars.' The hadith 'Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah' is answered by saying that it is a prohibition of tanzih, because the husband's right to her staying in the dwelling is obligatory, so she should not forgo it for a virtue." End of quote.

Al-Shinqiti, its author (may Allah pardon him and forgive him), said: What appears to me in this matter is that when a husband's wife asks his permission to go out to the mosque, and she is not wearing perfume and is not dressed in anything that would incite temptation (as will be clarified later, God willing), then it is obligatory for him to grant her permission, and it is forbidden for him to prevent her, because of the explicit prohibition from the Prophet (ﷺ) against preventing her from that, and because of the explicit command to grant her permission. A bare imperative form free of contextual indicators requires obligation, as we have explained in several places in this blessed book, and the prohibitive form likewise requires prohibition. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment strike them﴾ [al-Nur: 63]. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When I order you to do something, do of it what you are able; and when I forbid you from something, avoid it." And there are other proofs besides these, as we have already presented.

As for the statement of Ibn Hajar, that permission is not realised unless the one asked is given the choice in responding, this is not accepted, for there is no barrier, rational, legal or customary, to Allah making it obligatory upon him to grant his wife permission to go out to the mosque without choice. So making the granting of permission obligatory is not barred, and likewise making prevention prohibited. The authentic text has indicated its obligation, so there is no basis for rejecting it on a mere possibility, as you see.

As for the statement of al-Nawawi: "Because the husband's right to having the wife remain in the home is obligatory, so she may not abandon it for a mere virtue," this is not valid, since the explicit text from the Prophet (ﷺ) has come against it. His (ﷺ) command to the husband to grant her permission obliges him to do so and makes it binding upon him, so it cannot be opposed by what al-Nawawi mentioned, as you see.

As for what al-Nawawi reported from al-Bayhaqi, that the view of non-obligation is held by the majority of scholars, this too is not accepted. It is established in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, from Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them), that when he narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) the hadith we mentioned about the command to husbands to permit women to go out to the mosques, and his son said, "We will not let them go out," he became angry, reviled him, and struck him on the chest, objecting to his opposing the command of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is clear evidence of his belief that obeying that command by granting them permission is obligatory.

Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his Sahih: Harmalah ibn Yahya narrated to me, Ibn Wahb informed us, Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab, who said: Salim ibn Abdullah informed me that Abdullah ibn {Umar} said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Do not prevent your women from the mosques when they ask your permission to go to them.'" Bilal ibn Abdullah said: "By Allah, we will prevent them!" So Abdullah turned on him and reviled him with a severe insult the like of which I had never heard him use before, and said: "I tell you what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and you say: 'By Allah, we will prevent them!'" In another wording in Muslim: Ibn Umar rebuked him and said: "I say the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and you say: 'We will not let them.'" And in another wording also in Muslim: he struck him on the chest.

Know that the son of Abdullah ibn Umar who claimed that he did not comply with the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to permit women to go to the mosques, is named in Sahih Muslim as Bilal ibn Abdullah ibn Umar.

In another narration in Muslim, he is named as Waqid ibn Abdullah ibn Umar. The truth is that there were more than one, for both Bilal and Waqid, the two sons of Abdullah ibn Umar, said this, and Ibn Umar objected to each of them, as the authentic narrations in Muslim and elsewhere show. That Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) turned on his son Bilal, reviled him with a severe insult, and objected to him, saying, "I tell you what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and you say: 'We will prevent them'," is clear evidence that Ibn Umar held that granting them permission is binding and that preventing them is not permissible. Had he considered it permissible, he would not have rebuked his two sons so harshly, as is evident.

Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: His saying, "Abdullah turned on him and reviled him with a harsh insult," and in another narration "rebuked him," and in another "struck him on the chest," contains the discipline of one who objects to the Sunnah and opposes it with his opinion.

Al-Shinqiti said: This statement of al-Nawawi that you have seen is an acknowledgment by him that his school, which is the school of al-Shafi'i, and whoever holds his view, as al-Bayhaqi is reported to have said, is the view of the majority of scholars, that all who hold this view deserve discipline, as they object to the Sunnah and oppose it with their opinion. It is strange that he acknowledges that Bilal ibn Abdullah ibn Umar deserves discipline for objecting to the Sunnah and opposing it with his opinion, even though the school he supports, which he reports from al-Bayhaqi as the view of the majority of scholars, is exactly the view of Bilal ibn Abdullah ibn Umar, whom Ibn Umar himself declared deserving of discipline, and whose stance he described as objecting to the Sunnah and opposing it with opinion.

Al-Nawawi said: His saying "fa-zabarahu" means he rebuked him. Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: In the narration of Bilal in Muslim: "Abdullah turned on him and reviled him with a severe insult, the like of which I had never heard him use before." Abdullah ibn Hubayrah, in the narration of al-Tabarani, explained the mentioned reviling as cursing him three times. In a narration from al-A'mash with additional wording: "he rebuked him and said: 'Uff to you!'" And in another from Ibn al-A'mash: "May Allah do to you and do to you." A similar wording is in al-Tirmidhi from the narration of Isa ibn Yunus. In Muslim from the narration of Abu Mu'awiyah: "fa-zabarahu." In Abu Dawud from the narration of Jarir: "fa-sabbahu wa ghadiba alayhi." It was also said: from Ibn Umar's objection to his son is derived the discipline of one who objects to the Sunan with his opinion, which is also an acknowledgment by him that whoever opposes the mentioned hadith objects to the Sunan with his opinion.

By this you know that what we previously quoted from him, that the command to grant women permission to go to the mosques is not for obligation, is an objection to the Sunan with opinion, as you see.

By what we have mentioned, you know that the proof from the authentic Sunnah has indicated the obligation of granting women permission to go out to the mosques, as we have mentioned. This is supported by the fact that none of the Companions objected to Ibn Umar's condemnation of his two sons, as we have explained above. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

Once you know that what we have mentioned of the explicit texts regarding the command to grant them permission implies the permissibility of their going out to the mosques, know that it is established in the Sahih that they used to go out to the mosque and pray with the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih: Yahya ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: al-Layth informed us, from Uqayl, from Ibn Shihab, who said: Urwah ibn al-Zubayr informed me that Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) informed him, saying: "The believing women used to attend the dawn prayer with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrapped in their cloaks, then they would return to their homes when they had finished the prayer, and no one would recognise them because of the darkness." End of quote. This hadith was also related by Muslim and others. There are also authentic hadiths in the two Sahihs and elsewhere indicating what the hadith of Aisha indicates, the agreed-upon matter that women used to attend the prayer in the mosque with him (ﷺ).

Note.
